Which of the following statements are correct regarding Cauda equina syndrome?

I. Its presenting symptoms are perineal numbness, painless urinary retention and fecal incontinence.

IV. Confirmed cases require early surgical decompression.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is a neurosurgical emergency caused by compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris. The most common cause is a massive central lumbar disc prolapse (usually at L4–L5 or L5–S1). Prompt diagnosis and urgent surgical decompression are essential to prevent permanent neurological deficits.

The following statements are true:

  • I. Its presenting symptoms are perineal numbness, painless urinary retention and fecal incontinence: These are the hallmark features of CES:
    • Saddle (perineal) anesthesia
    • Painless urinary retention (earliest bladder symptom)
    • Overflow incontinence
    • Fecal incontinence
    • Bilateral leg weakness/sciatica
  • II. Urgent investigation with MRI is required: MRI of the lumbosacral spine is the gold standard investigation and should be performed urgently.
  • IV. Confirmed cases require early surgical decompression: Urgent decompressive surgery (ideally within 24–48 hours) offers the best chance of recovery of bladder, bowel, and neurological function.

Why is III incorrect?

  • III. It is present most commonly in the 45–60 year age group: Cauda equina syndrome can occur at any adult age, depending on the underlying cause. It is not defined by or restricted to the 45–60-year age group, making this statement incorrect.

Correct answer: A. Anterior cerebral artery

The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the paracentral lobule, which represents the motor and sensory areas for the lower limb (leg and foot).

Clinical features of ACA occlusion:

  • Contralateral weakness of the leg and foot
  • Contralateral sensory loss in the leg
  • Behavioral and personality changes due to medial frontal lobe involvement
  • Possible abulia (lack of motivation) and impaired judgment

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Middle cerebral artery (MCA): affects face and upper limb, aphasia or neglect.
  • Posterior cerebral artery (PCA): mainly causes visual deficits (contralateral homonymous hemianopia).
  • Internal carotid artery: produces combined ACA and MCA deficits.

Mechanism of Injury:

  • Usually caused by acceleration–deceleration injuries (e.g., road traffic accidents).
  • Brain moves within the skull, stretching and tearing the bridging veins.

Characteristic Features of Subdural Hemorrhage:

  • Crescent-shaped hematoma on CT scan
  • Venous bleeding → slower onset of symptoms
  • Can cross suture lines but does not cross the midline due to falx cerebri

questions.text: Match the following: Colum‍n II A. Distal median ner​ve; seen at rest/when ext‍ending fingers B. Proxima‌l ulnar nerve; seen when ‍closing the hand C. Dista​l ulnar nerve; seen at re‌st/when extending fingers​ D. Proximal median nerve​; seen when making a fist‍
questions.raw_text:
Match the following:

Column II 
A. Distal median nerve; seen at rest/when extending fingers
B. Proximal ulnar nerve; seen when closing the hand
C. Distal ulnar nerve; seen at rest/when extending fingers
D. Proximal median nerve; seen when making a fist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1-C, 2-D, 3-A, 4-B

  • 1. "Ulnar claw": Appears at rest/on extending the fingers, from a distal ulnar nerve lesion (e.g., Guyon canal). The FDP remains intact (innervated proximal to the lesion), so its unopposed pull produces a visible claw deformity even without active movement.
  • 2. "Hand of benediction": Appears when making a fist, from a proximal median nerve lesion (e.g., supracondylar fracture). The lateral two lumbricals and long flexors to the index/middle fingers are denervated, so those fingers fail to flex while the ulnar-innervated ring/little fingers flex normally — visible only during active fist-making.
  • 3. "Median claw": Appears at rest/on extending the fingers, from a distal median nerve lesion (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome), analogous to the ulnar claw but affecting the index/middle fingers via loss of the lateral two lumbricals with intact long flexors.
  • 4. "Trouble making a fist": Appears when closing the hand, from a proximal ulnar nerve lesion (e.g., at the elbow), where the FDP to the ring/little fingers is also denervated — these fingers fail to flex fully during active fist formation, unlike the resting claw deformity.
  • This reflects the paradox principle: distal lesions (sparing the long flexors) produce deformity at rest; proximal lesions (also denervating the long flexors) produce deficits only on active movement, since the unopposed flexor pull required for a resting claw is itself weakened.

In fetal circulation, the highest oxygen saturation is found in blood returning from the placenta through the umbilical vein. After passing through the ductus venosus, this relatively well-oxygenated blood enters the inferior vena cava (IVC) before reaching the right atrium.

Approximate descending order of oxygen saturation:

  1. Umbilical vein → highest (\~80%)
  2. Inferior vena cava → \~65–70% (mixture of oxygenated placental blood and systemic venous blood)
  3. Right atrium / left atrium mixture
  4. Pulmonary trunk / ductus arteriosus
  5. Descending aorta → lower due to mixing with deoxygenated blood

The IVC carries blood from the ductus venosus that bypassed the fetal liver, so it contains the most oxygenated blood among the listed options.

Which of the following are correctly matched?
1.	First arch – Maxillary artery
2.	Second arch – Hyoid or stapedial artery
3.	Third arch – Common carotid artery and distal internal carotid artery
4.	Sixth arch – Arch of the aorta
5.	Fourth arch – Right proximal subclavian artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, and 5

First arch forms the maxillary artery, second arch gives hyoid and stapedial arteries, and the right fourth arch forms the proximal right subclavian artery.

The third arch forms the common carotid and proximal internal carotid artery (not distal), while the sixth arch forms pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus, not the aortic arch.

The third arch gives the common carotid and the proximal internal carotid — not the distal ICA.

  • Third aortic arch artery → common carotid artery + proximal (first part of) internal carotid artery
  • Distal internal carotid artery → derived from the dorsal aorta cranial to the third arch (the persisting cranial portion of the ipsilateral dorsal aorta)

Other sources worth pairing:

  • External carotid → sprouts from the third arch / common carotid, not from the 1st arch proper.
  • Distal right subclavian → right 7th intersegmental artery + right dorsal aorta.
  • Left subclavian → left 7th intersegmental artery entirely (no arch contribution).

Why this asymmetry matters clinically

The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks the right subclavian (4th arch) because the right 5th and 6th arches regress distally. The left RLN hooks the ligamentum arteriosum (left 6th arch), which stays put — hence the left nerve's long thoracic descent and its vulnerability in aortic arch pathology.

Aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) = failure of the right 4th arch, with the right 7th intersegmental artery persisting off the descending aorta → dysphagia lusoria and a non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve (critical in thyroid surgery).

| 6th | Left: left pulmonary artery + ductus arteriosus Right: right pulmonary artery (distal part regresses — no ductus) |

The third arch forms the common carotid and proximal internal carotid artery (not distal), while the sixth arch forms pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus, not the aortic arch.

The third arch gives the common carotid and the proximal internal carotid — not the distal ICA.

The left RLN hooks the ligamentum arteriosum (left 6th arch), which stays put — hence the left nerve's long thoracic descent and its vulnerability in aortic arch pathology.

Column II 
A. Distal median nerve; seen at rest/when extending fingers
B. Proximal ulnar nerve; seen when closing the hand
C. Distal ulnar nerve; seen at rest/when extending fingers
D. Proximal median nerve; seen when making a fist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1-C, 2-D, 3-A, 4-B

  • 1. "Ulnar claw": Appears at rest/on extending the fingers, from a distal ulnar nerve lesion (e.g., Guyon canal). The FDP remains intact (innervated proximal to the lesion), so its unopposed pull produces a visible claw deformity even without active movement.
  • 2. "Hand of benediction": Appears when making a fist, from a proximal median nerve lesion (e.g., supracondylar fracture). The lateral two lumbricals and long flexors to the index/middle fingers are denervated, so those fingers fail to flex while the ulnar-innervated ring/little fingers flex normally — visible only during active fist-making.
  • 3. "Median claw": Appears at rest/on extending the fingers, from a distal median nerve lesion (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome), analogous to the ulnar claw but affecting the index/middle fingers via loss of the lateral two lumbricals with intact long flexors.
  • 4. "Trouble making a fist": Appears when closing the hand, from a proximal ulnar nerve lesion (e.g., at the elbow), where the FDP to the ring/little fingers is also denervated — these fingers fail to flex fully during active fist formation, unlike the resting claw deformity.
  • This reflects the paradox principle: distal lesions (sparing the long flexors) produce deformity at rest; proximal lesions (also denervating the long flexors) produce deficits only on active movement, since the unopposed flexor pull required for a resting claw is itself weakened.

Which of the following are correctly matched?
1.	First arch – Maxillary artery
2.	Second arch – Hyoid or stapedial artery
3.	Third arch – Common carotid artery and distal internal carotid artery
4.	Sixth arch – Arch of the aorta
5.	Fourth arch – Right proximal subclavian artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, and 5

First arch forms the maxillary artery, second arch gives hyoid and stapedial arteries, and the right fourth arch forms the proximal right subclavian artery.

The third arch forms the common carotid and proximal internal carotid artery (not distal), while the sixth arch forms pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus, not the aortic arch.

The third arch gives the common carotid and the proximal internal carotid — not the distal ICA.

  • Third aortic arch artery → common carotid artery + proximal (first part of) internal carotid artery
  • Distal internal carotid artery → derived from the dorsal aorta cranial to the third arch (the persisting cranial portion of the ipsilateral dorsal aorta)

Other sources worth pairing:

  • External carotid → sprouts from the third arch / common carotid, not from the 1st arch proper.
  • Distal right subclavian → right 7th intersegmental artery + right dorsal aorta.
  • Left subclavian → left 7th intersegmental artery entirely (no arch contribution).

Why this asymmetry matters clinically

The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks the right subclavian (4th arch) because the right 5th and 6th arches regress distally. The left RLN hooks the ligamentum arteriosum (left 6th arch), which stays put — hence the left nerve's long thoracic descent and its vulnerability in aortic arch pathology.

Aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) = failure of the right 4th arch, with the right 7th intersegmental artery persisting off the descending aorta → dysphagia lusoria and a non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve (critical in thyroid surgery).

| ---- | ------------- |
| 1st | Maxillary artery (mostly regresses); part of external carotid |
| 2nd | Stapedial + hyoid arteries (largely regress) |
| 3rd | Common carotid + proximal internal carotid |
| 4th | Left: arch of aorta (between left CCA and left subclavian) Right: proximal right subclavian artery |
| 5th | Never forms / regresses completely (no derivative) |
| 6th | Left: left pulmonary artery + ductus arteriosus Right: right pulmonary artery (distal part regresses — no ductus) |

Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is a neurosurgical emergency caused by compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris. The most common cause is a massive central lumbar disc prolapse (usually at L4–L5 or L5–S1).   • II. Urgent investigation with MRI is required: MRI of the lumbosacral spine is the gold standard investigation and should be performed urgently.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phase-I depolarizing neuromuscular blockade

A Phase-I depolarizing block, typically produced by standard doses of succinylcholine, results from persistent depolarization of the motor end plate. Since succinylcholine acts as a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist, neuromuscular transmission remains uniformly depressed without presynaptic receptor blockade.

Consequently:

  • Tetanic stimulation shows a sustained response without fade.
  • Train-of-four (TOF) stimulation shows equal reduction in all twitches.
  • Post-tetanic facilitation is absent.
  • Anticholinesterases prolong or enhance the block.

In contrast, Phase-II depolarizing block and non-depolarizing blockade both exhibit tetanic fade, TOF fade, and post-tetanic facilitation because they impair normal neuromuscular transmission in a manner similar to competitive blockade.

Other Options:

  • Option A. Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockade: Incorrect. Competitive neuromuscular blockers produce tetanic fade due to presynaptic inhibition of acetylcholine release.
  • Option C. Phase-II depolarizing neuromuscular blockade: Incorrect. With prolonged or repeated succinylcholine exposure, the block resembles a non-depolarizing block and demonstrates tetanic fade.
  • Option D. Both non-depolarizing and Phase-II depolarizing blockade: Incorrect. Both exhibit fade, not a sustained tetanic response.

Educational Objective:

  • A sustained response to tetanic stimulation without fade is the hallmark of Phase-I depolarizing neuromuscular blockade caused by standard-dose succinylcholine.

questions.raw_text: A 40-year-old man is administered succinylcholine to facilitate rapid sequence intubation. During intraoperative neuromuscular monitoring, a 50-Hz tetanic stimulus is applied. questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phase-I depolarizing neuromuscular blockade

A Phase-I depolarizing block, typically produced by standard doses of succinylcholine, results from persistent depolarization of the motor end plate. Since succinylcholine acts as a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist, neuromuscular transmission remains uniformly depressed without presynaptic receptor blockade.

Consequently:

  • Tetanic stimulation shows a sustained response without fade.
  • Train-of-four (TOF) stimulation shows equal reduction in all twitches.
  • Post-tetanic facilitation is absent.
  • Anticholinesterases prolong or enhance the block.

In contrast, Phase-II depolarizing block and non-depolarizing blockade both exhibit tetanic fade, TOF fade, and post-tetanic facilitation because they impair normal neuromuscular transmission in a manner similar to competitive blockade.

Other Options:

  • Option A. Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockade: Incorrect. Competitive neuromuscular blockers produce tetanic fade due to presynaptic inhibition of acetylcholine release.
  • Option C. Phase-II depolarizing neuromuscular blockade: Incorrect. With prolonged or repeated succinylcholine exposure, the block resembles a non-depolarizing block and demonstrates tetanic fade.
  • Option D. Both non-depolarizing and Phase-II depolarizing blockade: Incorrect. Both exhibit fade, not a sustained tetanic response.

Educational Objective:

  • A sustained response to tetanic stimulation without fade is the hallmark of Phase-I depolarizing neuromuscular blockade caused by standard-dose succinylcholine.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mivacurium

  • This patient has atypical (deficient) plasma pseudocholinesterase, resulting in impaired metabolism of certain neuromuscular blockers.
  • Mivacurium is a short-acting nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker that is hydrolyzed by plasma pseudocholinesterase. In patients with pseudocholinesterase deficiency, its metabolism is markedly delayed, leading to prolonged neuromuscular blockade and apnea.

Note: Succinylcholine is the classic drug associated with prolonged apnea due to pseudocholinesterase deficiency. Since it is not listed among the options, mivacurium is the correct answer.

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Pancuronium

  • Long-acting nondepolarizing blocker
  • Eliminated mainly by the kidneys
  • Not dependent on plasma pseudocholinesterase

B. Rocuronium

  • Intermediate-acting aminosteroid
  • Primarily eliminated via the liver
  • Reversal possible with sugammadex

D. Atracurium

  • Undergoes Hofmann elimination and nonspecific ester hydrolysis
  • Independent of pseudocholinesterase activity
  • Preferred in renal and hepatic failure

Among commonly used local anesthetics, bupivacaine has the greatest myotoxic potential, particularly after intramuscular infiltration or continuous infusion.

Mechanism of myotoxicity

Local anesthetics can directly injure skeletal muscle by:

  • Disrupting muscle cell membranes
  • Increasing intracellular calcium concentration
  • Causing mitochondrial dysfunction
  • Leading to myonecrosis, followed by regeneration over weeks

  • Localized muscle pain
  • Tenderness
  • Weakness of the injected muscle
  • Elevated CK (occasionally)

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Succinylcholine

The ECG changes indicate severe hyperkalemia:

  • Tall, peaked T waves
  • PR prolongation
  • Widened QRS complex
  • Sine-wave pattern
  • Ventricular fibrillation and asystole

In patients with major burns, there is upregulation of extrajunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors across skeletal muscle membranes. Administration of succinylcholine, a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, opens these receptors and causes massive potassium efflux from muscle cells.

This can produce sudden, life-threatening hyperkalemia and cardiac arrest.

Important timing

Succinylcholine is generally considered unsafe after the first 24–48 hours following a major burn, and the risk may persist for many months until receptor expression returns toward normal.

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Atracurium

  • Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker
  • Does not cause significant potassium release
  • May cause histamine release and hypotension

B. Baclofen

  • GABA-B receptor agonist used for spasticity
  • Does not cause acute hyperkalemia during anesthesia

C. Halothane

  • Volatile anesthetic associated with hepatotoxicity and malignant hyperthermia
  • Does not typically produce this classic hyperkalemic ECG sequence

Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS) is a rare but potentially fatal complication associated with prolonged (>48 hours) or high-dose (>4 mg/kg/hour) propofol infusion. It is believed to result from mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired fatty acid oxidation, leading to failure of cellular energy production.

Typical features include:

  • Severe metabolic (lactic) acidosis
  • Rhabdomyolysis
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Acute cardiac dysfunction (bradyarrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, cardiovascular collapse)
  • Acute kidney injury and elevated liver enzymes may also occur.

Therefore, hypokalemia is not a feature of PRIS.

Other Options:

  • Option B. Rhabdomyolysis: Correct. Skeletal muscle breakdown is common and contributes to elevated creatine kinase levels, renal injury, and hyperkalemia.
  • Option C. Cardiac dysfunction: Correct. PRIS can cause severe myocardial depression, arrhythmias, and refractory cardiovascular collapse, accounting for its high mortality.

  • Thiopentone protects the brain by decreasing cerebral metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, thereby reducing cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure while lowering neuronal oxygen demand during periods of cerebral ischemia.

Correct answer: C. Pethidine (Meperidine)

Pethidine (meperidine) is contraindicated in chronic renal failure because its active metabolite, norpethidine (normeperidine), is eliminated by the kidneys. Other Options:

  • Option B. Fentanyl: Incorrect. Fentanyl undergoes hepatic metabolism to inactive metabolites and has minimal dependence on renal excretion, making it the preferred opioid in patients with renal failure.
  • Option D. Atracurium: Incorrect. Atracurium is eliminated by Hofmann degradation and ester hydrolysis, processes that are independent of renal and hepatic function. Therefore, it is a preferred neuromuscular blocker in patients with renal impairment.

Educational Objective:

  • In patients with chronic kidney disease, pethidine should be avoided because of the accumulation of its neurotoxic metabolite, norpethidine.
  • Fentanyl and atracurium are preferred alternatives due to their organ-independent or minimally renal-dependent elimination and more predictable pharmacokinetics.

| --------------- | -------- | ---------------------------- |
| Pancuronium | Long-acting | Renal (80–90%) |

questions.raw_text: A 30-year-old woman is undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anesthesia. Shortly after intravenous administration of a neuromuscular blocking agent before induction is complete, she complains of severe burning pain at the injection site and withdraws her arm. Which of the following neuromuscular blocking agents is most commonly associated with marked pain on intravenous injection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rocuronium

  • Rocuronium is the non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker most frequently associated with pain on intravenous injection.
  • The pain is typically immediate, burning, or stinging and is thought to result from its low pH and direct irritation of the vascular endothelium. Without preventive measures, injection pain occurs in 50–80% of patients.
  • To reduce discomfort, intravenous lidocaine pretreatment or administration after induction with propofol is commonly employed.

Other Options:

  • Option A. Succinylcholine: Incorrect. Succinylcholine is more commonly associated with postoperative myalgia rather than significant pain on injection.
  • Option B. Vecuronium: Incorrect. Vecuronium causes minimal or no injection pain because of its relatively neutral formulation.
  • Option D. Cisatracurium: Incorrect. Cisatracurium is generally well tolerated on injection and rarely causes significant discomfort.

Educational Objective:

  • Among commonly used neuromuscular blocking agents, rocuronium is the most likely to cause severe pain on intravenous injection.
  • Pretreatment with lidocaine or administering the drug after induction of anesthesia significantly reduces this adverse effect.

During induction of anesthesia, the anesthesiologist administers thiopentone to provide cerebral protection. What is the primary mechanism responsible for the cerebroprotective effect of thiopentone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased cerebral metabolic rate

  • Thiopentone is a barbiturate that provides cerebral protection by markedly reducing the cerebral metabolic rate (CMR) and cerebral oxygen consumption (CMRO₂).
  • The resulting decrease in metabolic demand is accompanied by reduced cerebral blood flow (CBF) and intracranial pressure (ICP), while preserving the coupling between cerebral metabolism and blood flow.
  • By lowering the brain's oxygen requirements, thiopentone helps limit neuronal injury during focal cerebral ischemia, making it useful in selected neurosurgical and neurocritical care settings.

Other Options:

  • Option B. Reduction of cerebral vasospasm: Incorrect. Thiopentone does not relieve cerebral vasospasm. In fact, accidental intra-arterial injection may provoke vasospasm because of its highly alkaline solution.
  • Option C. Calcium channel blockade: Incorrect. Thiopentone acts primarily by enhancing GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission, not by blocking calcium channels.
  • Option D. Free radical scavenging: Incorrect. Thiopentone does not exert its neuroprotective effect through antioxidant or free radical scavenging activity.

Educational Objective:

  • Thiopentone protects the brain by decreasing cerebral metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, thereby reducing cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure while lowering neuronal oxygen demand during periods of cerebral ischemia.

During the pre-anesthetic planning, the anesthesiologist avoids an analgesic that can produce a neurotoxic metabolite which accumulates in renal failure and may precipitate seizures. Which of the following anesthetic drugs is contraindicated in patients with chronic renal failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pethidine (Meperidine)

Pethidine (meperidine) is contraindicated in chronic renal failure because its active metabolite, norpethidine (normeperidine), is eliminated by the kidneys. In patients with impaired renal function, this metabolite accumulates and can cause central nervous system toxicity, including agitation, tremors, myoclonus, and seizures.

Other Options:

  • Option A. Morphine: Incorrect. Morphine produces active metabolites that accumulate in renal impairment and may prolong sedation and respiratory depression. However, it is not absolutely contraindicated and may be used cautiously with dose reduction and close monitoring.
  • Option B. Fentanyl: Incorrect. Fentanyl undergoes hepatic metabolism to inactive metabolites and has minimal dependence on renal excretion, making it the preferred opioid in patients with renal failure.
  • Option D. Atracurium: Incorrect. Atracurium is eliminated by Hofmann degradation and ester hydrolysis, processes that are independent of renal and hepatic function. Therefore, it is a preferred neuromuscular blocker in patients with renal impairment.

Educational Objective:

  • In patients with chronic kidney disease, pethidine should be avoided because of the accumulation of its neurotoxic metabolite, norpethidine.
  • Fentanyl and atracurium are preferred alternatives due to their organ-independent or minimally renal-dependent elimination and more predictable pharmacokinetics.

While planning intraoperative neuromuscular blockade, the anesthesiologist decides to avoid a muscle relaxant that is predominantly eliminated by the kidneys, as it may result in prolonged paralysis. Which of the following neuromuscular blocking agents is primarily excreted via the renal route?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pancuronium

Pancuronium is a long-acting, non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that is primarily eliminated by the kidneys, with nearly 80–90% excreted unchanged in the urine. Consequently, its duration of action is significantly prolonged in patients with renal impairment, making it a poor choice in this setting.

Elimination of Common Neuromuscular Blocking Agents

| Muscle Relaxant | Duration | Primary Route of Elimination |
| --------------- | -------- | ---------------------------- |
| Pancuronium | Long-acting | Renal (80–90%) |
| Vecuronium | Intermediate | Hepatic metabolism and biliary excretion (major), partial renal excretion |
| Atracurium | Intermediate | Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis (organ-independent) |
| Rocuronium | Intermediate | Hepatic uptake and biliary excretion |

Other Options:

  • Option B. Vecuronium: Incorrect. It is eliminated mainly through hepatic metabolism and biliary excretion, with only a smaller proportion excreted by the kidneys.
  • Option C. Atracurium: Incorrect. It undergoes Hofmann elimination, a spontaneous plasma degradation that is independent of renal and hepatic function, making it an excellent choice in renal failure.
  • Option D. Rocuronium: Incorrect. Rocuronium is predominantly cleared by the liver and excreted in bile, with minimal renal elimination.

Educational Objective:

  • Among commonly used non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers, pancuronium is the most dependent on renal excretion and should generally be avoided in patients with significant renal dysfunction.
  • Atracurium, because of its organ-independent Hofmann elimination, is the preferred agent in patients with renal or hepatic failure.

questions.raw_text: A 32-year-old man undergoes elective surgery under general anesthesia. Following intravenous administration of succinylcholine (1 mg/kg) for endotracheal intubation, he develops prolonged apnea requiring continued mechanical ventilation. Laboratory evaluation reveals a normal serum pseudocholinesterase concentration, but the dibucaine number is 50. What is the most likely duration of neuromuscular paralysis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paralysis lasting 20–30 minutes

A dibucaine number of approximately 50 indicates a heterozygous atypical pseudocholinesterase variant. Although the amount of pseudocholinesterase is normal, the enzyme has reduced ability to hydrolyze succinylcholine, leading to an intermediate prolongation of neuromuscular blockade.

  • Normal dibucaine number (\~80): Paralysis lasts about 5–10 minutes (approximately 9–14 minutes).
  • Heterozygous atypical enzyme (dibucaine number \~50): Paralysis is prolonged to 20–30 minutes.
  • Homozygous atypical enzyme (dibucaine number \~20): Paralysis may persist for 1–3 hours or longer.

Other Options:

  • Option A. Hyperkalemic cardiac arrest: Although succinylcholine can precipitate life-threatening hyperkalemia in patients with burns, denervation injuries, or neuromuscular disorders, this complication is unrelated to the dibucaine number.
  • Option B. Paralysis lasting 5–10 minutes: This is the expected duration in individuals with normal pseudocholinesterase function and a dibucaine number of about 80.
  • Option D. Paralysis lasting more than 1–3 hours: Such marked prolongation is characteristic of homozygous atypical pseudocholinesterase deficiency (dibucaine number around 20), not a dibucaine number of 50.

Educational Objective:

  • The dibucaine number reflects the quality (functional activity) of pseudocholinesterase rather than its quantity.
  • A dibucaine number of 50 is consistent with heterozygous atypical pseudocholinesterase, resulting in intermediate prolongation of succinylcholine-induced paralysis (20–30 minutes).

Refeeding syndrome is a potentially life-threatening metabolic complication that occurs when nutrition is rapidly reintroduced after prolonged starvation or severe malnutrition. Refeeding syndrome is a potentially life-threatening metabolic complication that occurs when nutrition is rapidly reintroduced after prolonged starvation or severe malnutrition. The parents report that symptoms are most prominent after prolonged fasting, such as overnight. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly. This infant most likely has glycogen storage disease type III (Cori/Forbes disease), caused by deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme.

The key findings are:

  • Fasting hypoglycemia
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Elevated AST and ALT
  • Ketosis/ketoacidosis
  • Progressive muscle weakness
  • Excess accumulation of structurally abnormal glycogen in the liver

  • After an overnight fast: The outer glycogen chains have already been shortened to within four glucose residues of the branch points. Without the debranching enzyme, further glycogen breakdown cannot occur, so glucagon produces little or no rise in blood glucose.

You add malat​e and pyruvate, and respi​ration proceeds normally.‍ You then add succinate, ‍and respiration still rem‌ains normal. questions.raw_text: You are conducting an experiment on mitochondrial respiration. You add malate and pyruvate, and respiration proceeds normally. You then add succinate, and respiration still remains normal. However, after adding another substance in the presence of pyruvate, succinate, and malate, respiration is completely blocked. Which of the following substances was most likely added?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oligomycin

Respiration requires:

  • A functioning electron transport chain (ETC)
  • ATP synthase (Complex V) to allow protons to flow back into the mitochondrial matrix.

Why oligomycin is correct?

  • Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase (Complex V) by blocking its F₀ proton channel.
  • This prevents protons from re-entering the mitochondrial matrix.
  • As protons accumulate in the intermembrane space, the proton gradient becomes maximal.
  • Once the gradient is too high, the ETC can no longer pump additional protons, so electron transport and oxygen consumption stop completely.

Thus, respiration is completely blocked despite the presence of multiple substrates (pyruvate, malate, and succinate).

Why the other options are incorrect?
A. Rotenone ❌

  • Inhibits Complex I.
  • Pyruvate and malate donate electrons through Complex I, so their oxidation would stop.
  • However, succinate donates electrons directly to Complex II, bypassing Complex I.
  • Therefore, respiration would continue in the presence of succinate, not be completely blocked.

B. Antimycin A ❌

  • Inhibits Complex III.
  • This blocks electron flow from both Complex I and Complex II.
  • Respiration would indeed stop regardless of substrate.
  • However, in classic substrate-addition experiments, the inhibitor that blocks respiration by preventing proton re-entry despite intact electron donors is oligomycin. (If the question specifically emphasized inhibition of the ETC itself, antimycin A would be expected.)

D. 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) ❌

  • DNP is an uncoupler.
  • It dissipates the proton gradient by carrying protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
  • Electron transport and oxygen consumption increase, while ATP synthesis decreases.
  • Respiration is stimulated, not blocked.

Key Concept

| Inhibitor | Target | Effect on O₂ Consumption |
| --------- | ------ | ------------------------ |
| Rotenone | Complex I | Blocked unless electrons enter via Complex II (succinate) |
| Antimycin A | Complex III | Completely blocks ETC and respiration |
| Oligomycin | ATP synthase (Complex V) | Stops ATP synthesis and secondarily halts respiration |
| DNP | Uncoupler | Increases oxygen consumption, decreases ATP synthesis |

Correct answer: A. β-Oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids within peroxisomes

This infant has features suggestive of Zellweger syndrome, the prototype peroxisome biogenesis disorder.

Key clinical clues

  • Severe hypotonia ("floppy infant")
  • Developmental delay
  • Seizures
  • Dysmorphic facial features
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Hyporeflexia
  • Defective extramitochondrial lipid metabolism

The defect lies in the PEX genes, which are responsible for the formation and function of peroxisomes.

What do peroxisomes do?
Peroxisomes are responsible for:

  • β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs; ≥22 carbons)
  • α-Oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids (e.g., phytanic acid)
  • Synthesis of plasmalogens (important for myelin)
  • Detoxification of hydrogen peroxide by catalase

Because VLCFAs cannot initially be degraded in mitochondria, they must first undergo β-oxidation in peroxisomes.

Correct answer: A. Primary structure

Most inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs) are caused by mutations in genes encoding metabolic enzymes, leading to alterations in the primary structure of proteins—the linear sequence of amino acids. Even a single amino acid substitution can impair protein folding, stability, or catalytic activity, resulting in enzyme deficiency and accumulation of toxic metabolites or deficiency of essential metabolic products.

The altered primary structure may subsequently affect the protein's secondary, tertiary, or quaternary structure, but the initial defect lies in the amino acid sequence.

Other Options:

  • B. Secondary structure: Incorrect. Secondary structure refers to local protein folding into α-helices and β-pleated sheets through hydrogen bonding. These changes are usually secondary to alterations in the primary structure.
  • C. Tertiary structure: Incorrect. Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional conformation of a single polypeptide chain formed by interactions among amino acid side chains. Although often disrupted in IEMs, the primary genetic defect usually affects the amino acid sequence first.
  • D. Quaternary structure: Incorrect. Quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits. While some inherited disorders affect multimeric proteins, this is not the most common structural defect in inborn errors of metabolism.

High-yield:

  • Primary structure: Amino acid sequence (determined by DNA sequence)
  • Secondary structure: α-Helices and β-sheets
  • Tertiary structure: Three-dimensional folding of a single polypeptide
  • Quaternary structure: Association of two or more polypeptide chains
  • Most inborn errors of metabolism: Caused by mutations altering the primary structure of metabolic enzymes, leading to loss or reduction of enzyme function.

  • Option C. Tertiary structure: Incorrect. Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional folding of a single polypeptide chain. Each heavy and light chain individually possesses tertiary structure, but the complete immunoglobulin is formed by the association of multiple chains.

  • Redissolve on boiling (≈100°C)
  • Reprecipitate on cooling

Examination shows multiple bruises on the forehead and several healing wounds over the fingers. There is increased muscle tone in all extremities. Laboratory studies show an increased serum uric acid concentration. The serum concentration of which of the following substances is most likely to also be increased in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate

This child has Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, caused by deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). HGPRT normally salvages hypoxanthine and guanine to IMP and GMP. Its deficiency leads to:

  • Hyperuricemia (excess purine degradation)
  • Self-mutilation, intellectual disability, dystonia, spasticity

The lack of purine salvage causes PRPP accumulation, because it is not being used in the salvage pathway. Elevated PRPP stimulates de novo purine synthesis, further increasing uric acid production.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. HGPRT: This enzyme is deficient, not increased.
  • C. dATP (deoxyadenosine triphosphate): Increased dATP occurs in ADA deficiency, not Lesch-Nyhan.
  • D. Branched-chain amino acids: Not related to HGPRT deficiency; elevated in maple syrup urine disease.

Correct answer: D. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase

What is a ping-pong (double-displacement) reaction?
In a ping-pong mechanism, the reaction occurs in two sequential steps:

  1. First substrate binds to the enzyme.
  2. The enzyme is chemically modified, and the first product is released.
  3. Second substrate binds to the modified enzyme.
  4. The enzyme transfers the intermediate to the second substrate, forming the second product, and the enzyme returns to its original state.

Key feature: The two substrates are never bound to the enzyme at the same time.

| ------ | -------------------- | ------------------- |
| Serine proteases | ✅ Yes | Acyl-enzyme intermediate |
| Aminotransferases (ALT/AST) | ✅ Yes | PLP ⇌ PMP intermediate |
| Pyruvate carboxylase | ✅ Yes | Carboxybiotin intermediate |
| Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase | ❌ No | No ping-pong mechanism |

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Competitive inhibition

In a Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/V vs 1/[S]), competitive inhibition is identified by the following features:

  • Vmax remains unchanged because increasing substrate concentration can overcome the inhibitor.
  • Km increases (apparent Km ↑), indicating that a higher substrate concentration is required to reach half of Vmax.
  • Since 1/Vmax is unchanged, the Y-intercept remains the same.

questions.raw_text:
Regarding alternative splicing of pre-mRNA, consider the following statements:

1. It allows a single gene to give rise to multiple protein isoforms.
2. The calcitonin/CGRP gene is a classic example, producing calcitonin in thyroid C-cells and CGRP in neurons.
3. It occurs in the nucleus and is carried out by the spliceosome.
4. It increases the coding capacity of the genome without increasing the number of genes.

Which of the above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Distractor-by-distractor analysis:

  • Statement 1. It allows a single gene to give rise to multiple protein isoforms: True. Different combinations of exons are retained or excluded, so one gene → several mRNAs → several protein isoforms. This is the core definition.
  • Statement 2. The calcitonin/CGRP gene is a classic example, producing calcitonin in thyroid C-cells and CGRP in neurons: True. The single CALC I gene is the textbook example. Tissue-specific splicing yields calcitonin in thyroid parafollicular (C) cells and CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) in neural tissue. This exact example is the most frequently tested instance in PG entrances — worth memorizing as the go-to answer.
  • Statement 3. It occurs in the nucleus and is carried out by the spliceosome: True. Splicing is a nuclear, co-/post-transcriptional event performed by the spliceosome (snRNPs: U1, U2, U4, U5, U6). Regulation is via cis elements (splice enhancers/silencers) and trans factors (SR proteins, hnRNPs).
  • Statement 4. It increases the coding capacity of the genome without increasing the number of genes: True. This explains the "proteome > genome" paradox — humans have \~20,000 genes but a far larger proteome, largely because of alternative splicing.

High-yield pearls to attach in the bank:

  • Other classic examples: tropomyosin, immunoglobulin heavy chain (membrane-bound vs secreted forms), and Dscam (extreme diversity).
  • Disease link — splice-site mutations cause β-thalassemia; SMN1/SMN2 splicing underlies spinal muscular atrophy (basis of nusinersen therapy).
  • Common trap: alternative splicing is distinct from RNA editing (e.g., apolipoprotein B — C→U deamination creating a stop codon). Examiners love pairing these two as distractors.

    • Cas9 is an RNA-guided endonuclease that introduces site-specific double-stranded DNA breaks.
    • It is widely used for precise genome editing.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the HPRT1 (HGPRT) gene located on the X chromosome (Xq26–q27), not chromosome 6. Deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) impairs the purine salvage pathway, leading to increased degradation of purines into uric acid, resulting in hyperuricemia. Excess PRPP also stimulates de novo purine synthesis, further worsening uric acid overproduction.

The syndrome is characterized by a triad of:

  • Hyperuricemia (gout, nephrolithiasis, orange "sand" crystals in diapers)
  • Neurological dysfunction (dystonia, choreoathetosis, spasticity)
  • Behavioral abnormalities, especially self-mutilation and compulsive aggressive behavior.

Other Options:

  • A. Hyperuricemia: Correct. Excess uric acid production leads to gout, uric acid nephrolithiasis, and urate crystal deposition.
  • B. Self-mutilative behavior: Correct. Self-biting of the lips, tongue, and fingers is a hallmark feature of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
  • C. Compulsive aggression: Correct. Behavioral disturbances, including compulsive aggression and self-injurious behavior, are common neurological manifestations.

  • Inheritance: X-linked recessive
  • Enzyme deficiency: HGPRT (Hypoxanthine-Guanine Phosphoribosyltransferase)
  • Pathway affected: Purine salvage pathway
  • Biochemical findings: ↑ PRPP, ↓ IMP/GMP, ↑ de novo purine synthesis, ↑ uric acid
  • Classic presentation: Hyperuricemia + dystonia/choreoathetosis + self-mutilation
  • Treatment: Allopurinol or febuxostat lowers uric acid but does not improve the neurological manifestations.

Correct answer: D. The patient's son most likely inherited the mutation.

ZVRecommendation: Watch the video explanation for this one for a better understanding!

Step 1 — Identify the disease allele

The patient's mutation came from the paternal line (father + grandfather affected). Compare the patient with his affected father:

  • Patient = 12 + 8; Father = 10 + 8 → the only shared band is 8 kb.
  • Since the patient must have inherited one allele from his father, and he shares only the 8 kb band with him, the 8 kb fragment is the paternally-transmitted disease allele.
  • The 12 kb band is therefore maternal (mother has a normal lipid profile → normal allele).

Mutant allele = 8 kb. This is the linchpin of the whole question.

Step 2 — Track the son and brother

Son (20 + 8):

  • Wife (20 + 10) → son got the 20 kb from mother.
  • Patient (12 + 8) → son got the 8 kb from father = disease allele. ✔️ Inherited the mutation → D correct.

Brother (12 + 10):

  • Father (10 + 8) → brother got the 10 kb (normal), not the 8 kb disease allele.
  • 12 kb came from their shared mother.
  • → Brother did not inherit the mutation.

Distractor analysis

A. X-linked recessive — Wrong on two counts. FH is autosomal dominant, and the pedigree shows clear male-to-male (father→patient→son) transmission, which formally excludes X-linkage.
B. Mutation in the 10 kb band — Trap for students who don't establish the disease allele first. The 10 kb band is the father's normal allele (and one of the wife's normal alleles). The mutation segregates with 8 kb, not 10 kb.
C. Brother inherited the mutation — He received the father's 10 kb normal allele, so he's unaffected. Tempting only if a student assumes "shares a band with patient (12 kb) = affected," forgetting the 12 kb is the maternal/normal allele.
D. Son inherited the mutation — ✔️ He carries the paternal 8 kb disease allele.

A 4-month-old infant who appeared healthy at birth is brought for evaluation of recurrent episodes of fasting hypoglycemia and progressive muscle weakness. The parents report that symptoms are most prominent after prolonged fasting, such as overnight. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly. Laboratory investigations demonstrate elevated AST and ALT levels along with ketoacidosis (arterial pH 7.25). Liver biopsy shows excessive glycogen accumulation, accounting for approximately 8% of liver weight. A glucagon stimulation test is performed:
•	After a carbohydrate-rich meal: Blood glucose rises appropriately. 
•	After an overnight fast: No significant increase in blood glucose is observed. 
Which enzyme deficiency best explains these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Debranching enzyme

This infant most likely has glycogen storage disease type III (Cori/Forbes disease), caused by deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme.

The key findings are:

  • Fasting hypoglycemia
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Elevated AST and ALT
  • Ketosis/ketoacidosis
  • Progressive muscle weakness
  • Excess accumulation of structurally abnormal glycogen in the liver

Glucagon stimulation test

  • After a carbohydrate-rich meal: Blood glucose rises because recently synthesized glycogen has relatively long outer chains. Glycogen phosphorylase can initially break these α-1,4 bonds and release glucose-1-phosphate.
  • After an overnight fast: The outer glycogen chains have already been shortened to within four glucose residues of the branch points. Without the debranching enzyme, further glycogen breakdown cannot occur, so glucagon produces little or no rise in blood glucose.

This characteristic response supports debranching enzyme deficiency.

Why the other options are incorrect?

  • B. Muscle glycogen phosphorylase: Causes McArdle disease, presenting with exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, and myoglobinuria. It does not cause hepatomegaly or fasting hypoglycemia.
  • C. Glucose-6-phosphatase: Causes von Gierke disease. It produces severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia, but muscle weakness is not a prominent feature. Glucagon fails to raise blood glucose in both fed and fasting states.
  • D. Liver glycogen phosphorylase: Causes Hers disease. It leads to mild fasting hypoglycemia, ketosis, and hepatomegaly but generally does not cause progressive muscle weakness.

You add malat​e and pyruvate, and respi‍ration proceeds normally.​ You then add succinate, ​and respiration still rem‌ains normal. questions.raw_text: You are conducting an experiment on mitochondrial respiration. You add malate and pyruvate, and respiration proceeds normally. You then add succinate, and respiration still remains normal. However, after adding another substance in the presence of pyruvate, succinate, and malate, respiration is completely blocked. Which of the following substances was most likely added?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oligomycin

Respiration requires:

  • A functioning electron transport chain (ETC)
  • ATP synthase (Complex V) to allow protons to flow back into the mitochondrial matrix.

Why oligomycin is correct?

  • Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase (Complex V) by blocking its F₀ proton channel.
  • This prevents protons from re-entering the mitochondrial matrix.
  • As protons accumulate in the intermembrane space, the proton gradient becomes maximal.
  • Once the gradient is too high, the ETC can no longer pump additional protons, so electron transport and oxygen consumption stop completely.

Thus, respiration is completely blocked despite the presence of multiple substrates (pyruvate, malate, and succinate).

Why the other options are incorrect?
A. Rotenone ❌

  • Inhibits Complex I.
  • Pyruvate and malate donate electrons through Complex I, so their oxidation would stop.
  • However, succinate donates electrons directly to Complex II, bypassing Complex I.
  • Therefore, respiration would continue in the presence of succinate, not be completely blocked.

B. Antimycin A ❌

  • Inhibits Complex III.
  • This blocks electron flow from both Complex I and Complex II.
  • Respiration would indeed stop regardless of substrate.
  • However, in classic substrate-addition experiments, the inhibitor that blocks respiration by preventing proton re-entry despite intact electron donors is oligomycin. (If the question specifically emphasized inhibition of the ETC itself, antimycin A would be expected.)

D. 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) ❌

  • DNP is an uncoupler.
  • It dissipates the proton gradient by carrying protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
  • Electron transport and oxygen consumption increase, while ATP synthesis decreases.
  • Respiration is stimulated, not blocked.

Key Concept

| Inhibitor | Target | Effect on O₂ Consumption |
| --------- | ------ | ------------------------ |
| Rotenone | Complex I | Blocked unless electrons enter via Complex II (succinate) |
| Antimycin A | Complex III | Completely blocks ETC and respiration |
| Oligomycin | ATP synthase (Complex V) | Stops ATP synthesis and secondarily halts respiration |
| DNP | Uncoupler | Increases oxygen consumption, decreases ATP synthesis |

Correct answer: D. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase

What is a ping-pong (double-displacement) reaction?
In a ping-pong mechanism, the reaction occurs in two sequential steps:

  1. First substrate binds to the enzyme.
  2. The enzyme is chemically modified, and the first product is released.
  3. Second substrate binds to the modified enzyme.
  4. The enzyme transfers the intermediate to the second substrate, forming the second product, and the enzyme returns to its original state.

Key feature: The two substrates are never bound to the enzyme at the same time.

| ------ | -------------------- | ------------------- |
| Serine proteases | ✅ Yes | Acyl-enzyme intermediate |

| Pyruvate carboxylase | ✅ Yes | Carboxybiotin intermediate |

questions.raw_text:
Regarding alternative splicing of pre-mRNA, consider the following statements:

1. It allows a single gene to give rise to multiple protein isoforms.
2. The calcitonin/CGRP gene is a classic example, producing calcitonin in thyroid C-cells and CGRP in neurons.
3. It occurs in the nucleus and is carried out by the spliceosome.
4. It increases the coding capacity of the genome without increasing the number of genes.

Which of the above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Distractor-by-distractor analysis:

  • Statement 1. It allows a single gene to give rise to multiple protein isoforms: True. Different combinations of exons are retained or excluded, so one gene → several mRNAs → several protein isoforms. This is the core definition.
  • Statement 2. The calcitonin/CGRP gene is a classic example, producing calcitonin in thyroid C-cells and CGRP in neurons: True. The single CALC I gene is the textbook example. Tissue-specific splicing yields calcitonin in thyroid parafollicular (C) cells and CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) in neural tissue. This exact example is the most frequently tested instance in PG entrances — worth memorizing as the go-to answer.
  • Statement 3. It occurs in the nucleus and is carried out by the spliceosome: True. Splicing is a nuclear, co-/post-transcriptional event performed by the spliceosome (snRNPs: U1, U2, U4, U5, U6). Regulation is via cis elements (splice enhancers/silencers) and trans factors (SR proteins, hnRNPs).
  • Statement 4. It increases the coding capacity of the genome without increasing the number of genes: True. This explains the "proteome > genome" paradox — humans have \~20,000 genes but a far larger proteome, largely because of alternative splicing.

High-yield pearls to attach in the bank:

  • Other classic examples: tropomyosin, immunoglobulin heavy chain (membrane-bound vs secreted forms), and Dscam (extreme diversity).
  • Disease link — splice-site mutations cause β-thalassemia; SMN1/SMN2 splicing underlies spinal muscular atrophy (basis of nusinersen therapy).
  • Common trap: alternative splicing is distinct from RNA editing (e.g., apolipoprotein B — C→U deamination creating a stop codon). Examiners love pairing these two as distractors.

  • Neurological dysfunction (dystonia, choreoathetosis, spasticity)

B. Hemoglobin C: Lys82 mutation in β-globin causes mild hemolysis and crystal formation, but does not cause high-affinity hemoglobin or erythrocytosis.
D. Hemoglobin S: Glu6→Val mutation causes sickling, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusive crises, not erythrocytosis.

questions.raw_text: A 34-year-old man is found to have an LDL level of 310 mg/dl and a normal serum triglyceride level. His father suffered a myocardial infarction at age 39, and his paternal grandfather died of a heart attack at age 40. The patient's wife has a normal lipid profile. DNA samples are obtained from several family members for genetic analysis. Southern blotting of restriction fragments from a region containing the LDL receptor gene shows the following pattern. Identify the correct statement:

options.text: The disease is transmitted‌ in an X-linked recessive​ fashion.
The mutation is probably l‌ocated in the 10 kb band.​
The patient's brother most‌ likely inherited the mut​ation.
The patient's son most lik‌ely inherited the mutatio​n.

questions.correct_answer: D. The patient's son most likely inherited the mutation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The patient's son most likely inherited the mutation.

ZVRecommendation: Watch the video explanation for this one for a better understanding!

Step 1 — Identify the disease allele

The patient's mutation came from the paternal line (father + grandfather affected). Compare the patient with his affected father:

  • Patient = 12 + 8; Father = 10 + 8 → the only shared band is 8 kb.
  • Since the patient must have inherited one allele from his father, and he shares only the 8 kb band with him, the 8 kb fragment is the paternally-transmitted disease allele.
  • The 12 kb band is therefore maternal (mother has a normal lipid profile → normal allele).

Mutant allele = 8 kb. This is the linchpin of the whole question.

Step 2 — Track the son and brother

Son (20 + 8):

  • Wife (20 + 10) → son got the 20 kb from mother.
  • Patient (12 + 8) → son got the 8 kb from father = disease allele. ✔️ Inherited the mutation → D correct.

Brother (12 + 10):

  • Father (10 + 8) → brother got the 10 kb (normal), not the 8 kb disease allele.
  • 12 kb came from their shared mother.
  • → Brother did not inherit the mutation.

Distractor analysis

A. X-linked recessive — Wrong on two counts. FH is autosomal dominant, and the pedigree shows clear male-to-male (father→patient→son) transmission, which formally excludes X-linkage.
B. Mutation in the 10 kb band — Trap for students who don't establish the disease allele first. The 10 kb band is the father's normal allele (and one of the wife's normal alleles). The mutation segregates with 8 kb, not 10 kb.
C. Brother inherited the mutation — He received the father's 10 kb normal allele, so he's unaffected. Tempting only if a student assumes "shares a band with patient (12 kb) = affected," forgetting the 12 kb is the maternal/normal allele.
D. Son inherited the mutation — ✔️ He carries the paternal 8 kb disease allele.

CRISPR-Cas9 introduces double-strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA. The cell repairs these DSBs via:

  • Microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ): Uses short homologous sequences to repair DSBs.
  • Single-strand annealing (SSA): Uses repeated sequences flanking the break to repair.

Mismatch repair (MMR), on the other hand, corrects base mispairings after DNA replication and does not repair DSBs, so it is not used in CRISPR-Cas9–mediated gene editing.

Why other options are incorrect:

1.	Endonuclease excises the sugar backbone
2.	Glycosylase removes the altered base
3.	DNA-polymerase adds a nucleotide
4.	Creation of apurinic/apyrimidinic site
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 → 4 → 1 → 3

Base excision repair (BER) proceeds in the following order:

1.  Glycosylase removes the altered base (2): Recognizes and excises the damaged base, leaving an apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) site.

2.  Creation of AP site (4): The sugar-phosphate backbone remains intact, now missing the base.

3.  Endonuclease excises the sugar backbone (1): AP endonuclease cleaves the phosphodiester bond at the AP site.

4.  DNA polymerase adds a nucleotide (3): Fills in the gap using the complementary strand as a template.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary structure

Most inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs) are caused by mutations in genes encoding metabolic enzymes, leading to alterations in the primary structure of proteins—the linear sequence of amino acids. Even a single amino acid substitution can impair protein folding, stability, or catalytic activity, resulting in enzyme deficiency and accumulation of toxic metabolites or deficiency of essential metabolic products.

The altered primary structure may subsequently affect the protein's secondary, tertiary, or quaternary structure, but the initial defect lies in the amino acid sequence.

Other Options:

  • B. Secondary structure: Incorrect. Secondary structure refers to local protein folding into α-helices and β-pleated sheets through hydrogen bonding. These changes are usually secondary to alterations in the primary structure.
  • C. Tertiary structure: Incorrect. Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional conformation of a single polypeptide chain formed by interactions among amino acid side chains. Although often disrupted in IEMs, the primary genetic defect usually affects the amino acid sequence first.
  • D. Quaternary structure: Incorrect. Quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits. While some inherited disorders affect multimeric proteins, this is not the most common structural defect in inborn errors of metabolism.

High-yield:

  • Primary structure: Amino acid sequence (determined by DNA sequence)
  • Secondary structure: α-Helices and β-sheets
  • Tertiary structure: Three-dimensional folding of a single polypeptide
  • Quaternary structure: Association of two or more polypeptide chains
  • Most inborn errors of metabolism: Caused by mutations altering the primary structure of metabolic enzymes, leading to loss or reduction of enzyme function.

  • Option C. Tertiary structure: Incorrect. Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional folding of a single polypeptide chain. Each heavy and light chain individually possesses tertiary structure, but the complete immunoglobulin is formed by the association of multiple chains.

Bence Jones proteins are free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (κ or λ) produced in excess by malignant plasma cells in disorders such as multiple myeloma and light-chain amyloidosis. These proteins are filtered by the kidneys and can be detected in urine.

A classic laboratory feature is their thermoreversible precipitation:

  • Precipitate at 40–60°C
  • Redissolve on boiling (≈100°C)
  • Reprecipitate on cooling

2.	End products are ribose-5-P, O₂ and NADH
3.	No ATP produced in oxidative phase
4.	Transketolase requires thiamine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3 and 4

The HMP shunt (Pentose Phosphate Pathway) is an alternative pathway of glucose metabolism that occurs in the cytosol and primarily functions to produce NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate.

1. Non-oxidative phase is reversible – TRUE
The non-oxidative phase interconverts pentose phosphates with glycolytic intermediates (fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate), allowing flexibility depending on cellular needs.

3. No ATP is produced in the oxidative phase – TRUE
The oxidative phase generates NADPH, not ATP. NADPH is used for:

  • Fatty acid synthesis
  • Cholesterol synthesis
  • Maintenance of reduced glutathione in RBCs

4. Transketolase requires thiamine – TRUE
The enzyme transketolase in the non-oxidative phase requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) as a cofactor. Reduced transketolase activity is seen in thiamine deficiency.

Why statement 2 is incorrect: The end products of the oxidative phase are ribulose-5-phosphate, CO₂, and NADPH, not O₂ or NADH.

questions.raw_text: Which intermediate of the TCA cycle participates in fatty acid synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Citrate

Citrate is the TCA cycle intermediate that links carbohydrate metabolism with fatty acid synthesis.

Role of citrate in fatty acid synthesis

  • In the mitochondria, acetyl-CoA enters the TCA cycle and combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
  • When cellular energy is abundant, citrate is transported from the mitochondria to the cytosol.
  • In the cytosol, ATP-citrate lyase cleaves citrate into:
    • Acetyl-CoA
    • Oxaloacetate

The acetyl-CoA produced in the cytosol is the precursor for fatty acid synthesis.

Citrate also Activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carnitine

Long-chain fatty acids cannot directly cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Their transport into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation requires the carnitine shuttle system.

Mechanism (Carnitine shuttle):
1.      Fatty acids are activated to fatty acyl-CoA in the cytosol.
2.      Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I) converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine (outer mitochondrial membrane).
3.      Acyl-carnitine is transported across the inner membrane via a translocase.
4.      CPT-II reconverts acyl-carnitine to acyl-CoA inside the mitochondria for β-oxidation.
Defects in the carnitine shuttle (e.g., CPT deficiency) lead to impaired fatty acid oxidation → hypoketotic hypoglycemia and muscle weakness.

  • Acyl carrier protein: Involved in fatty acid synthesis, not transport.
  • Cholesterol transporter: Not related to fatty acid mitochondrial entry.
  • LCAT (Lecithin–cholesterol acyltransferase): Involved in cholesterol metabolism (HDL function).

Correct answer: B. https://assets.corebtr.com/questions_image/option/01KXMR22ET2S7GB2B8P3EVQKWM.jpeg

Uncompetitive inhibition occurs when the inhibitor binds only to the enzyme–substrate (ES) complex, forming an inactive ESI complex. This decreases both the maximum velocity (Vmax) and the Michaelis constant (Km) by the same proportion. As a result, on a Lineweaver–Burk plot, the inhibited and uninhibited lines are parallel because the slope (Km/Vmax) remains unchanged.

  • In uncompetitive inhibition:
    • Vmax decreases → Y-intercept (1/Vmax) increases
    • Km decreases → X-intercept (-1/Km) shifts further to the left
    • Slope (Km/Vmax) remains unchanged
  • Therefore, the Lineweaver–Burk plot shows parallel lines, as seen in Option B

Why not the other options?

  • A. Competitive inhibition: Vmax is unchanged, Km increases; lines intersect on the Y-axis.
  • B. Mixed inhibition: Both Km and Vmax change, but not proportionally; lines intersect left of the Y-axis.
  • D. Noncompetitive inhibition (pure): Vmax decreases while Km remains unchanged; lines intersect on the X-axis.

questions.raw_text:
A 12-year-old boy presented to a health centre in Telangana along with his parents, with complaints of recurrent diarrhoea and skin changes on areas of the body exposed to sunlight. There is a history of progressive disorientation and increasing irritability. The child and his family ate sorghum cereal, there was very little consumption of milk and no consumption of foods of animal origin like meat, though the family is not strictly vegetarian by food habit. Consider the following plans of action:

1.	Absolute avoidance of milk in the child’s diet
2.	Encouraging shift of cereal consumption from sorghum to maize
3.	Encouraging consumption of meat in the child’s diet, if the family can afford
4.	Supplementation with nicotinic acid or nicotinamide

Which of the plans of action given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 and 4 only

The child has the classic 3 Ds of pellagra:

  • Diarrhea
  • Dermatitis — photosensitive skin lesions
  • Dementia — irritability, disorientation and neuropsychiatric changes

Why sorghum (jowar) causes pellagra:
Sorghum-based diets (common in parts of the Deccan plateau, including Telangana) are strongly associated with pellagra due to the "leucine excess theory" — sorghum is unusually rich in the amino acid leucine, which interferes with the enzymes involved in the tryptophan → niacin conversion pathway, precipitating niacin deficiency even when dietary intake isn't grossly inadequate. Lack of milk and animal-source foods (both good tryptophan/niacin sources) compounds the deficiency.

Evaluating the options:

  1. Absolute avoidance of milk — Incorrect. Milk is actually a good source of tryptophan and should be encouraged, not avoided. Avoiding it would worsen the deficiency.
  2. Shift from sorghum to maize — Incorrect. This is a classic distractor. Maize is equally, if not more strongly, associated with pellagra — its niacin is present in a biologically unavailable bound form (niacytin), and it too is deficient in tryptophan. Shifting from sorghum to maize does not solve the problem and may worsen it.
  3. Encouraging meat consumption — Correct. Meat is rich in both tryptophan and preformed niacin, directly addressing the deficiency.
  4. Supplementation with nicotinic acid/nicotinamide — Correct. This is the definitive treatment for established pellagra.

Exam pearl: Both sorghum and maize are classically linked to pellagra (via different mechanisms — leucine excess in sorghum vs. bound/unavailable niacin in maize) — so "switching cereals" is never the fix; the fix is adding tryptophan/niacin-rich foods (milk, eggs, meat, groundnuts) and direct niacin supplementation.

questions.text: Which of the following sta‌tements regarding folate ​deficiency is FALSE?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following statements regarding folate deficiency is FALSE?

options.text: High homocysteine and norm‌al methyl malonic acid
If given at the diagnosis ‌of pregnancy - can preven​t neural tube defects
Folate supplementation is ‌required in children with​ chronic hemolytic anemia‍
Vitamin B12 deficiency sho‌uld be corrected before s​upplementing folate

questions.correct_answer: B. If given at the diagnosis of pregnancy - can prevent neural tube defects
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. If given at the diagnosis of pregnancy - can prevent neural tube defects

Neural tube closure occurs very early in embryonic development (between days 21–28 after conception, around the 4th week of gestation). By the time most women realize they are pregnant (usually 5–6 weeks gestation), neural tube closure has already occurred.
Therefore, folic acid must be taken before conception and continued through the first trimester to effectively reduce the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs).

  • Recommended dose for low-risk women: 400 µg/day, beginning at least 1 month before conception.
  • High-risk women (previous pregnancy with NTD, certain antiepileptic drugs, etc.): 4–5 mg/day before conception.

Why are the other options correct

A. High homocysteine with normal methylmalonic acid levels

Folate deficiency impairs the conversion of homocysteine → methionine, leading to:

  • ↑ Homocysteine
  • Normal methylmalonic acid (MMA)

In contrast:

| Deficiency | Homocysteine | Methylmalonic acid |
| ---------- | ------------ | ------------------ |
| Folate deficiency | ↑ | Normal |
| Vitamin B12 deficiency | ↑ | ↑ |

High-yield pearl: MMA differentiates vitamin B12 deficiency from folate deficiency.

C. Folate supplementation is required in children with chronic hemolytic anemia

Children with chronic hemolytic disorders (e.g., sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassemia) have:

  • Increased RBC destruction
  • Increased bone marrow activity
  • Increased DNA synthesis
  • Increased folate requirement

Hence, routine folate supplementation is recommended to support erythropoiesis.

D. Vitamin B12 deficiency should be corrected before folate supplementation

This is an important clinical principle.
Giving folic acid alone to a patient with unrecognized vitamin B12 deficiency:

  • Corrects the megaloblastic anemia
  • Does not treat the neurological damage
  • May allow neurological complications to progress unnoticed, sometimes irreversibly

Therefore:

  • Always exclude or treat vitamin B12 deficiency first, or give both B12 and folate if both deficiencies are suspected.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Denaturation → Annealing → Extension

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is a laboratory technique used to amplify a specific segment of DNA, producing millions of copies from a small DNA sample.
Sequence of steps in PCR

  1. Denaturation (≈94–98°C)
    • Double-stranded DNA separates into two single strands due to breaking of hydrogen bonds.
  2. Annealing (≈50–65°C)
    • Primers bind to complementary sequences on the single-stranded DNA template.
  3. Extension / Elongation (≈72°C)
    • DNA polymerase synthesizes new DNA strands by adding nucleotides complementary to the template.

These steps are repeated for multiple cycles, resulting in exponential amplification of the target DNA.

questions.raw_text:
A 12-year-old boy presented to a health centre in Telangana along with his parents, with complaints of recurrent diarrhoea and skin changes on areas of the body exposed to sunlight. There is a history of progressive disorientation and increasing irritability. The child and his family ate sorghum cereal, there was very little consumption of milk and no consumption of foods of animal origin like meat, though the family is not strictly vegetarian by food habit. Consider the following plans of action:

1.	Absolute avoidance of milk in the child’s diet
2.	Encouraging shift of cereal consumption from sorghum to maize
3.	Encouraging consumption of meat in the child’s diet, if the family can afford
4.	Supplementation with nicotinic acid or nicotinamide

Which of the plans of action given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 and 4 only

The child has the classic 3 Ds of pellagra:

  • Diarrhea
  • Dermatitis — photosensitive skin lesions
  • Dementia — irritability, disorientation and neuropsychiatric changes

Why sorghum (jowar) causes pellagra:
Sorghum-based diets (common in parts of the Deccan plateau, including Telangana) are strongly associated with pellagra due to the "leucine excess theory" — sorghum is unusually rich in the amino acid leucine, which interferes with the enzymes involved in the tryptophan → niacin conversion pathway, precipitating niacin deficiency even when dietary intake isn't grossly inadequate. Lack of milk and animal-source foods (both good tryptophan/niacin sources) compounds the deficiency.

Evaluating the options:

  1. Absolute avoidance of milk — Incorrect. Milk is actually a good source of tryptophan and should be encouraged, not avoided. Avoiding it would worsen the deficiency.
  2. Shift from sorghum to maize — Incorrect. This is a classic distractor. Maize is equally, if not more strongly, associated with pellagra — its niacin is present in a biologically unavailable bound form (niacytin), and it too is deficient in tryptophan. Shifting from sorghum to maize does not solve the problem and may worsen it.
  3. Encouraging meat consumption — Correct. Meat is rich in both tryptophan and preformed niacin, directly addressing the deficiency.
  4. Supplementation with nicotinic acid/nicotinamide — Correct. This is the definitive treatment for established pellagra.

Exam pearl: Both sorghum and maize are classically linked to pellagra (via different mechanisms — leucine excess in sorghum vs. bound/unavailable niacin in maize) — so "switching cereals" is never the fix; the fix is adding tryptophan/niacin-rich foods (milk, eggs, meat, groundnuts) and direct niacin supplementation.

Correct answer: A. Conversion of glycine to serine

The clue is defective one-carbon metabolism.

One-carbon metabolism is mediated by tetrahydrofolate (THF), which carries one-carbon units in different oxidation states. These one-carbon units are essential for:

  • Purine synthesis
  • Thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis
  • Methionine synthesis
  • Interconversion of serine and glycine

  • Tetrahydrofolate (THF)
  • Pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B₆)

This is one of the most important THF-dependent one-carbon transfer reactions in amino acid metabolism.

Why this reaction is important
The serine–glycine interconversion:

  • Generates N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene THF, the one-carbon donor required for:
    • dTMP synthesis (thymidylate synthase)
    • Purine synthesis
  • Links amino acid metabolism with DNA synthesis.

Defects in folate metabolism impair this reaction, leading to reduced DNA synthesis and megaloblastic anemia.

  • Catalyzed by tyrosine hydroxylase.
  • Requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄), not THF.

  • Requires pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B₆).
  • No one-carbon transfer occurs.

Correct answer: B. If given at the diagnosis of pregnancy - can prevent neural tube defects

Neural tube closure occurs very early in embryonic development (between days 21–28 after conception, around the 4th week of gestation). By the time most women realize they are pregnant (usually 5–6 weeks gestation), neural tube closure has already occurred.
Therefore, folic acid must be taken before conception and continued through the first trimester to effectively reduce the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs).

  • Recommended dose for low-risk women: 400 µg/day, beginning at least 1 month before conception.
  • High-risk women (previous pregnancy with NTD, certain antiepileptic drugs, etc.): 4–5 mg/day before conception.

  • Normal methylmalonic acid (MMA)

| Deficiency | Homocysteine | Methylmalonic acid |
| ---------- | ------------ | ------------------ |
| Folate deficiency | ↑ | Normal |
| Vitamin B12 deficiency | ↑ | ↑ |

High-yield pearl: MMA differentiates vitamin B12 deficiency from folate deficiency.

C. Folate supplementation is required in children with chronic hemolytic anemia

Children with chronic hemolytic disorders (e.g., sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassemia) have:

  • Increased RBC destruction
  • Increased bone marrow activity
  • Increased DNA synthesis
  • Increased folate requirement

Hence, routine folate supplementation is recommended to support erythropoiesis.

D. Vitamin B12 deficiency should be corrected before folate supplementation

This is an important clinical principle.
Giving folic acid alone to a patient with unrecognized vitamin B12 deficiency:

  • Corrects the megaloblastic anemia
  • Does not treat the neurological damage
  • May allow neurological complications to progress unnoticed, sometimes irreversibly

questions.raw_text: You are conducting an experiment on mitochondrial respiration. You add malate and pyruvate, and respiration proceeds normally. You then add succinate, and respiration still remains normal. However, after adding another substance in the presence of pyruvate, succinate, and malate, respiration is completely blocked. Which of the following substances was most likely added?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oligomycin

Respiration requires:

  • A functioning electron transport chain (ETC)
  • ATP synthase (Complex V) to allow protons to flow back into the mitochondrial matrix.

Why oligomycin is correct?

  • Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase (Complex V) by blocking its F₀ proton channel.
  • This prevents protons from re-entering the mitochondrial matrix.
  • As protons accumulate in the intermembrane space, the proton gradient becomes maximal.
  • Once the gradient is too high, the ETC can no longer pump additional protons, so electron transport and oxygen consumption stop completely.

Thus, respiration is completely blocked despite the presence of multiple substrates (pyruvate, malate, and succinate).

Why the other options are incorrect?
A. Rotenone ❌

  • Inhibits Complex I.
  • Pyruvate and malate donate electrons through Complex I, so their oxidation would stop.
  • However, succinate donates electrons directly to Complex II, bypassing Complex I.
  • Therefore, respiration would continue in the presence of succinate, not be completely blocked.

B. Antimycin A ❌

  • Inhibits Complex III.
  • This blocks electron flow from both Complex I and Complex II.
  • Respiration would indeed stop regardless of substrate.
  • However, in classic substrate-addition experiments, the inhibitor that blocks respiration by preventing proton re-entry despite intact electron donors is oligomycin. (If the question specifically emphasized inhibition of the ETC itself, antimycin A would be expected.)

D. 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) ❌

  • DNP is an uncoupler.
  • It dissipates the proton gradient by carrying protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
  • Electron transport and oxygen consumption increase, while ATP synthesis decreases.
  • Respiration is stimulated, not blocked.

Key Concept

| --------- | ------ | ------------------------ |
| Rotenone | Complex I | Blocked unless electrons enter via Complex II (succinate) |
| Antimycin A | Complex III | Completely blocks ETC and respiration |
| Oligomycin | ATP synthase (Complex V) | Stops ATP synthesis and secondarily halts respiration |
| DNP | Uncoupler | Increases oxygen consumption, decreases ATP synthesis |
