  • Bind to the anionic site of AChE

Statement 3. Clinical benefit of oximes does not depend on the type of organophosphate poisoning: False. Clinical efficacy DOES depend on:

questions.raw_text: A 1-year-old infant accidentally ingests an organophosphate pesticide. Which drug reverses acetylcholinesterase enzyme blockade?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pralidoxime

Mechanism of Action of Pralidoxime (2-PAM)

  • Pralidoxime is a cholinesterase reactivator used in the treatment of organophosphate (OP) poisoning. It restores the activity of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) by removing the organophosphate bound to the enzyme before the process of aging occurs.

Stepwise Mechanism
1. Organophosphate poisoning

  • Organophosphates phosphorylate the active serine residue at the esteratic site of acetylcholinesterase.
  • This inactivates AChE, preventing the breakdown of acetylcholine.

  • Acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS synapses, producing a cholinergic crisis.

  • Binding of pralidoxime

  • Pralidoxime binds to the unoccupied anionic site of the inhibited acetylcholinesterase enzyme.

  • Its oxime (-NOH) group is a potent nucleophile.

  • Removal of the organophosphate

  • The oxime group attacks the phosphorus atom of the enzyme-bound organophosphate.

  • The organophosphate is displaced from the active serine residue and forms a stable pralidoxime–organophosphate complex.
  • This frees the enzyme and reactivates acetylcholinesterase, allowing normal hydrolysis of acetylcholine.

Important distinction:

  • Atropine blocks muscarinic effects only
  • Pralidoxime reverses the enzyme inhibition itself

questions.raw_text: A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer and found on genetic testing to carry a pathogenic BRCA1 mutation. Her mother, who carries the same BRCA1 mutation (confirmed on cascade testing), is now 74 years old and has never developed breast, ovarian, or any other BRCA-associated cancer. Which genetic principle best explains why the mother, despite carrying the identical disease-causing mutation, never developed the expected phenotype?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Incomplete penetrance

Rationale: Penetrance refers to the proportion of individuals carrying a given genotype who actually go on to express the associated phenotype at all — it is an all-or-none, population-level concept ("does the trait show up or not?"). BRCA1 mutations are classically incompletely penetrant: not every carrier develops cancer, even though the mutation substantially increases lifetime risk (e.g., roughly 55–72% lifetime breast cancer risk, not 100%). The mother in this vignette carries the identical pathogenic mutation as her daughter but has remained unaffected — exactly illustrating incomplete penetrance, since the genotype has not "penetrated" into a phenotype in her case, possibly due to protective modifier genes, hormonal/reproductive factors, or simply chance. Variable expressivity (A) would instead apply if both mother and daughter developed cancer, but with differing severity, age of onset, or tumor characteristics — that describes a spectrum of severity among those who are affected, not whether the disease appears at all. Pleiotropy (C) describes one gene causing multiple different unrelated phenotypic effects (e.g., BRCA1 mutations increasing both breast AND ovarian cancer risk) — not relevant to why the mother is asymptomatic. Anticipation (D) refers to a genetic disease worsening or presenting earlier in successive generations (classically seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders like Huntington disease or myotonic dystrophy) — not applicable here.
Quick reference — Penetrance vs Expressivity vs Pleiotropy:

| Concept | Key question it answers | Classic example |
| ------- | ----------------------- | --------------- |
| Penetrance | Does the phenotype appear at all in carriers? (all-or-none, population-level) | BRCA1/2 mutations; incomplete penetrance |
| Expressivity | Among those affected, how severe/variable is the phenotype? | Neurofibromatosis type 1; sickle cell anemia severity |
| Pleiotropy | Does one gene cause multiple different types of effects? | Marfan syndrome (eyes, heart, skeleton); sickle cell (crises + malaria resistance) |
| Anticipation | Does severity worsen / onset occur earlier in successive generations? | Huntington disease, myotonic dystrophy, Fragile X |

Correct answer: C. Upregulation of pro-apoptotic Fas ligand

In chronic viral hepatitis (HBV and HCV), hepatocyte injury is primarily immune-mediated rather than due to direct viral cytotoxicity.

  • Cytotoxic CD8⁺ T lymphocytes recognize viral antigens expressed on infected hepatocytes.
  • These T cells express Fas ligand (FasL), which binds to the Fas (CD95) receptor on hepatocytes.

  • Histologically, apoptotic hepatocytes appear as Councilman (acidophilic) bodies.

  • B. Activation of caspase-3 – Caspase-3 is an executioner caspase involved in the final phase of apoptosis. It is not the initiating molecular event.
  • D. Inhibition of p53 – p53 promotes apoptosis in response to DNA damage. Its inhibition decreases, rather than increases, apoptotic cell death.

| Pathway | Initiating event | Key mediator |
| ------- | ---------------- | ------------ |
| Extrinsic pathway | Fas–FasL or TNF receptor activation | Caspase-8 |
| Intrinsic pathway | Mitochondrial injury, DNA damage | BAX/BAK → Cytochrome c → Caspase-9 |
| Common pathway | Activation of executioner caspases | Caspase-3 |

Enclysis is a recently described cell-in-cell phenomenon in which hepatocytes selectively internalize live CD4⁺ T cells, particularly regulatory T cells (Tregs), playing a role in hepatic immune homeostasis and immune tolerance.

Unlike classical phagocytosis, the engulfed lymphocytes are viable at the time of uptake, and the process is unique to hepatocytes.

  • B. Entosis: A live cell actively invades another live cell, most commonly seen in epithelial tumors. It is associated with cell competition rather than immune regulation.
  • D. Emperipolesis: Describes the passage of intact viable cells through the cytoplasm of another cell without being digested. It is classically seen with megakaryocytes containing neutrophils or lymphocytes (e.g., Rosai–Dorfman disease).

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intracellular calcium overload

During myocardial ischemia followed by reperfusion (e.g., after PCI in STEMI), the most critical mechanism of early myocardial cell injury is intracellular calcium overload.

Pathophysiology:
1.      Ischemia → ATP depletion → failure of Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase.
2.      Na⁺ accumulates intracellularly, which activates the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger.
3.      This causes excess Ca²⁺ influx into cardiomyocytes.
4.      Calcium overload leads to:

  • Activation of proteases, phospholipases, and endonucleases
  • Mitochondrial damage
  • Hypercontracture of myofibrils
  • Cell death

Labile Cells

  • These cells are continuously being lost and replaced by maturation from tissue stem cells and by the proliferation of mature cells.
  • Labile cells include hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow and the majority of surface epithelia.

Stable Cells

  • They are quiescent and have minimal proliferative activity from progenitor cells.
  • They divide only when required but have limited regeneration compared to labile cells.
  • Stable cells constitute the parenchyma of most solid tissues (e.g., liver), endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and smooth muscle cells.

Permanent Cells

  • These cells are considered to be terminally differentiated and non-proliferative in postnatal life.
  • Permanent cells include neurons and cardiac and skeletal muscle cells.

Anoikis is a specialized form of apoptosis that occurs when epithelial or anchorage-dependent cells lose attachment to the extracellular matrix (ECM). This mechanism prevents detached cells from surviving and colonizing other tissues.

In malignant tumors, especially carcinomas, cancer cells often develop resistance to anoikis, allowing them to survive after detaching from the primary tumor, circulate in blood or lymph, and establish metastases at distant sites.

B. Pyroptosis: inflammatory cell death mediated by caspase-1 with IL-1β release.

D. Ferroptosis: iron-dependent cell death due to lipid peroxidation.

questions.raw_text: Which of the following statements about apoptosis is false?

options.text: Characterized by the activ​ation of caspases leading‌ to DNA fragmentation.
Inflammatory response and ​release of damage-associa‌ted molecular patterns (D​AMPs).
Chromatin condensation and​ formation of cytoplasmic‌ blebs.
Eliminates cells that are ​injured beyond repair wit‌hout eliciting a host rea​ction.

questions.correct_answer: B. Inflammatory response and release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs).
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inflammatory response and release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs).

Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death characterized by activation of caspases, DNA fragmentation, chromatin condensation, and membrane blebbing with formation of apoptotic bodies that are rapidly phagocytosed. Because the cell contents remain membrane-bound and are cleared efficiently, apoptosis does not trigger an inflammatory response. In contrast, necrosis leads to cell membrane rupture, release of intracellular components (including DAMPs), and inflammation.

  • Apoptosis: caspase activation, cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, membrane blebbing, no inflammation.
  • Necrosis: cell swelling, membrane rupture, DAMP release → inflammation.

So, the false statement is B, because inflammatory response with DAMP release is a feature of necrosis, not apoptosis.

  • B. Endometrial carcinoma: Malignancy of the endometrial glands; histology shows malignant glandular structures rather than spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells.
  • C. Adenomyosis: Presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium causing dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia; it is a benign, non-neoplastic condition.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medial calcific sclerosis

  • Age-classic: Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis typically affects patients >50 years, often incidental, seen in muscular (medium-sized) arteries — radial, ulnar, femoral, tibial vessels are classic sites.
  • X-ray correlate: Produces a characteristic "pipe-stem" or railroad-track calcification — visible radiographically as linear, tram-track calcific densities along the artery, which is exactly why an X-ray would be paired with a biopsy in this vignette.
  • Biopsy/histology correlate: Calcification is deposited in the tunica media, NOT the intima. Crucially, it does not narrow the lumen and is non-inflammatory — a key distractor point since it can look dramatic on imaging but is often clinically silent.

Quick differentiation from the distractors:

| Option | Vessel layer | Vessel size | Key association |
| ------ | ------------ | ----------- | --------------- |
| B. Medial calcific sclerosis | Media | Muscular arteries | Age >50, incidental, no luminal narrowing |
| A. Hyaline arteriolosclerosis | Intima/wall (hyaline thickening) | Arterioles | Chronic hypertension, diabetes |
| D. Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis | Intima (onion-skin) | Arterioles | Malignant hypertension |
| C. Metastatic calcification | Normal tissue, deposition d/t hypercalcemia | Various tissues (not vessel-specific) | Hypercalcemia (hyperparathyroidism, renal failure, etc.) |

The tram-track X-ray appearance + tunica media localization on histology is the pairing that clinches medial calcific sclerosis over the others — hyaline/hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis are hypertension-driven arteriolar lesions, and metastatic calcification is calcium deposition in otherwise normal tissue due to elevated serum calcium, not a primary vascular medial process.

Her mot​her, who carries the same​ BRCA1 mutation (confirme​d on cascade testing), is​ now 74 years old and has​ never developed breast, ​ovarian, or any other BRC‍A-associated cancer. questions.raw_text: A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer and found on genetic testing to carry a pathogenic BRCA1 mutation. Her mother, who carries the same BRCA1 mutation (confirmed on cascade testing), is now 74 years old and has never developed breast, ovarian, or any other BRCA-associated cancer. Which genetic principle best explains why the mother, despite carrying the identical disease-causing mutation, never developed the expected phenotype?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Incomplete penetrance

Rationale: Penetrance refers to the proportion of individuals carrying a given genotype who actually go on to express the associated phenotype at all — it is an all-or-none, population-level concept ("does the trait show up or not?"). BRCA1 mutations are classically incompletely penetrant: not every carrier develops cancer, even though the mutation substantially increases lifetime risk (e.g., roughly 55–72% lifetime breast cancer risk, not 100%). The mother in this vignette carries the identical pathogenic mutation as her daughter but has remained unaffected — exactly illustrating incomplete penetrance, since the genotype has not "penetrated" into a phenotype in her case, possibly due to protective modifier genes, hormonal/reproductive factors, or simply chance. Variable expressivity (A) would instead apply if both mother and daughter developed cancer, but with differing severity, age of onset, or tumor characteristics — that describes a spectrum of severity among those who are affected, not whether the disease appears at all. Pleiotropy (C) describes one gene causing multiple different unrelated phenotypic effects (e.g., BRCA1 mutations increasing both breast AND ovarian cancer risk) — not relevant to why the mother is asymptomatic. Anticipation (D) refers to a genetic disease worsening or presenting earlier in successive generations (classically seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders like Huntington disease or myotonic dystrophy) — not applicable here.
Quick reference — Penetrance vs Expressivity vs Pleiotropy:

| Concept | Key question it answers | Classic example |
| ------- | ----------------------- | --------------- |
| Penetrance | Does the phenotype appear at all in carriers? (all-or-none, population-level) | BRCA1/2 mutations; incomplete penetrance |
| Expressivity | Among those affected, how severe/variable is the phenotype? | Neurofibromatosis type 1; sickle cell anemia severity |
| Pleiotropy | Does one gene cause multiple different types of effects? | Marfan syndrome (eyes, heart, skeleton); sickle cell (crises + malaria resistance) |
| Anticipation | Does severity worsen / onset occur earlier in successive generations? | Huntington disease, myotonic dystrophy, Fragile X |

questions.raw_text: A researcher is investigating the restriction (R) point, the first major checkpoint of the cell cycle that determines whether a cell will commit to DNA synthesis or exit the cell cycle into a quiescent (G₀) state. This checkpoint is located immediately before which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. S phase

The G₁/S checkpoint (Restriction point or R point) is the first and most important checkpoint of the cell cycle. It occurs in late G₁ phase, immediately before the S phase, where the cell decides whether to:

  • Proceed to DNA replication (S phase), or
  • Exit the cell cycle and enter the quiescent G₀ phase

Once a cell crosses this checkpoint, it is committed to completing the cell cycle, even if external growth factors are withdrawn.

The checkpoint assesses:

  • Cell size
  • Nutrient and energy availability
  • Growth factor stimulation
  • DNA damage

It is regulated by:

  • Cyclin D–CDK4/6
  • Cyclin E–CDK2
  • Retinoblastoma (Rb) protein
  • p53 (via p21 in response to DNA damage)

Why not the other options?

  • A. G₂ phase: Incorrect. The G₂/M checkpoint occurs after DNA replication, ensuring DNA has been completely and accurately replicated before mitosis.
  • B. M phase: Incorrect. The spindle assembly checkpoint occurs during metaphase, ensuring proper chromosome attachment before anaphase.
  • C. S phase: ✅ Correct. The restriction point is located immediately before the S phase.
  • D. G₀ phase: Incorrect. G₀ is not a phase that follows the checkpoint; rather, cells exit from G₁ into G₀ if they do not receive the signals required to pass the checkpoint.

High-yield pearl

| Cell cycle checkpoint | Location | Function |
| --------------------- | -------- | -------- |
| G₁/S (Restriction point) | End of G₁, before S phase | Determines commitment to DNA replication; checks DNA damage, nutrients, growth factors |
| G₂/M checkpoint | End of G₂ | Ensures DNA replication is complete and DNA is undamaged before mitosis |
| Spindle checkpoint | Metaphase | Ensures all chromosomes are attached to spindle fibers before anaphase |

Exam tip:
The G₁/S checkpoint is the commitment checkpoint of the cell cycle:

  • Pass → Enter S phase and replicate DNA
  • Fail → Cell arrests for repair or exits into G₀.

questions.text: A researcher is investigat​ing the restriction (R) p​oint, the first major che‌ckpoint of the cell cycle‌ that determines whether ​a cell will commit to DNA‍ synthesis or exit the ce‌ll cycle into a quiescent‍ (G₀) state. questions.raw_text: A researcher is investigating the restriction (R) point, the first major checkpoint of the cell cycle that determines whether a cell will commit to DNA synthesis or exit the cell cycle into a quiescent (G₀) state. This checkpoint is located immediately before which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. S phase

The G₁/S checkpoint (Restriction point or R point) is the first and most important checkpoint of the cell cycle. It occurs in late G₁ phase, immediately before the S phase, where the cell decides whether to:

  • Proceed to DNA replication (S phase), or
  • Exit the cell cycle and enter the quiescent G₀ phase

Once a cell crosses this checkpoint, it is committed to completing the cell cycle, even if external growth factors are withdrawn.

The checkpoint assesses:

  • Cell size
  • Nutrient and energy availability
  • Growth factor stimulation
  • DNA damage

It is regulated by:

  • Cyclin D–CDK4/6
  • Cyclin E–CDK2
  • Retinoblastoma (Rb) protein
  • p53 (via p21 in response to DNA damage)

Why not the other options?

  • A. G₂ phase: Incorrect. The G₂/M checkpoint occurs after DNA replication, ensuring DNA has been completely and accurately replicated before mitosis.
  • B. M phase: Incorrect. The spindle assembly checkpoint occurs during metaphase, ensuring proper chromosome attachment before anaphase.
  • C. S phase: ✅ Correct. The restriction point is located immediately before the S phase.
  • D. G₀ phase: Incorrect. G₀ is not a phase that follows the checkpoint; rather, cells exit from G₁ into G₀ if they do not receive the signals required to pass the checkpoint.

High-yield pearl

| Cell cycle checkpoint | Location | Function |
| --------------------- | -------- | -------- |
| G₁/S (Restriction point) | End of G₁, before S phase | Determines commitment to DNA replication; checks DNA damage, nutrients, growth factors |
| G₂/M checkpoint | End of G₂ | Ensures DNA replication is complete and DNA is undamaged before mitosis |
| Spindle checkpoint | Metaphase | Ensures all chromosomes are attached to spindle fibers before anaphase |

Exam tip:
The G₁/S checkpoint is the commitment checkpoint of the cell cycle:

  • Pass → Enter S phase and replicate DNA
  • Fail → Cell arrests for repair or exits into G₀.

Which genetic principle best explains why the mother, despite carrying the identical disease-causing mutation, never developed the expected phenotype?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Incomplete penetrance

Rationale: Penetrance refers to the proportion of individuals carrying a given genotype who actually go on to express the associated phenotype at all — it is an all-or-none, population-level concept ("does the trait show up or not?"). BRCA1 mutations are classically incompletely penetrant: not every carrier develops cancer, even though the mutation substantially increases lifetime risk (e.g., roughly 55–72% lifetime breast cancer risk, not 100%). The mother in this vignette carries the identical pathogenic mutation as her daughter but has remained unaffected — exactly illustrating incomplete penetrance, since the genotype has not "penetrated" into a phenotype in her case, possibly due to protective modifier genes, hormonal/reproductive factors, or simply chance. Variable expressivity (A) would instead apply if both mother and daughter developed cancer, but with differing severity, age of onset, or tumor characteristics — that describes a spectrum of severity among those who are affected, not whether the disease appears at all. Pleiotropy (C) describes one gene causing multiple different unrelated phenotypic effects (e.g., BRCA1 mutations increasing both breast AND ovarian cancer risk) — not relevant to why the mother is asymptomatic. Anticipation (D) refers to a genetic disease worsening or presenting earlier in successive generations (classically seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders like Huntington disease or myotonic dystrophy) — not applicable here.
Quick reference — Penetrance vs Expressivity vs Pleiotropy:

| Concept | Key question it answers | Classic example |
| ------- | ----------------------- | --------------- |
| Penetrance | Does the phenotype appear at all in carriers? (all-or-none, population-level) | BRCA1/2 mutations; incomplete penetrance |
| Expressivity | Among those affected, how severe/variable is the phenotype? | Neurofibromatosis type 1; sickle cell anemia severity |
| Pleiotropy | Does one gene cause multiple different types of effects? | Marfan syndrome (eyes, heart, skeleton); sickle cell (crises + malaria resistance) |
| Anticipation | Does severity worsen / onset occur earlier in successive generations? | Huntington disease, myotonic dystrophy, Fragile X |

The medication charts reveal that he was taking digoxin, potassium chloride, clarithromycin, atenolol, and triamterene. Suspecting the symptoms to be due to digoxin overdose, plasma levels of digoxin were ordered. It was found that his blood levels of digoxin have increased significantly. Which of his medications is most likely responsible for this increase in digoxin levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clarithromycin

Mechanism:
Clarithromycin (a macrolide) raises digoxin levels through two mechanisms, both classic teaching points:

  1. P-glycoprotein inhibition: Digoxin is a substrate of P-gp (efflux transporter) in the gut wall and renal tubules. Macrolides like clarithromycin and erythromycin inhibit P-gp, reducing digoxin's efflux back into the gut lumen and its renal excretion → increased absorption and decreased clearance → increased plasma levels.
  2. Elimination of gut flora: In about 10% of the population, gut bacteria (notably Eubacterium lentum) metabolize digoxin in the intestine before it can be absorbed. Clarithromycin wipes out this flora, so more unmetabolized digoxin gets absorbed, further raising levels.

This is a well-documented and clinically significant interaction — macrolide + digoxin is a classic "avoid or monitor closely" combination.

Why the others are distractors, not the answer?

| Option | Relevance to the vignette |
| ------ | ------------------------- |
| A) Potassium chloride | Doesn't raise digoxin levels — in fact, hypokalemia (not hyperkalemia) potentiates digoxin toxicity by increasing its binding to Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. KCl would be protective against toxicity, not causative of elevated levels |
| C) Atenolol | Beta-blocker; additive AV nodal blockade with digoxin (bradycardia risk) but doesn't alter digoxin pharmacokinetics/levels |
| D) Triamterene | Potassium-sparing diuretic; relevant because it prevents hypokalemia (again protective against toxicity), not a P-gp inhibitor — doesn't raise digoxin levels |

High-yield takeaway for the question bank: Any question testing "drug that increases digoxin levels" should trigger recall of the P-gp inhibitor list — quinidine, verapamil, amiodarone, and macrolides (clarithromycin/erythromycin) are the classic culprits. This is a frequently recycled PYQ theme across NEET PG/INICET.

→ 2 half-lives

  • Vd = 150 L

  • Initial concentration = Measured concentration × 2ⁿ (where n = number of half-lives elapsed)
  • Dose = Initial concentration × Vd

Correct answer: D. X: Methotrexate Y: Fluorouracil

Both drugs ultimately inhibit thymidylate synthase (TS), the enzyme that converts dUMP → dTMP (thymidylate), but they hit the pathway at different points — which is exactly why their rescue requirements differ.

Drug X = Methotrexate

Mechanism: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking the regeneration of tetrahydrofolate (THF) from dihydrofolate (DHF).

  • Thymidylate synthase requires N5,N10-methylene-THF as a cofactor to convert dUMP → dTMP
  • When MTX blocks DHFR, the cell runs out of usable THF → no folate cofactor available → thymidylate synthase can't function → indirect inhibition of TS due to cofactor depletion

Why N5-formyl-THF (Leucovorin) rescues it:

  • Leucovorin = N5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate, a fully reduced folate that bypasses DHFR entirely
  • It gets converted intracellularly to N5,N10-methylene-THF, replenishing the folate cofactor pool
  • This is literally the basis of "Leucovorin rescue" used clinically with high-dose MTX therapy to protect normal cells while preserving the antitumor effect in cancer cells (which have differential uptake/retention)

Drug Y = Fluorouracil (5-FU)

Mechanism: 5-FU is converted to FdUMP (5-fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate), which forms a stable covalent ternary complex with:

  1. Thymidylate synthase enzyme itself, AND
  2. The folate cofactor N5,N10-methylene-THF

This ternary complex directly and covalently inhibits TS — it's a direct enzyme inhibitor, not a cofactor-depletion mechanism.
Why Leucovorin does NOT reverse 5-FU toxicity:

  • Since 5-FU/FdUMP binds TS directly, simply adding more folate doesn't displace the inhibitor
  • In fact — clinically important twist — Leucovorin is often co-administered WITH 5-FU, but for the opposite reason: it enhances/potentiates 5-FU's cytotoxicity by stabilizing the ternary complex (more folate → more stable inhibitory complex → ↑ TS inhibition). This is the basis of the FOLFOX/FOLFIRI regimens.

| Mechanism | Folate cofactor depletion | Covalent ternary complex formation |
| Effect of Leucovorin | Reverses/rescues toxicity | Potentiates cytotoxicity (no rescue) |

Correct answer: C. Ondansetron

Apomorphine + Ondansetron = profound, severe hypotension and loss of consciousness (syncope) — this is a well-documented, black-box/contraindicated combination.
Mechanism: Both drugs act on 5-HT3 receptor pathways involved in blood pressure regulation via the Bezold-Jarisch reflex (a cardioinhibitory reflex triggered by 5-HT3 receptor activation in the heart/vagal afferents → bradycardia + hypotension). When apomorphine (which itself can cause hypotension via central D2 effects) is combined with a 5-HT3 antagonist like ondansetron, this reflex is potentiated → severe synergistic hypotension and syncope.
This is why apomorphine + ondansetron (or any 5-HT3 antagonist: granisetron, palonosetron) is an absolute contraindication.

questions.raw_text: Which drug acts by inhibiting calcineurin and thereby decreasing IL-2 synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cyclosporine

Cyclosporine binds the intracellular immunophilin cyclophilin; the drug–cyclophilin complex inhibits the phosphatase calcineurin. Calcineurin normally dephosphorylates NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T cells), allowing it to enter the nucleus and transcribe IL-2. Blocking calcineurin therefore prevents IL-2 gene transcription → failure of T-helper cell activation and clonal proliferation. Tacrolimus works identically but binds FKBP-12 instead.

Other options:

  • A. Sirolimus: Also binds FKBP-12, but the complex inhibits mTOR, blocking the signal from the IL-2 receptor — i.e., it blocks IL-2 response, not IL-2 synthesis.
  • C. Glucocorticoids: Inhibit NF-κB → broadly ↓ cytokines (IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, TNF-α); not a calcineurin action.
  • D. Azathioprine → converted to 6-MP → inhibits purine synthesis → antiproliferative (S-phase).

Toxicity pearl:

  • Cyclosporine → nephrotoxicity, hypertension, gum hyperplasia, hirsutism.
  • Tacrolimus → more neurotoxicity and diabetogenicity, but no gum hyperplasia or hirsutism.

questions.text: Two antineoplastic drugs a​re shown to inhibit intra​cellular thymidylate form‌ation. The chemotherapeut‌ic effect of drug X can b​e overcome by Ns-formyl-t​etrahydrofolate supplemen‌tation, but that of drug ‌Y is not affected. questions.raw_text: Two antineoplastic drugs are shown to inhibit intracellular thymidylate formation. The chemotherapeutic effect of drug X can be overcome by Ns-formyl-tetrahydrofolate supplementation, but that of drug Y is not affected. The drugs described in this scenario are most likely which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. X: Methotrexate Y: Fluorouracil

Both drugs ultimately inhibit thymidylate synthase (TS), the enzyme that converts dUMP → dTMP (thymidylate), but they hit the pathway at different points — which is exactly why their rescue requirements differ.

Drug X = Methotrexate

Mechanism: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking the regeneration of tetrahydrofolate (THF) from dihydrofolate (DHF).

  • Thymidylate synthase requires N5,N10-methylene-THF as a cofactor to convert dUMP → dTMP
  • When MTX blocks DHFR, the cell runs out of usable THF → no folate cofactor available → thymidylate synthase can't function → indirect inhibition of TS due to cofactor depletion

Why N5-formyl-THF (Leucovorin) rescues it:

  • Leucovorin = N5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate, a fully reduced folate that bypasses DHFR entirely
  • It gets converted intracellularly to N5,N10-methylene-THF, replenishing the folate cofactor pool
  • This is literally the basis of "Leucovorin rescue" used clinically with high-dose MTX therapy to protect normal cells while preserving the antitumor effect in cancer cells (which have differential uptake/retention)

Drug Y = Fluorouracil (5-FU)

Mechanism: 5-FU is converted to FdUMP (5-fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate), which forms a stable covalent ternary complex with:

  1. Thymidylate synthase enzyme itself, AND
  2. The folate cofactor N5,N10-methylene-THF

This ternary complex directly and covalently inhibits TS — it's a direct enzyme inhibitor, not a cofactor-depletion mechanism.
Why Leucovorin does NOT reverse 5-FU toxicity:

  • Since 5-FU/FdUMP binds TS directly, simply adding more folate doesn't displace the inhibitor
  • In fact — clinically important twist — Leucovorin is often co-administered WITH 5-FU, but for the opposite reason: it enhances/potentiates 5-FU's cytotoxicity by stabilizing the ternary complex (more folate → more stable inhibitory complex → ↑ TS inhibition). This is the basis of the FOLFOX/FOLFIRI regimens.

Side-by-Side Comparison

| Feature | Methotrexate (X) | Fluorouracil (Y) |
| ------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| Target | DHFR (indirect TS inhibition) | TS directly (via FdUMP) |
| Mechanism | Folate cofactor depletion | Covalent ternary complex formation |
| Effect of Leucovorin | Reverses/rescues toxicity | Potentiates cytotoxicity (no rescue) |
| Clinical use of Leucovorin | "Leucovorin rescue" in high-dose MTX | Combined for synergy (FOLFOX, FOLFIRI) |

questions.raw_text: A 60-year-old male patient was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate. The medication charts reveal that he was taking digoxin, potassium chloride, clarithromycin, atenolol, and triamterene. Suspecting the symptoms to be due to digoxin overdose, plasma levels of digoxin were ordered. It was found that his blood levels of digoxin have increased significantly. Which of his medications is most likely responsible for this increase in digoxin levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clarithromycin

Mechanism:
Clarithromycin (a macrolide) raises digoxin levels through two mechanisms, both classic teaching points:

  1. P-glycoprotein inhibition: Digoxin is a substrate of P-gp (efflux transporter) in the gut wall and renal tubules. Macrolides like clarithromycin and erythromycin inhibit P-gp, reducing digoxin's efflux back into the gut lumen and its renal excretion → increased absorption and decreased clearance → increased plasma levels.
  2. Elimination of gut flora: In about 10% of the population, gut bacteria (notably Eubacterium lentum) metabolize digoxin in the intestine before it can be absorbed. Clarithromycin wipes out this flora, so more unmetabolized digoxin gets absorbed, further raising levels.

This is a well-documented and clinically significant interaction — macrolide + digoxin is a classic "avoid or monitor closely" combination.

Why the others are distractors, not the answer?

| Option | Relevance to the vignette |
| ------ | ------------------------- |
| A) Potassium chloride | Doesn't raise digoxin levels — in fact, hypokalemia (not hyperkalemia) potentiates digoxin toxicity by increasing its binding to Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. KCl would be protective against toxicity, not causative of elevated levels |
| C) Atenolol | Beta-blocker; additive AV nodal blockade with digoxin (bradycardia risk) but doesn't alter digoxin pharmacokinetics/levels |
| D) Triamterene | Potassium-sparing diuretic; relevant because it prevents hypokalemia (again protective against toxicity), not a P-gp inhibitor — doesn't raise digoxin levels |

High-yield takeaway for the question bank: Any question testing "drug that increases digoxin levels" should trigger recall of the P-gp inhibitor list — quinidine, verapamil, amiodarone, and macrolides (clarithromycin/erythromycin) are the classic culprits. questions.raw_text:
A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 8 hours after an intentional overdose of morphine. He is drowsy, has pinpoint pupils, and a respiratory rate of 8/min. The following pharmacokinetic parameters are known:

•	Half-life (t½) of morphine = 4 hours 
•	Volume of distribution (Vd) = 150 L 
•	Current plasma morphine concentration = 0.5 µg/mL 

Assuming first-order elimination, what was the approximate initial dose of morphine ingested?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 300 mg

Step 1: Determine the number of half-lives elapsed

  • Time since ingestion = 8 hours
  • Half-life = 4 hours

→ 2 half-lives

After 2 half-lives:

  • Remaining fraction = 1/4

Therefore, Initial concentration = 0.5 × 4 = 2 µg/mL

Step 2: Calculate the initial amount of drug

  • Dose = Initial concentration × Volume of distribution

Convert units:

  • 2 µg/mL = 2 mg/L
  • Vd = 150 L

Dose = 2 mg/L × 150 L = 300 mg
✅ Correct answer: 300 mg

High-yield formula

  • Initial concentration = Measured concentration × 2ⁿ (where n = number of half-lives elapsed)
  • Dose = Initial concentration × Vd

questions.text: A medication is administer​ed orally and has a 40% a‍bsorption rate. If the he‍patic extraction ratio of‌ the drug is 0.6, what wo​uld be its systemic bioav​ailability?
questions.raw_text: A medication is administered orally and has a 40% absorption rate. If the hepatic extraction ratio of the drug is 0.6, what would be its systemic bioavailability?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 16 percent

Systemic bioavailability depends on the fraction of drug absorbed and the fraction escaping first-pass metabolism. For an orally administered drug, the systemic bioavailability (F) is calculated as:
 F = Fractional absorption × (1 - Hepatic extraction ratio)

In this case:

  • Fractional absorption = 0.40 (40%)
  • Hepatic extraction ratio = 0.60
  • F = 0.40 × (1 - 0.60)
  • F = 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.16 or 16%

Other Options:

  • Option B - 24% would result if we used 0.60 instead of 0.40 for the fraction escaping first-pass metabolism.
  • Option C - 4% would result if we multiplied the absorption rate by the hepatic extraction ratio (0.40 × 0.10)\, which is the incorrect formula.
  • Option D - 60% is simply the hepatic extraction ratio\, not the bioavailability.

Educational Objective:

  • Systemic bioavailability of orally administered drugs depends on both the fraction absorbed from the GI tract and the fraction that escapes first-pass metabolism in the liver, calculated as: F = Fractional absorption × (1 - Hepatic extraction ratio)

questions.text: A medication is administer​ed orally and has a 40% a​bsorption rate. If the he​patic extraction ratio of‌ the drug is 0.6, what wo‍uld be its systemic bioav​ailability?
questions.raw_text: A medication is administered orally and has a 40% absorption rate. If the hepatic extraction ratio of the drug is 0.6, what would be its systemic bioavailability?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 16 percent

Systemic bioavailability depends on the fraction of drug absorbed and the fraction escaping first-pass metabolism. For an orally administered drug, the systemic bioavailability (F) is calculated as:
 F = Fractional absorption × (1 - Hepatic extraction ratio)

In this case:

  • Fractional absorption = 0.40 (40%)
  • Hepatic extraction ratio = 0.60
  • F = 0.40 × (1 - 0.60)
  • F = 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.16 or 16%

Other Options:

  • Option B - 24% would result if we used 0.60 instead of 0.40 for the fraction escaping first-pass metabolism.
  • Option C - 4% would result if we multiplied the absorption rate by the hepatic extraction ratio (0.40 × 0.10)\, which is the incorrect formula.
  • Option D - 60% is simply the hepatic extraction ratio\, not the bioavailability.

Educational Objective:

  • Systemic bioavailability of orally administered drugs depends on both the fraction absorbed from the GI tract and the fraction that escapes first-pass metabolism in the liver, calculated as: F = Fractional absorption × (1 - Hepatic extraction ratio)

questions.text: A medication is administer‌ed orally and has a 40% a‍bsorption rate. If the he‌patic extraction ratio of​ the drug is 0.6, what wo‍uld be its systemic bioav‍ailability?
questions.raw_text: A medication is administered orally and has a 40% absorption rate. If the hepatic extraction ratio of the drug is 0.6, what would be its systemic bioavailability?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 16 percent

Systemic bioavailability depends on the fraction of drug absorbed and the fraction escaping first-pass metabolism. For an orally administered drug, the systemic bioavailability (F) is calculated as:
 F = Fractional absorption × (1 - Hepatic extraction ratio)

In this case:

  • Fractional absorption = 0.40 (40%)
  • Hepatic extraction ratio = 0.60
  • F = 0.40 × (1 - 0.60)
  • F = 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.16 or 16%

Other Options:

  • Option B - 24% would result if we used 0.60 instead of 0.40 for the fraction escaping first-pass metabolism.
  • Option C - 4% would result if we multiplied the absorption rate by the hepatic extraction ratio (0.40 × 0.10)\, which is the incorrect formula.
  • Option D - 60% is simply the hepatic extraction ratio\, not the bioavailability.

Educational Objective:

  • Systemic bioavailability of orally administered drugs depends on both the fraction absorbed from the GI tract and the fraction that escapes first-pass metabolism in the liver, calculated as: F = Fractional absorption × (1 - Hepatic extraction ratio)

questions.raw_text: Two antineoplastic drugs are shown to inhibit intracellular thymidylate formation. The chemotherapeutic effect of drug X can be overcome by Ns-formyl-tetrahydrofolate supplementation, but that of drug Y is not affected. The drugs described in this scenario are most likely which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. X: Methotrexate Y: Fluorouracil

Both drugs ultimately inhibit thymidylate synthase (TS), the enzyme that converts dUMP → dTMP (thymidylate), but they hit the pathway at different points — which is exactly why their rescue requirements differ.

Drug X = Methotrexate

Mechanism: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking the regeneration of tetrahydrofolate (THF) from dihydrofolate (DHF).

  • Thymidylate synthase requires N5,N10-methylene-THF as a cofactor to convert dUMP → dTMP
  • When MTX blocks DHFR, the cell runs out of usable THF → no folate cofactor available → thymidylate synthase can't function → indirect inhibition of TS due to cofactor depletion

Why N5-formyl-THF (Leucovorin) rescues it:

  • Leucovorin = N5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate, a fully reduced folate that bypasses DHFR entirely
  • It gets converted intracellularly to N5,N10-methylene-THF, replenishing the folate cofactor pool
  • This is literally the basis of "Leucovorin rescue" used clinically with high-dose MTX therapy to protect normal cells while preserving the antitumor effect in cancer cells (which have differential uptake/retention)

Drug Y = Fluorouracil (5-FU)

Mechanism: 5-FU is converted to FdUMP (5-fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate), which forms a stable covalent ternary complex with:

  1. Thymidylate synthase enzyme itself, AND
  2. The folate cofactor N5,N10-methylene-THF

This ternary complex directly and covalently inhibits TS — it's a direct enzyme inhibitor, not a cofactor-depletion mechanism.
Why Leucovorin does NOT reverse 5-FU toxicity:

  • Since 5-FU/FdUMP binds TS directly, simply adding more folate doesn't displace the inhibitor
  • In fact — clinically important twist — Leucovorin is often co-administered WITH 5-FU, but for the opposite reason: it enhances/potentiates 5-FU's cytotoxicity by stabilizing the ternary complex (more folate → more stable inhibitory complex → ↑ TS inhibition). This is the basis of the FOLFOX/FOLFIRI regimens.

| Mechanism | Folate cofactor depletion | Covalent ternary complex formation |
| Effect of Leucovorin | Reverses/rescues toxicity | Potentiates cytotoxicity (no rescue) |
| Clinical use of Leucovorin | "Leucovorin rescue" in high-dose MTX | Combined for synergy (FOLFOX, FOLFIRI) |

questions.raw_text: Researchers are studying ion movement across the membrane of a resting skeletal muscle cell. The resting membrane potential (RMP) is measured at −70 mV. The equilibrium potentials of the major ions are given below. If selective ion channels are opened while all concentration gradients remain unchanged, which of the following ions would be expected to move out of the cell?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Potassium only

The direction of ion movement depends on the relationship between the membrane potential (Vm) and the equilibrium potential (Eion).

Rule:

  • If Vm > Eion (membrane is more positive than the ion's equilibrium potential), positive ions move out of the cell.
  • If Vm < Eion, positive ions move into the cell.
  • For Cl⁻ (a negative ion), the direction is opposite because of its negative charge.

Given:

  • Vm = −70 mV

Potassium (K⁺)

  • EK = −90 mV
  • Vm (−70) is more positive than EK (−90).
  • Therefore, K⁺ moves out of the cell.

Sodium (Na⁺)

  • ENa = +60 mV
  • Vm is much more negative than ENa.
  • Na⁺ moves into the cell.

Calcium (Ca²⁺)

  • ECa = +125 mV
  • Strong electrochemical gradient drives Ca²⁺ into the cell.

Magnesium (Mg²⁺)

  • EMg = 0 mV
  • Vm is more negative than EMg.
  • Mg²⁺ would move into the cell.

Chloride (Cl⁻)

  • ECl = −75 mV
  • Vm is slightly more positive than ECl.
  • Because chloride is negatively charged, it moves into the cell (opposite to the electrical driving force for cations).

Thus, only potassium leaves the cell.

Why the other options are incorrect?

  • A. Magnesium and calcium: Both would move into the cell.
  • B. Magnesium and chloride: Magnesium enters; chloride tends to move into the cell under these conditions.
  • C. Potassium and chloride: Potassium exits, but chloride does not.

High-yield pearl:
The driving force for an ion is: Driving force = Vm − Eion

  • Positive driving force → Cations move out
  • Negative driving force → Cations move in
  • Anions move in the opposite direction

If the diameter is reduced by 50%, the radius also becomes half of the original.

Small decreases in vessel radius dramatically increase resistance, which significantly reduces blood flow.

Hyperventilation-driven re‌spiratory alkalosis, caus‍ing a leftward shift of t‍he oxygen-hemoglobin diss‌ociation curve, followed ‍by renal compensation

| --------- | ----- | ------ |

| Size limit | Permits molecules <1 kDa (ions, cAMP, IP3, small metabolites) |
| Key locations | Cardiac muscle (intercalated discs), smooth muscle, lens fibers, hepatocytes, neurons (electrical synapses), beta cells of pancreas |
| Functional role | Electrical coupling, metabolic coupling, synchronized contraction |
| Regulation | Closed by ↑intracellular Ca²⁺, ↓pH (acidosis); important in limiting injury spread after cell damage |

The equilibrium potentials of the major ions are given below. If selective ion channels are opened while all concentration gradients remain unchanged, which of the following ions would be expected to move out of the cell?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Potassium only

The direction of ion movement depends on the relationship between the membrane potential (Vm) and the equilibrium potential (Eion).

Rule:

  • If Vm > Eion (membrane is more positive than the ion's equilibrium potential), positive ions move out of the cell.
  • If Vm < Eion, positive ions move into the cell.
  • For Cl⁻ (a negative ion), the direction is opposite because of its negative charge.

Given:

  • Vm = −70 mV

Potassium (K⁺)

  • EK = −90 mV
  • Vm (−70) is more positive than EK (−90).
  • Therefore, K⁺ moves out of the cell.

Sodium (Na⁺)

  • ENa = +60 mV
  • Vm is much more negative than ENa.
  • Na⁺ moves into the cell.

Calcium (Ca²⁺)

  • ECa = +125 mV
  • Strong electrochemical gradient drives Ca²⁺ into the cell.

Magnesium (Mg²⁺)

  • EMg = 0 mV
  • Vm is more negative than EMg.
  • Mg²⁺ would move into the cell.

Chloride (Cl⁻)

  • ECl = −75 mV
  • Vm is slightly more positive than ECl.
  • Because chloride is negatively charged, it moves into the cell (opposite to the electrical driving force for cations).

Thus, only potassium leaves the cell.

Why the other options are incorrect?

  • A. Magnesium and calcium: Both would move into the cell.
  • B. Magnesium and chloride: Magnesium enters; chloride tends to move into the cell under these conditions.
  • C. Potassium and chloride: Potassium exits, but chloride does not.

High-yield pearl:
The driving force for an ion is: Driving force = Vm − Eion

  • Positive driving force → Cations move out
  • Negative driving force → Cations move in
  • Anions move in the opposite direction

According to the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction occurs because thin (actin) filaments slide inward over thick (myosin) filaments. The filaments themselves do not shorten; instead, the degree of overlap between them increases.

  1. Skeletal muscle contraction is initiated by calcium binding to troponin T. ❌ Incorrect
    • Calcium binds to troponin C (TnC), not troponin T (TnT).

  2. Skeletal muscle fibers contain a single nucleus. ❌ Incorrect
    • Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated due to fusion of myoblasts during development.
    • The nuclei are located peripherally beneath the sarcolemma.
  3. Skeletal muscle contractions are voluntary. ✅ Correct
    • Skeletal muscle is supplied by the somatic nervous system, making its contractions voluntary.
  4. Gap junctions are present in skeletal muscle. ❌ Incorrect
    • Skeletal muscle fibers function independently and lack gap junctions.
    • Gap junctions are characteristic of cardiac muscle (intercalated discs) and single-unit smooth muscle.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Little dependence on extracellular calcium influx

Skeletal muscle contraction is relatively resistant to calcium channel blockers such as verapamil because it relies primarily on intracellular calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum rather than extracellular calcium influx. In contrast, cardiac and smooth muscle require extracellular calcium entry through L-type calcium channels, making them sensitive to calcium channel blockade.

  • In skeletal muscle, depolarization of the T-tubule activates the dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR).
  • DHPR is mechanically coupled to the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  • This direct coupling triggers massive calcium release from intracellular stores.
  • Therefore, skeletal muscle contraction has minimal dependence on extracellular calcium influx, explaining its resistance to verapamil.

Why not the others?

  • A. Calmodulin-independent excitation-contraction coupling → True for skeletal muscle, but this does not explain resistance to calcium channel blockers.
  • B. Decreased troponin affinity to calcium → Not the mechanism responsible for verapamil resistance.
  • C. Elaborate T-tubular system → Facilitates excitation-contraction coupling but does not explain the lack of dependence on extracellular calcium.

All the following are properties of ventricular muscle fibers:

2.	Length-tension relation

All-or-None Law

  • Cardiac muscle behaves as a functional syncytium
  • Once threshold reached → entire ventricle contracts maximally
  • No graded contraction like skeletal motor units

Length–Tension Relationship

  • Mechanism:

    • ↑ Ca²⁺ sensitivity of myofilaments

Ventricular muscle behaves like a syncytium with unique electrical discipline.
It contracts as a unit, obeys Frank–Starling law, and absolutely refuses tetanus.
Cardiac action potential (with plateau)
↓
Prolonged Ca²⁺ influx (L-type channels)
↓
Long absolute refractory period
↓
No re-excitation possible
↓
No summation → No tetanus

  • Cardiac AP duration: \~200–300 ms
  • Contraction duration: overlaps with refractory period

So:

  • Second stimulus cannot trigger contraction
  • Prevents sustained contraction (which would be fatal)

| 1 | All-or-none law | ✅ YES | Entire myocardium contracts as a syncytium via gap junctions |

| 3 | Tetanus | ❌ NO | Prevented due to long refractory period |

The latent period of a muscle twitch is the short delay (≈2–5 ms) between stimulus application and start of contraction.
This period includes all events before actual cross-bridge cycling begins. The latent period represents the time between stimulus and onset of contraction and includes electrical and coupling events before tension develops. It covers impulse transmission to the NMJ, opening of Na⁺ channels with depolarization, and excitation–contraction coupling with Ca²⁺ release. Pumping Ca²⁺ back into the SR occurs during relaxation, not latency. Hence a, b, and c contribute to the latent period.
Stimulus applied
     ↓
Impulse travels along motor nerve (c)
     ↓
Acetylcholine release at NMJ → Na⁺ channels open (b)
     ↓
End plate potential → Muscle action potential
     ↓
T-tubule depolarization
     ↓
Ca²⁺ release from SR (Excitation-Contraction Coupling) (a)
     ↓
Actin-myosin interaction begins → Contraction starts
Latent period reflects 3 physiological delays:

  1. Neural delay
    • Nerve conduction time
  2. Synaptic delay (\~0.5 ms)
    • ACh release, diffusion, receptor binding
  3. E-C coupling delay
    • T-tubule depolarization
    • DHPR–RyR interaction
    • Ca²⁺ release

  • Maintains homeostasis

2. Feedforward Mechanism (Anticipatory)

  • Activated before actual disturbance
  • Based on prediction / external cues

  • Trigger: ↓ O₂ delivery
  • Body responds after deficit occurs

  • Trigger: ↑ plasma osmolality

Long absolute refractory period

No re-excitation possible

  • Prevents sustained contraction (which would be fatal)

Hyperventilation-driven re​spiratory alkalosis, caus‍ing a leftward shift of t‍he oxygen-hemoglobin diss‌ociation curve, followed ​by renal compensation
Increased renal erythropoi​etin secretion, causing a‍n immediate rise in hemog‍lobin concentration withi‌n hours

  • The earliest acclimatization response to high altitude hypoxia is hyperventilation, triggered by peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies) sensing the fall in arterial PO2. | --------- | ----- | ------ |
| Hyperventilation (chemoreceptor-driven) | Minutes–hours | ↓ PaCO2, respiratory alkalosis, ↑ PaO2 |
| Renal bicarbonate excretion | Days | Corrects pH toward normal, permits further hyperventilation |
| ↑ 2,3-BPG in RBCs | Days | Rightward shift of O2-Hb curve, improves tissue O2 unloading |
| ↑ Erythropoietin → ↑RBC mass | Days to weeks | ↑ Hemoglobin concentration, ↑O2-carrying capacity |
| ↑ Pulmonary vasoconstriction (hypoxic) | Hours–days | Can contribute to high-altitude pulmonary edema if excessive |

Correct answer: B. SAAG = 2.2 g/dL; suggests portal hypertension as the cause

Rationale: SAAG = Serum albumin − Ascitic fluid albumin = 3.2 − 1.0 = 2.2 g/dL. A SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension as the underlying mechanism (due to increased hydrostatic pressure pushing albumin-poor fluid into the peritoneal cavity, while albumin itself remains largely retained intravascularly) — classically seen in cirrhosis (as in this patient with a history of alcohol use), congestive heart failure, and Budd-Chiari syndrome. A SAAG <1.1 g/dL instead points toward non-portal hypertensive causes, where the peritoneum itself is diseased and "leaky" to albumin, such as peritoneal tuberculosis, peritoneal carcinomatosis, or pancreatitis-related ascites. Since this patient's SAAG is 2.2 g/dL (≥1.1), portal hypertension — not a non-portal hypertensive cause — is the correct interpretation, making options C and D incorrect despite their correct arithmetic of "high SAAG," and option A incorrect on calculation.
Quick reference — SAAG Interpretation:

| SAAG | Interpretation | Common Causes |
| ---- | -------------- | ------------- |
| ≥1.1 g/dL (High gradient) | Portal hypertension | Cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, CHF, Budd-Chiari syndrome, constrictive pericarditis, massive liver metastases |
| <1.1 g/dL (Low gradient) | Non-portal hypertensive (peritoneal disease) | Peritoneal tuberculosis, peritoneal carcinomatosis, pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome, serositis |

Formula: SAAG = Serum albumin − Ascitic fluid albumin (both measured on the same day)
Note: SAAG is far more accurate than the older "exudate vs transudate" (total protein-based) classification of ascites.

A 52-year-old man presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, migratory arthralgia, and intermittent fever. He also has hyperpigmentation and generalized lymphadenopathy. Duodenal biopsy is performed. Which of the following statements regarding Whipple disease are CORRECT?

E. Long-term antibiotic therapy is required for definitive treatment
F. Causes disturbance in lymphatic transport of absorbed lipids

options.text: A, B, C,‌ D, E, F

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A, C, E, F

Whipple disease is a rare systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that primarily affects the small intestine and can involve multiple organ systems.

  • Chronic diarrhea and weight loss
  • Migratory polyarthritis (often precedes GI symptoms)
  • Fever, lymphadenopathy, hyperpigmentation
  • Malabsorption

Pathophysiology:

  • Infiltration of the intestinal mucosa by infected macrophages
  • Leads to impaired lymphatic transport of absorbed lipids, causing malabsorption.

Diagnosis:

  • Duodenal biopsy (classically PAS-positive macrophages, though not included in the correct set here)
  • PCR for Tropheryma whipplei

Treatment:

  • Requires prolonged antibiotic therapy (often ≥1 year) to prevent relapse and CNS involvement.

Wilson's disease (Hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13.

  • ↑ 24-hour urinary copper excretion (>100 μg/day)
  • ↑ Hepatic copper concentration (>250 μg/g dry weight)
  • Increased free (non-ceruloplasmin-bound) serum copper

1. Hepatocyte injury

  • Ballooning degeneration – most characteristic finding; hepatocytes swollen with clear, rarefied cytoplasm, sometimes with wispy strands ("moth-eaten" appearance)
  • Councilman bodies (acidophil bodies) – individual apoptotic hepatocytes, shrunken, deeply eosinophilic, with pyknotic or absent nucleus
  • Spotty (focal) necrosis – scattered single-cell death throughout the lobule
  • Confluent necrosis in more severe disease — may bridge portal-portal, portal-central, or central-central regions
  • Panacinar/massive necrosis in fulminant hepatitis

2. Inflammation

  • Lobular disarray with mixed mononuclear infiltrate — predominantly lymphocytes, plus macrophages and occasional plasma cells
  • Inflammation involves both lobules and portal tracts (unlike chronic hepatitis where portal/periportal predominates)
  • Kupffer cell hypertrophy/hyperplasia with pigment (lipofuscin) — reflects phagocytosis of debris from dead hepatocytes

3. Cholestasis

  • Mild canalicular cholestasis (bile plugs) can occur, more marked in cholestatic variants of hepatitis (e.g., Hepatitis A)

4. Regeneration

  • Hepatocyte regeneration with mitotic figures, occasional rosette formation
  • Variation in hepatocyte size (anisocytosis) as regenerating cells proliferate

5. Architecture

  • Lobular architecture usually preserved
  • No fibrosis in uncomplicated acute disease (fibrosis = chronic hepatitis)

He has a history of alcohol abuse, peptic ulcer disease, and acute pancreatitis. Physical examination shows a distended abdomen with shifting dullness and 1+ ankle edema. •	Albumin-2.5 g/dL
•	Neutrophils-200/uL

•	Albumin-3.8 g/dL
•	Glucose-120 mg/dL

•	Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)-40 units/L

questions.correct_answer: B. Increased hepatic capillary hydrostatic pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased hepatic capillary hydrostatic pressure

Ascites can be evaluated using the serum–ascites albumin gradient (SAAG), which helps determine whether portal hypertension is present.

SAAG = Serum albumin − Ascitic fluid albumin = 3.8 − 2.5 = 1.3 g/dL

  • SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension.
  • SAAG < 1.1 g/dL suggests non–portal hypertensive causes (eg, malignancy, pancreatitis, tuberculosis).

In portal hypertension, ascites forms due to increased hydrostatic pressure in hepatic sinusoids, causing fluid to leak into the peritoneal cavity.

Clinical context:

  • History of alcohol abuse suggests alcoholic liver disease leading to portal hypertension.
  • Neutrophil count <250 cells/µL excludes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) enhances the absorption of non-heme iron by reducing ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to the more readily absorbable ferrous form (Fe²⁺) and maintaining an acidic gastric environment.   • Vitamin B₁₂: Required for DNA synthesis and treatment of megaloblastic anemia, not iron deficiency anemia unless B₁₂ deficiency also exists.
  • Vitamin D: Important for calcium and bone metabolism; has no significant role in improving iron absorption.

Correct answer: C. HCl deficiency

Long-term proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy suppresses gastric acid (HCl) secretion, which reduces the conversion of dietary ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to the absorbable ferrous form (Fe²⁺). As a result, iron absorption decreases, predisposing patients to iron deficiency anemia, which presents with pallor and fatigue. Prolonged PPI use may also reduce the absorption of vitamin B₁₂, calcium, and magnesium.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Gastrin deficiency: Incorrect. PPIs actually cause hypergastrinemia due to loss of acid-mediated negative feedback.
  • B. Secretin overactivity: Incorrect. Secretin regulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and has no significant role in iron absorption or PPI-induced anemia.
  • D. Intrinsic factor deficiency: Incorrect. Intrinsic factor is produced by parietal cells and is required for vitamin B₁₂ absorption. PPIs do not directly reduce intrinsic factor production, although prolonged acid suppression can impair the release of vitamin B₁₂ from dietary proteins.

  • Erythromycin

The liver is palpated 1.5 cm below the right costal margin. A biopsy specimen of this patient's liver would most likely show which of the following findings?

Correct answer: B. Ballooning degeneration

1. Hepatocyte injury

  • Ballooning degeneration – most characteristic finding; hepatocytes swollen with clear, rarefied cytoplasm, sometimes with wispy strands ("moth-eaten" appearance)
  • Councilman bodies (acidophil bodies) – individual apoptotic hepatocytes, shrunken, deeply eosinophilic, with pyknotic or absent nucleus
  • Spotty (focal) necrosis – scattered single-cell death throughout the lobule
  • Confluent necrosis in more severe disease — may bridge portal-portal, portal-central, or central-central regions
  • Panacinar/massive necrosis in fulminant hepatitis

2. Inflammation

  • Lobular disarray with mixed mononuclear infiltrate — predominantly lymphocytes, plus macrophages and occasional plasma cells
  • Inflammation involves both lobules and portal tracts (unlike chronic hepatitis where portal/periportal predominates)
  • Kupffer cell hypertrophy/hyperplasia with pigment (lipofuscin) — reflects phagocytosis of debris from dead hepatocytes

3. Cholestasis

  • Mild canalicular cholestasis (bile plugs) can occur, more marked in cholestatic variants of hepatitis (e.g., Hepatitis A)

4. Regeneration

  • Hepatocyte regeneration with mitotic figures, occasional rosette formation
  • Variation in hepatocyte size (anisocytosis) as regenerating cells proliferate

5. Architecture

  • Lobular architecture usually preserved
  • No fibrosis in uncomplicated acute disease (fibrosis = chronic hepatitis)

  • Organism is fragile
  • Killed by storage at 4°C
  • Transmission mainly via fresh blood only

Correct answer: D. Multiple myeloma with elevated IgM

How to Read This Immunofixation Electrophoresis (IFE)

The lanes are: ELP \| G \| A \| M \| K \| L

  • ELP = total protein (all bands visible)
  • G = IgG, A = IgA, M = IgM, K = Kappa, L = Lambda

What the image shows:

| Lane | Band Present? | Interpretation |
| ---- | ------------- | -------------- |
| ELP | ✅ Strong band | M-spike confirmed |
| G (IgG) | ✅ Faint/broad | Non-specific, polyclonal background |
| A (IgA) | ❌ Very faint | Negative |
| M (IgM) | ✅ Distinct dark band | Monoclonal IgM ✅ |
| K (Kappa) | ✅ Distinct dark band | Monoclonal Kappa ✅ |
| L (Lambda) | ❌ Absent | Negative |

Monoclonal IgM-Kappa = the paraprotein is IgM with Kappa light chain

Why Students Pick IgG (Option C) — The Trap

The G lane appears to have a band, but it is broad and diffuse — this is polyclonal background, not a monoclonal spike.

| Monoclonal band | Polyclonal band |
| --------------- | --------------- |
| Sharp, discrete, well-defined | Broad, smeared, diffuse |
| Aligns perfectly across ELP + heavy chain + light chain | Doesn't co-migrate cleanly |
| Seen in myeloma/Waldenström | Seen in infection, inflammation |

The rule: A true monoclonal protein shows a band in ELP + one heavy chain lane + one light chain lane, all at the same migration level.
Here: ELP + M + K all align → IgM-Kappa monoclonal protein.

questions.raw_text: A 12-year-old boy presents with recurrent bleeding into the joints since childhood. There is no history of mucocutaneous bleeding. Family history reveals similar symptoms in a maternal male relative. Laboratory investigations show normal platelet count, normal bleeding time, prolonged aPTT, normal PT, normal ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation, and a 50% reduction in Factor VIII levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hemophilia A

Hemophilia A, an X-linked recessive deficiency of Factor VIII, which presents with deep tissue bleeding, especially recurrent hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints) and intramuscular hematomas. The diagnosis is suggested by a positive family history in maternal male relatives, isolated prolonged aPTT, normal PT and platelet function, and reduced Factor VIII levels.
•        Laboratory findings: ↑ aPTT, normal PT, normal bleeding time, normal platelet count, normal ristocetin test.
•        Diagnosis: Low Factor VIII activity; mixing study corrects the prolonged aPTT (unless inhibitors are present).
•        Treatment: Recombinant Factor VIII replacement, desmopressin (DDAVP) for mild disease, and emicizumab for prophylaxis in selected patients.
Why not the other options?

  • B. Von Willebrand disease: Causes mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, easy bruising), prolonged bleeding time, abnormal ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation, and may have mildly reduced Factor VIII.
  • C. Glanzmann thrombasthenia: Defect of GpIIb/IIIa causing impaired platelet aggregation; presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, normal platelet count, prolonged bleeding time, and normal coagulation tests.
  • D. Bernard–Soulier syndrome: Defect of GpIb causing impaired platelet adhesion; presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, thrombocytopenia with giant platelets, prolonged bleeding time, and abnormal ristocetin test.

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia due to IgG-mediated destruction of platelets. The bone marrow responds with compensatory megakaryocytic hyperplasia, resulting in increased megakaryocytes. Since the coagulation cascade is unaffected, PT and aPTT remain normal.

Key differentiating features:

  • ITP:
    • Isolated thrombocytopenia
    • Normal PT and aPTT
    • Increased megakaryocytes in bone marrow
    • Petechiae, purpura, mucosal bleeding
  • Dengue:
    • Thrombocytopenia with fever, often accompanied by leukopenia, hemoconcentration, and positive NS1/IgM tests.
  • Hemophilia:
    • Normal platelet count
    • Prolonged aPTT
    • Deep tissue and joint bleeding (hemarthrosis)
  • Thalassemia:
    • Microcytic hemolytic anemia, not isolated thrombocytopenia.

questions.raw_text:
With regard to management of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, consider the following statements:

I. All patients with ITP with platelet count less than 100 × 10⁹/L should receive high dose glucocorticoids.
II. For patient with spontaneous bleeding, 40 mg of dexamethasone daily is indicated for 4 days.
III. Intravenous immunoglobulin can raise the platelet count.
IV. Life-threatening bleeding should be treated with platelet transfusion.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II, III and IV

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100 × 10⁹/L) due to autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction and impaired platelet production. Treatment is based on the severity of thrombocytopenia and the presence of bleeding, not the platelet count alone.

  • I. All patients with ITP with platelet count <100 × 10⁹/L should receive high-dose glucocorticoids:
    • Incorrect. Not all patients require treatment. Patients with mild thrombocytopenia and no bleeding may be observed. Treatment is indicated for clinically significant bleeding or platelet count <20–30 × 10⁹/L.
  • II. For patients with spontaneous bleeding, 40 mg of dexamethasone daily is indicated for 4 days:
    • High-dose dexamethasone (40 mg/day for 4 days) is a standard first-line corticosteroid regimen in adults with symptomatic ITP.
  • III. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) can raise the platelet count:
    • IVIG rapidly increases platelet counts by blocking Fc receptor-mediated platelet destruction and is used when a rapid platelet rise is required.
  • IV. Life-threatening bleeding should be treated with platelet transfusion:
    • Platelet transfusion is indicated only in life-threatening bleeding and should be combined with IV corticosteroids and IVIG, as transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed.

How to Read This Immunofixation Electrophoresis (IFE)

The lanes are: ELP \| G \| A \| M \| K \| L

  • ELP = total protein (all bands visible)
  • G = IgG, A = IgA, M = IgM, K = Kappa, L = Lambda

What the image shows:

| Lane | Band Present? | Interpretation |
| ---- | ------------- | -------------- |
| ELP | ✅ Strong band | M-spike confirmed |
| G (IgG) | ✅ Faint/broad | Non-specific, polyclonal background |
| A (IgA) | ❌ Very faint | Negative |
| M (IgM) | ✅ Distinct dark band | Monoclonal IgM ✅ |
| K (Kappa) | ✅ Distinct dark band | Monoclonal Kappa ✅ |
| L (Lambda) | ❌ Absent | Negative |

Monoclonal IgM-Kappa = the paraprotein is IgM with Kappa light chain

Why Students Pick IgG (Option C) — The Trap

The G lane appears to have a band, but it is broad and diffuse — this is polyclonal background, not a monoclonal spike.

| Monoclonal band | Polyclonal band |
| --------------- | --------------- |
| Sharp, discrete, well-defined | Broad, smeared, diffuse |
| Aligns perfectly across ELP + heavy chain + light chain | Doesn't co-migrate cleanly |
| Seen in myeloma/Waldenström | Seen in infection, inflammation |

The rule: A true monoclonal protein shows a band in ELP + one heavy chain lane + one light chain lane, all at the same migration level.
Here: ELP + M + K all align → IgM-Kappa monoclonal protein.

The lanes are: ELP \| G \| A \| M \| K \| L

  • ELP = total protein (all bands visible)

| Lane | Band Present? | Interpretation |

| K (Kappa) | ✅ Distinct dark band | Monoclonal Kappa ✅ |
| L (Lambda) | ❌ Absent | Negative |

Monoclonal IgM-Kappa = the paraprotein is IgM with Kappa light chain

Why Students Pick IgG (Option C) — The Trap

The G lane appears to have a band, but it is broad and diffuse — this is polyclonal background, not a monoclonal spike.

| Monoclonal band | Polyclonal band |
| --------------- | --------------- |
| Sharp, discrete, well-defined | Broad, smeared, diffuse |
| Aligns perfectly across ELP + heavy chain + light chain | Doesn't co-migrate cleanly |
| Seen in myeloma/Waldenström | Seen in infection, inflammation |

The rule: A true monoclonal protein shows a band in ELP + one heavy chain lane + one light chain lane, all at the same migration level.

I. All patients with ITP with platelet count less than 100 × 10⁹/L should receive high dose glucocorticoids.

III. Intravenous immunoglobulin can raise the platelet count.
IV. Life-threatening bleeding should be treated with platelet transfusion.

Correct answer: B. II, III and IV

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100 × 10⁹/L) due to autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction and impaired platelet production. Treatment is based on the severity of thrombocytopenia and the presence of bleeding, not the platelet count alone.

  • I. All patients with ITP with platelet count <100 × 10⁹/L should receive high-dose glucocorticoids:
    • Incorrect. Not all patients require treatment. Patients with mild thrombocytopenia and no bleeding may be observed. Treatment is indicated for clinically significant bleeding or platelet count <20–30 × 10⁹/L.
  • II. For patients with spontaneous bleeding, 40 mg of dexamethasone daily is indicated for 4 days:
    • High-dose dexamethasone (40 mg/day for 4 days) is a standard first-line corticosteroid regimen in adults with symptomatic ITP.
  • III. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) can raise the platelet count:
    • IVIG rapidly increases platelet counts by blocking Fc receptor-mediated platelet destruction and is used when a rapid platelet rise is required.
  • IV. Life-threatening bleeding should be treated with platelet transfusion:
    • Platelet transfusion is indicated only in life-threatening bleeding and should be combined with IV corticosteroids and IVIG, as transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed.

2.	Macrophages 
3.	Neutrophils 
4.	Eosinophils
5.	CD4 lymphocytes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3, 4

Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is an immune mechanism in which effector cells destroy antibody-coated target cells.

  • Target cells are coated with IgG antibodies.
  • Immune cells bind the Fc portion of IgG via Fc receptors.
  • This triggers release of cytotoxic substances, leading to destruction of the target cell.

Cells involved in ADCC:

  • Natural killer (NK) cells
  • Neutrophils
  • Eosinophils (especially against parasites)

Not involved:

  • CD4 T lymphocytes, which function mainly in helper and regulatory roles, not cytotoxic killing.

Correct answer: D. Omenn syndrome

Omenn syndrome is a leaky (hypomorphic) form of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) caused by hypomorphic mutations in the RAG1 or RAG2 genes, resulting in defective V(D)J recombination.

Unlike classic SCID, some oligoclonal autoreactive T cells develop. These T cells infiltrate tissues and cause autoimmune-like manifestations.

Characteristic features include:

  • Recurrent severe infections
  • Generalized erythroderma
  • Chronic diarrhea
  • Failure to thrive
  • Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly
  • Eosinophilia and markedly elevated IgE
  • Absent or markedly reduced B cells
  • Presence of activated, oligoclonal T cells

Why the other options are incorrect?

  • A. X-linked agammaglobulinemia: Caused by BTK mutation, leading to absent mature B cells and recurrent bacterial infections after 6 months of age. Erythroderma, eosinophilia, and activated T cells are not typical.
  • B. DiGeorge syndrome: Results from 22q11.2 deletion causing thymic hypoplasia with T-cell deficiency, congenital heart defects, and hypocalcemia, but not elevated IgE with erythroderma.
  • C. Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID): Classic SCID is characterized by profound deficiency of functional T cells (often with absent T cells), whereas Omenn syndrome is a variant with autoreactive oligoclonal T cells, producing features of both immunodeficiency and immune dysregulation.

High-yield pearl
Omenn syndrome = "Leaky SCID"

  • Cause: Hypomorphic RAG1/RAG2 mutations
  • Defect: Impaired V(D)J recombination
  • Immune profile: ↓/Absent B cells + oligoclonal autoreactive T cells
  • Classic findings: Erythroderma + eosinophilia + ↑IgE + failure to thrive + recurrent infections
  • Definitive treatment: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)

| ------- | ------ |
| Inheritance | X-linked recessive (WAS gene, Xp11.23) |

| Mnemonic | "WIPE" — WAS gene, Immunodeficiency, Platelets low/small, Eczema |

Laboratory studies reveal marked eosinophilia, elevated serum IgE levels, markedly reduced B lymphocytes, and circulating activated oligoclonal T cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Omenn syndrome

Omenn syndrome is a leaky (hypomorphic) form of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) caused by hypomorphic mutations in the RAG1 or RAG2 genes, resulting in defective V(D)J recombination.

Unlike classic SCID, some oligoclonal autoreactive T cells develop. These T cells infiltrate tissues and cause autoimmune-like manifestations.

Characteristic features include:

  • Recurrent severe infections
  • Generalized erythroderma
  • Chronic diarrhea
  • Failure to thrive
  • Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly
  • Eosinophilia and markedly elevated IgE
  • Absent or markedly reduced B cells
  • Presence of activated, oligoclonal T cells

Why the other options are incorrect?

  • A. X-linked agammaglobulinemia: Caused by BTK mutation, leading to absent mature B cells and recurrent bacterial infections after 6 months of age. Erythroderma, eosinophilia, and activated T cells are not typical.
  • B. DiGeorge syndrome: Results from 22q11.2 deletion causing thymic hypoplasia with T-cell deficiency, congenital heart defects, and hypocalcemia, but not elevated IgE with erythroderma.
  • C. Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID): Classic SCID is characterized by profound deficiency of functional T cells (often with absent T cells), whereas Omenn syndrome is a variant with autoreactive oligoclonal T cells, producing features of both immunodeficiency and immune dysregulation.

High-yield pearl
Omenn syndrome = "Leaky SCID"

  • Cause: Hypomorphic RAG1/RAG2 mutations
  • Defect: Impaired V(D)J recombination
  • Immune profile: ↓/Absent B cells + oligoclonal autoreactive T cells
  • Classic findings: Erythroderma + eosinophilia + ↑IgE + failure to thrive + recurrent infections
  • Definitive treatment: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)

Myeloablative conditioning before allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) uses high-dose chemotherapy ± total body irradiation to:

Allelic exclusion ensures that each B cell expresses a single antigen receptor specificity by allowing productive rearrangement of only one immunoglobulin heavy-chain allele and one light-chain allele.

C) Alternative polyadenylation: Determines membrane-bound vs secreted antibody forms. Not related to allelic exclusion.
D) Somatic hypermutation: Occurs after antigen stimulation in germinal centers to increase antibody affinity. Not involved in initial allele selection.

Correct answer: A. Nitrofurantoin

A urinary antiseptic is a drug that achieves antibacterial concentrations only in urine, with negligible systemic (plasma/tissue) levels — hence it treats lower UTI/cystitis but never pyelonephritis or systemic infection.

Nitrofurantoin is the prototype: it is rapidly absorbed, concentrated by the kidney, and excreted into urine where it is reduced by bacterial nitroreductases into reactive intermediates that damage bacterial ribosomes, DNA and metabolic enzymes — a multi-target action, which explains its remarkably low resistance rate. It is safe in the first and second trimesters and is a preferred agent for asymptomatic bacteriuria/cystitis in pregnancy.

Other options:

  • B. Ciprofloxacin → fluoroquinolone; contraindicated in pregnancy (cartilage/arthropathy risk); it is a systemic antibiotic, not an antiseptic.
  • C. Doxycycline → contraindicated in pregnancy — teeth staining, enamel hypoplasia, bone growth inhibition, maternal hepatotoxicity.
  • D. Cotrimoxazole → avoid in 1st trimester (folate antagonism → neural tube defects) and near term (kernicterus).

Pearl:

  • Urinary antiseptics = Nitrofurantoin, Methenamine, Nalidixic acid.
  • Avoid nitrofurantoin at term (38 wk onwards) → risk of neonatal hemolysis (G6PD deficiency).

Microorganisms vary in their resistance to sterilization and disinfectants. The order from most resistant to least resistant is:

Prions > Bacterial spores > Mycobacteria > Naked (non-enveloped) viruses > Enveloped viruses

  • Prions are most resistant because they are misfolded proteins without nucleic acids, resistant to heat, radiation, and many disinfectants.
  • Bacterial spores (e.g., Bacillus, Clostridium) resist heat and chemicals due to thick protective coats and low metabolic activity.
  • Mycobacteria are moderately resistant because of their lipid-rich mycolic acid cell wall.
  • Naked viruses are more resistant than enveloped viruses since they lack a fragile lipid envelope.
  • Enveloped viruses are least resistant because their lipid envelope is easily destroyed by detergents, alcohol, and drying.
