questions.text: A woman receiving oxytocin‌ develops ≥5 uterine cont​ractions in 10 minutes as‌sociated with the followi‌ng pattern on CTG. What i‍s the next best step?
questions.raw_text: A woman receiving oxytocin develops ≥5 uterine contractions in 10 minutes associated with the following pattern on CTG. What is the next best step?

options.text: Intrauterine resuscitation‌ with stopping oxytocin a​nd left lateral position

questions.correct_answer: C. Intrauterine resuscitation with stopping oxytocin and left lateral position
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intrauterine resuscitation with stopping oxytocin and left lateral position

This CTG demonstrates uterine tachysystole/hyperstimulation (≥5 contractions in 10 minutes) associated with recurrent fetal heart rate decelerations, most likely due to excessive uterine activity from oxytocin.

  • ≥5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes
  • May reduce uteroplacental blood flow
  • Can lead to fetal hypoxia and abnormal CTG patterns

Immediate Management (Intrauterine Resuscitation)

  • Stop oxytocin infusion immediately
  • Place the mother in left lateral position
  • Administer IV fluids
  • Consider oxygen if maternal hypoxia is present
  • Consider tocolysis (e.g., terbutaline) if tachysystole persists

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

  • Increase oxytocin infusion: Worsens uterine hyperstimulation and fetal compromise.
  • Immediate forceps delivery: Only if delivery is imminent and indicated.
  • Artificial rupture of membranes: Does not correct tachysystole and may worsen fetal distress.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The cervicograph status suggests that intervention is likely to be required

A partograph (cervicograph) is used to monitor the progress of labor by plotting cervical dilatation against time. Important lines on the partograph:

  • Alert line → represents expected normal cervical dilatation
  • Action line → placed 4 hours to the right of the alert line and indicates need for intervention if crossed

In this patient:

  • Cervical dilatation progressed only from 4 cm to 5 cm in 4 hours
  • Fetal station remained unchanged
  • Cervicograph lies to the right of the alert line

This indicates abnormal or slow progress of labor and suggests that intervention may soon be required (eg, augmentation or operative delivery).
Additional concepts:

  • “3/5 head palpable per abdomen” means the head is not fully engaged
  • Engaged head usually corresponds to ≤2/5 palpable abdominally

The biophysical profile (BPP) is used to assess fetal well-being and includes five parameters, each scored as 0 or 2. Normal BPP parameters:

  2. Gross body movements

  3. Fetal tone

  • AFI 5–25 → not the standard BPP criterion
  • FHR acceleration >15 bpm → criterion for NST in term fetus but incomplete description
  • Two episodes of limb extension/flexion → only one episode is required for normal fetal tone

questions.text: A 28-year-old multigravida‌ is taught fetal movement​ counting. She asks what ‌“Cardiff count of 10” pra‌ctically means. Which ins‍truction is most accurate‍?
questions.raw_text: A 28-year-old multigravida is taught fetal movement counting. She asks what “Cardiff count of 10” practically means. Which instruction is most accurate?

options.text: 10 movements in 10 minutes‌ after a meal is reassuri​ng
At rest, 10 fetal movement‌s within 2 hours is reass​uring
10 movements in 12 hours i‌s required in all women
Maximum fetal movements oc‌cur at term, so counting ​is most useful after 40 w‌eeks

questions.correct_answer: B. At rest, 10 fetal movements within 2 hours is reassuring
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. At rest, 10 fetal movements within 2 hours is reassuring

The Cardiff “count-to-10” method instructs that fetal movements are counted daily, usually starting in the late 2nd to early 3rd trimester. The practical reassuring threshold is that 10 distinct fetal movements are perceived within 12 hours, and most fetuses achieve this much sooner. In day-to-day counselling and many exam stems, this is operationalized as “10 movements within 2 hours is reassuring,” and if 10 movements are not felt within the chosen counting window, reassessment and evaluation are advised. Among the given options, the most accurate practical instruction is that 10 movements within 2 hours at rest is reassuring.

Other options:
A. 10 movements in 10 minutes after a meal is reassuring
Incorrect. Ten movements in 10 minutes is not the Cardiff instruction and is too stringent and variable.

C. 10 movements in 12 hours is required in all women
This is closer to the original Cardiff framework, but the wording “required in all women” is not practical counselling. The method is to count until 10 are felt, usually within 12 hours, and the commonly used practical instruction is the 2-hour reassurance threshold.

D. Maximum fetal movements occur at term, so counting is most useful after 40 weeks
Incorrect. Counting is useful in the third trimester well before 40 weeks, and movements do not peak at 40 weeks in a way that makes counting uniquely useful only then.

questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravida‌ is in labor. The baselin​e FHR is 110bpm. All of t‌he following are possible‌ causes of fetal bradycar‍dia, except:
questions.raw_text: A 24-year-old primigravida is in labor. The baseline FHR is 110bpm. All of the following are possible causes of fetal bradycardia, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Maternal fever

Fetal bradycardia is defined as baseline fetal heart rate (FHR) <110 bpm for ≥10 minutes. It usually occurs due to reduced fetal oxygenation, fetal cardiac suppression, or maternal factors affecting fetal circulation.

Common causes of fetal bradycardia include:
• Maternal β-blocker therapy → crosses placenta and suppresses fetal heart rate
• Maternal hypothermia → decreases fetal metabolic rate and FHR
• Maternal hypoglycemia → reduces fetal energy supply leading to decreased FHR
• Fetal hypoxia/acidosis
• Cord compression
• Congenital heart block

Maternal fever, however, typically causes fetal tachycardia (>160 bpm) due to increased fetal metabolic rate and sympathetic stimulation (often seen in chorioamnionitis or maternal infection).

questions.text: During fetal heart rate mo‌nitoring, variable decele​rations are noted on the ‌CTG trace. What is the mo‌st likely cause or mechan‍ism of this finding?
questions.raw_text: During fetal heart rate monitoring, variable decelerations are noted on the CTG trace. What is the most likely cause or mechanism of this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cord compression

Cardiotocography detects changes in fetal heart rate patterns during labor.
Variable decelerations are abrupt decreases in fetal heart rate caused by Umbilical Cord Compression.
Variable decelerations on CTG indicate umbilical cord compression and are commonly associated with oligohydramnios. Early decelerations indicate fetal head compression, while late decelerations indicate fetal hypoxia from uteroplacental insufficiency.

Mechanism of Variable Decelerations
Umbilical cord compression
         ↓
Reduced blood flow to fetus
         ↓
Baroreceptor stimulation
         ↓
Sudden drop in fetal heart rate
This produces the characteristic abrupt V-shaped deceleration on CTG.

| Type | Cause | Pattern |
| ---- | ----- | ------- |
| Early deceleration | Head compression | Mirror of contraction |
| Variable deceleration | Cord compression | Abrupt V-shaped |
| Late deceleration | Uteroplacental insufficiency | Delayed after contraction |

Conditions Causing Cord Compression
Common causes include:

  • Oligohydramnios
  • Cord prolapse
  • Nuchal cord
  • Cord around limbs

Management of Variable Decelerations
Initial steps include:

  • Maternal position change
  • Oxygen administration
  • IV fluids
  • Amnioinfusion if severe

This leads to:

  • Fetal hypoxia
  • Maternal shock

| ---- | ----------- |
| Severe abdominal/suprapubic pain | Scar tearing |
| Maternal tachycardia | Blood loss |
| Fetal bradycardia | Fetal hypoxia |
| Loss of fetal station | Indicates complete rupture |

Fetal bradycardia is the most common early sign of uterine dehiscence/ rupture.

        ↓
Immediate resuscitation
        ↓
Emergency laparotomy
        ↓
Cesarean delivery
        ↓
Repair uterus or hysterectomy

The goal is rapid delivery to save the fetus and prevent maternal hemorrhage.

Bradycardia generally indicates fetal hypoxia or cardiac abnormalities.
Causes of Fetal Bradycardia

1. Placental Abruption
In Placental Abruption:

  • Placenta separates prematurely.
  • Causes acute fetal hypoxia.

2. Fetal Head Compression
Head compression during labor causes:

  • Vagal stimulation
  • Resulting in early decelerations on CTG.

These appear as temporary fetal heart rate slowing.

3. Congenital Heart Disease
Congenital cardiac defects can affect the fetal conduction system, producing:

  • Complete heart block
  • Persistent fetal bradycardia

Example:

  • Congenital AV block
  • Seen in maternal lupus (anti-Ro antibodies).

Maternal fever, especially in chorioamnionitis, causes:

  • Increased fetal metabolic rate
  • Sympathetic stimulation

Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR) is commonly caused by uteroplacental insufficiency, resulting in chronic fetal hypoxia. The fetus adapts by redistributing blood flow (“brain-sparing effect”) to vital organs such as the brain, heart, and adrenal glands, at the expense of the kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, and peripheral tissues.

She denies any rupture of membranes or vaginal bleeding. Fetal movements have been perceived normally. On initial examination, the cervix is 4 cm dilated, 80% effaced, with the fetal vertex at 0 station. She requests pain relief and receives epidural analgesia. Two hours after epidural placement, repeat examination shows the cervix to be 5 cm dilated and 100% effaced with the vertex at 0 station. A subsequent examination 2 hours later reveals no change in cervical dilation or fetal descent. Fetal heart rate tracing demonstrates:
•	Baseline: 138/min
•	Variability: moderate
•	Accelerations: present
•	Decelerations: sporadic early decelerations only
Uterine activity on tocometry shows contractions occurring every 6–8 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Proceed with cesarean deli‍very for arrest of active​ labor
Continue expectant managem‍ent for another 2 hours
Begin oxytocin infusion fo‍r augmentation of labor
Administer intravaginal mi‍soprostol for cervical ri​pening

questions.correct_answer: C. Begin oxytocin infusion for augmentation of labor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Begin oxytocin infusion for augmentation of labor

This patient is in the active phase of labor and has demonstrated inadequate labor progress after epidural analgesia.
Active Labor Arrest Criteria

  • No cervical change despite:
    • ≥6 cm dilatation and
    • Adequate uterine contractions for ≥4 hours, or
    • Inadequate contractions despite oxytocin for ≥6 hours

This patient does not yet meet criteria for active-phase arrest because contractions are inadequate.
Interpretation:

  • Labor progress is inadequate due to hypotonic uterine contractions (power dysfunction)
  • There is no evidence of fetal distress or cephalopelvic disproportion

Management:

  • Oxytocin augmentation should be initiated to increase contraction frequency and strength
  • Continuous fetal and uterine monitoring should be maintained

Why other options are incorrect?

  • Proceed with cesarean delivery for arrest of active labor: Cesarean delivery is not indicated because active-phase arrest requires adequate contractions before diagnosing labor arrest
  • Continue expectant management for another 2 hours: Expectant management may unnecessarily prolong labor when contractions are inadequate
  • Administer intravaginal misoprostol for cervical ripening: Misoprostol is used for cervical ripening and labor induction, not for augmentation of established labor

Correct answer: B. 2 mg

Prostaglandin F2 alpha (PGF2α), also known as carboprost, is used for the treatment of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) due to uterine atony. The therapeutic regimen and maximum dosage are crucial for effective management and patient safety.

  • Dose and Administration: The approved dose for treating uterine atony with PGF2α is 0.25 mg administered intramuscularly (IM).
  • Maximum Dose: The maximum cumulative dose is 2 mg. This is achieved by administering a total of 8 doses of 0.25 mg each.
  • Dosing Interval: These doses can be repeated at intervals of 15 to 90 minutes, depending on the clinical response and the patient's condition.

Contraindications

  • Bronchial Asthma: PGF2α can cause bronchoconstriction, which makes it contraindicated in patients with bronchial asthma.
  • Suspected Amniotic Fluid Embolism: Due to its potential to cause pulmonary airway and vascular constriction, it is also contraindicated in cases of suspected amniotic fluid embolism.

questions.text: Which of the following is ‍an absolute contraindicat​ion to TOLAC? (NEET PG 20‍15)
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to TOLAC? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prior classical hysterotomy

Trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC) is contraindicated in women with a prior classical cesarean section because the vertical incision in the upper uterine segment carries a high risk of uterine rupture during labor.

Types of uterine incisions:

  • Classical hysterotomy: Vertical upper-segment incision → absolute contraindication to TOLAC
  • Kerr hysterotomy: Low transverse incision → safest and commonly eligible for VBAC
  • Kronig hysterotomy: Low vertical incision → relative risk depends on extent

Why classical incision is dangerous:

  • Upper uterine segment contracts strongly during labor
  • Scar has poor tensile strength
  • Increased risk of catastrophic uterine rupture, fetal distress, and maternal hemorrhage

Therefore, prior classical hysterotomy is an absolute contraindication to TOLAC/VBAC.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rh isoimmunization

Golden-yellow discoloration of amniotic fluid is classically associated with Rh isoimmunization due to severe fetal hemolysis.

  • Maternal anti-D antibodies cross the placenta
  • Cause fetal RBC destruction
  • Breakdown of hemoglobin increases bilirubin pigments in amniotic fluid
  • This produces the characteristic golden/yellow (“saffron-colored”) amniotic fluid

Important associations:

  • Fetal anemia
  • Hydrops fetalis
  • Elevated bilirubin in amniotic fluid
  • Positive indirect Coombs test in mother

Different amniotic fluid colors:

  • Green → Meconium staining/fetal distress
  • Foul-smelling or turbid → Chorioamnionitis/infection
  • Golden yellow → Rh incompatibility with hemolysis
  • Dark red/brown → Concealed abruption or old blood

  • Fetal head at –1 station
  • Occipitoanterior position

  • Fully dilated cervix
  • Ruptured membranes
  • Engaged head
  • Known fetal position
  • Adequate pelvis
  • No cephalopelvic disproportion

  • Fetal injury
  • Failed operative delivery.

Correct answer: C. 5

The Modified Bishop score is used to assess cervical favorability before induction of labor and predicts the likelihood of successful vaginal delivery.

| Cervical Feature | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| ---------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cervical dilatation | ˂ 1cm | 1-2 cm | 3-4 cm | 5+cm |
| Cervical length | 4 cm | 2-4 cm | 1-2 cm | ˂ 1 cm |
| Effacement* | 30 | 40-50 | 60-70 | >80 |
| Station of presenting part | -3 cm | -2 cm | -1/0 cm | +1/+2 cm |
| Consistency of the cervix | Firm | Average | Soft | |
| Position of cervix | Posterior | Mid position | Anterior | |

Scoring in this patient:

  • Dilation: 1 cm → 1 point
  • Effacement: 30% → 1 point
  • Station: –1 → 2 points
  • Consistency: Soft → 1 point
  • Position: Posterior → 0 points

Interpretation:

  • Score ≥6–8: Favorable cervix (successful induction likely)
  • Score <6: Unfavorable cervix → cervical ripening needed (e.g., prostaglandins or Foley catheter)

The staff nurse prepares oxytocin in a dextrose 5% bottle because normal saline is out of stock. After starting the infusion, the patient develops headache, nausea, confusion, and a generalized tonic clonic seizure. What is the most likely mechanism?

options.text: Water intoxication due to ‍hypotonic free water load​
Pulmonary edema due to oxy‍tocin-induced myocardial ​depression

questions.correct_answer: B. Water intoxication due to hypotonic free water load
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Water intoxication due to hypotonic free water load

Oxytocin has an ADH-like effect because it is structurally similar to vasopressin and can promote water retention. When oxytocin is infused in 5% dextrose, the dextrose is rapidly metabolized, leaving free water, creating a hypotonic water load. This can precipitate acute hyponatremia, leading to headache, nausea, confusion, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. The mechanism is therefore water intoxication from hypotonic free water plus oxytocin-related antidiuretic effect.

Other options:
A. Acute hyperglycemia triggering ketoacidosis:
Unlikely. Dextrose infusion could raise glucose, but acute ketoacidosis requires insulin deficiency and typically presents with dehydration, Kussmaul breathing, and metabolic acidosis rather than acute seizures from neurologic symptoms soon after infusion.

C. Pulmonary edema due to oxytocin-induced myocardial depression:
Oxytocin can cause hypotension and fluid-related pulmonary edema in some contexts, but the dominant picture here is acute neurotoxicity and seizure, which is classic for acute hyponatremia.

D. Anaphylaxis to oxytocin preservative:
Anaphylaxis would present with hypotension, bronchospasm, urticaria, angioedema, and respiratory compromise rather than a hyponatremic encephalopathy pattern.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Huntington method

In uterine inversion refractory to manual replacement, operative correction can be performed at laparotomy. If the surgeon applies upward traction on the round ligaments or the inverted uterine fundus using clamps, gradually “walking” the uterus back through the cervical ring without incising the constriction ring, this is the Huntington procedure. The stem explicitly states that the uterus is restored without incising the ring, which distinguishes Huntington from Haultain.

● Huntington method: laparotomy, identify the cup-shaped inversion, apply traction on round ligaments or fundus, progressively elevating the uterus through the ring without cutting the ring.
●  Haultain method: used when the cervical ring is tight and replacement fails. It involves posterior incision of the constriction ring to allow reposition.

Other options:

B. Haultain method
Incorrect here because Haultain requires incision of the constriction ring (usually posterior). The stem states no incision was needed.

C. B-Lynch suture
Used for uterine atony causing postpartum hemorrhage as a uterine compression suture, not for inversion reduction.

D. Hayman suture
Another uterine compression suture for atonic postpartum hemorrhage, not a method for inversion correction.

  • Negative station (−1, −2, etc.): Head not engaged
  • Positive station (+1, +2 etc.): Head descending toward outlet

  • Fully dilated cervix
  • Ruptured membranes
  • Engaged fetal head (≥0 station)
  • Known fetal position
  • Adequate pelvis
  • No suspicion of cephalopelvic disproportion

  • Station −1 → head not engaged
  • Attempting forceps with a high head is contraindicated

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Observe: Already prolonged second stage with maternal exhaustion.
  • Forceps: Contraindicated when head is above ischial spines.
  • Fetal blood sampling: Used for abnormal CTG, but CTG here is normal.

Uterine rupture should be suspected in a laboring woman with a previous cesarean scar who suddenly develops:

  • Loss of fetal station (fetal head moves from 0 station to −3 station)
  • Vaginal bleeding
  • Arrest of labor progress

questions.correct_answer: B. Two finger breadths below umbilicus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Two finger breadths below umbilicus

Uterus is at the umbilicus after delivery and involutes \~1 fingerbreadth per day. Therefore, on day 2 it lies 2 fingerbreadths below.

| Postpartum Day | Fundal Position |
| -------------- | --------------- |
| Immediately after delivery | At the level of the umbilicus |
| Day 1 | 1 finger breadth below umbilicus |
| Day 2 | 2 finger breadths below umbilicus |
| Each subsequent day | Descends \~1 cm/day |
| 10–14 days | Not palpable abdominally |

The controversy:

  • The dispute is entirely about the day-counting convention, not the physiology. Both camps agree on \~1 FB/day. They disagree on when the clock starts.

The two models

| | Model A | Model B |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| Reckoning | Day of delivery = Day 0, fundus at umbilicus | Fundus static for first 24 h; descent begins on day 2 |
| Day 1 | 1 FB below | at umbilicus |
| Day 2 | 2 FB below ✅ | 1 FB below |
| Day 7 | 7 FB below | 6 FB below |
| Day 12–14 | \~12–13 FB below = pelvic organ ✅ | 13 FB below — overshoots |

Why Model A wins on internal consistency

  • Immediately postpartum, fundus ≈ 13.5 cm above symphysis (DC Dutta) — i.e., roughly umbilical level.
  • Involution rate = 1.25 cm (½ inch)/day ≈ 1 fingerbreadth/day.
  • Umbilicus → symphysis ≈ 12–13 cm.
  • 13.5 cm ÷ 1.25 cm/day ≈ day 11–12 → uterus reaches the pelvis.
  • This lands squarely on the universally-agreed endpoint: "pelvic organ by the end of the 2nd week."

Magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) is the drug of choice for prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures, but it should be used with extreme caution or avoided in certain neuromuscular disorders.

  • Reduces muscle fiber excitability

  • Significant renal failure (risk of magnesium toxicity)

  • Gestational diabetes: Not a contraindication.

Magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) is utilized across several obstetric contexts:
1.      Eclampsia — MgSO4 serves as the drug of choice for both the prevention and treatment of seizures in eclamptic patients.
2.      Severe Pre-eclampsia — It is administered prophylactically to reduce the risk of seizure progression in women diagnosed with severe pre-eclampsia.

A pansystolic murmur is not a normal finding in pregnancy. It suggests pathological regurgitation — mitral, tricuspid, or a ventricular septal defect — and warrants full cardiac evaluation.

Why the other three are normal:
A. Left axis deviation — as the uterus enlarges, the diaphragm is pushed upward, mechanically displacing the heart to the left and superiorly. This produces an average \~15° left axis shift on ECG, which is entirely physiological.
B. Mild ST changes in inferior leads — the same diaphragmatic elevation alters the heart's positional relationship to the chest wall, producing mild non-specific ST and T-wave changes in the inferior leads. These are positional, not ischaemic.
C. Atrial and ventricular premature contractions — the hyperdynamic circulation, increased sympathetic tone, and expanded plasma volume of pregnancy make ectopic beats relatively common and generally benign in structurally normal hearts.

| Heart sounds | Loud, widely split S1 | Increased flow + hyperdynamic state |

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased glomerular filtration rate

During normal pregnancy, there is a physiologic increase in renal plasma flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by approximately 40–50%.
Because of this increased GFR, a larger amount of glucose is filtered at the glomerulus.
The renal tubules may not completely reabsorb this increased glucose load, resulting in mild physiologic glucosuria, even when serum glucose levels are normal.

Key features of physiologic glucosuria in pregnancy:
• Occurs due to increased GFR
• Normal blood glucose levels
• Common finding in pregnancy
• Not diagnostic of gestational diabetes

Why other options are incorrect:
• Decreased SGLT2 expression → not the physiologic change in pregnancy
• Increased glomerular filtration barrier permeability → would cause proteinuria, not glucosuria
• Splay phenomenon → refers to variability in nephron glucose reabsorption but is not the primary mechanism here

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spiral artery by extravillous trophoblasts

During early pregnancy, Extravillous Trophoblast invade the maternal uterine vessels. Their role is to remodel the maternal spiral arteries.
Extravillous trophoblast invasion
            ↓
Remodeling of spiral arteries
            ↓
Low resistance vessels
            ↓
Adequate placental blood flow
This transformation converts narrow spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance vessels.
In Preeclampsia:
Failure of trophoblastic invasion
            ↓
Spiral arteries remain narrow
            ↓
High resistance blood flow
            ↓
Placental ischemia
            ↓
Release of antiangiogenic factors
            ↓
Maternal endothelial dysfunction
            ↓
Hypertension and proteinuria
Preeclampsia results from abnormal spiral artery remodeling.

Spiral arteries supply the placenta and intervillous space. Their remodeling is crucial for:

  • Adequate uteroplacental circulation
  • Proper fetal growth

Failure leads to:

  • Preeclampsia
  • Fetal growth restriction

A) Spiral artery by villous trophoblasts
Villous Trophoblast

  • Responsible for maternal–fetal exchange, not arterial invasion.

B) Radial artery by cytotrophoblasts

  • Radial arteries are not the primary vessels remodeled in pregnancy.

D) Arcuate artery by extravillous trophoblasts

  • Arcuate arteries lie deeper in the uterus and do not undergo trophoblastic remodeling.

Correct answer: C. Preterm labor

A 29-year-old pregnant woman in the first trimester has asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) detected on routine screening with E. coli growth on urine culture.
Correct Answer:C) Preterm labor

Physiological changes during pregnancy predispose to infection:

  • Progesterone → ureteric dilation
  • Urinary stasis
  • Reduced bladder tone
  • Vesicoureteral reflux

These changes allow bacteria to ascend from bladder to kidneys.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is defined as:

  • ≥10⁵ colony-forming units/mL bacteria in urine culture
  • No urinary symptoms

It occurs in 2–10% of pregnancies.
Most common organism: Escherichia coli (\~80–90%)              
Untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria may lead to:

| Complication | Mechanism |
| ------------ | --------- |
| Acute pyelonephritis | Ascending infection |
| Preterm labor | Infection-induced inflammatory mediators |
| Low birth weight | Placental inflammation |
| Preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) | Infection weakening membranes |

Treatment
Common safe antibiotics in pregnancy:

| Drug | Example |
| ---- | ------- |
| Beta-lactams | Amoxicillin |
| Cephalosporins | Cephalexin |
| Nitrofurantoin | Used except near term |
| Fosfomycin | Single dose therapy |

Drugs avoided in pregnancy:

  • Fluoroquinolones
  • Tetracyclines

questions.text: Which of the following is ​not a recognized clinical​ use of magnesium sulfate‌ (MgSO₄)?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is not a recognized clinical use of magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase renal perfusion

Magnesium sulfate acts primarily as a central nervous system depressant and anticonvulsant.
Mechanism of action

  • Blocks NMDA receptors
  • Reduces acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junction
  • Stabilizes neuronal membranes

This results in seizure prevention and neuroprotection.
Recognized Clinical Uses
1. Prevention and Treatment of Eclampsia
Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for seizure prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia and treatment of eclampsia.
MgSO₄ is superior to diazepam and phenytoin for eclamptic seizures.
2  Fetal Neuroprotection
Magnesium sulfate is given in imminent preterm delivery (<32 weeks).
Purpose:

  • Protects fetal brain
  • Reduces risk of cerebral palsy

Exam pearl:
MgSO₄ is used for fetal neuroprotection in preterm labor.

3. Prevention of Eclamptic Seizures
In severe preeclampsia, magnesium sulfate prevents progression to eclampsia (seizures).
Indications include:

  • Severe hypertension
  • Visual disturbances
  • Severe headache
  • Epigastric pain

Because MgSO₄ can cause respiratory depression, monitoring is essential.

| Parameter | Normal value |
| --------- | ------------ |
| Respiratory rate | >12/min |
| Urine output | >25–30 mL/hr |
| Patellar reflex | Present |

·         Antidote for toxicity:
·         ➡ Calcium Gluconate
Magnesium sulfate does not improve renal blood flow or renal perfusion.
In fact, in severe preeclampsia:

  • Renal perfusion is reduced
  • MgSO₄ is given only for seizure prevention, not for renal function improvement.

Preeclampsia 
A pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder occurring after 20 weeks of gestation characterized by: 

  • Hypertension ≥140/90 mmHg 
  • Proteinuria ≥300 mg/day 

Severe disease can progress to eclampsia, which involves generalized tonic-clonic seizures. 
Severe hypertension with heavy proteinuria at 36 weeks raises concern for imminent eclampsia. The true warning signs are headache, visual disturbances, and epigastric/RUQ pain from hepatic capsular stretch. 

1. Headache 
Mechanism 

  • Cerebral vasospasm 

  • Increased intracranial pressure 

  • Cerebral edema 

Clinical clue 

  • Severe frontal or occipital headache 

  • Often persistent and not relieved by analgesics 

2. Blurring of Vision 
Cause 

  • Retinal arteriolar spasm 

  • Cerebral edema affecting visual cortex 

Symptoms 

  • Blurring of vision 

  • Scotomas 

  • Photophobia 

  • Temporary blindness 

3. Epigastric Pain  
Mechanism 

  • Liver ischemia 

  • Stretching of Glisson’s capsule 

  • Associated with HELLP syndrome 

Clinical significance 

  • Indicates severe preeclampsia 

  • Often precedes seizures or hepatic rupture 

Although pedal edema is nonspecific in pregnancy, persistent or sudden worsening edema is a worsening sign but not included in criteria for impending eclampsia.

questions.text: Which one of the following‌ statements explains self‍-priming of gonadotrophs?​
questions.raw_text: Which one of the following statements explains self-priming of gonadotrophs?

options.text: Lower GnRH pulse frequenci‌es favour FSH secretion a‍nd higher frequencies fav​our LH secretion.
Lower GnRH pulse frequenci‌es favour LH secretion an‍d higher frequencies favo​ur FSH secretion.
Higher GnRH pulse frequenc‌ies favour LH as well as ‍FSH secretion.
Lower GnRH pulse frequenci‌es favour LH as well as F‍SH secretion.

questions.correct_answer: A. Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour FSH secretion and higher frequencies favour LH secretion.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour FSH secretion and higher frequencies favour LH secretion.

GnRH is released in a pulsatile manner, and the frequency of GnRH pulses determines the relative secretion of LH and FSH:

  • Low-frequency GnRH pulses → preferentially stimulate FSH
  • High-frequency GnRH pulses → preferentially stimulate LH

This differential response is called GnRH pulse-frequency modulation.

Self-priming of gonadotrophs refers to the phenomenon whereby repeated GnRH stimulation enhances the gonadotroph response, particularly during the preovulatory GnRH/LH surge.

Why the other options are incorrect?

  • B. Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH secretion and higher frequencies favour FSH secretion: Reverses the normal frequency relationship.
  • C. Higher GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH as well as FSH secretion: Does not explain differential regulation by GnRH pulse frequency.
  • D. Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH as well as FSH secretion: Incorrect; low-frequency pulses do not preferentially stimulate both LH and FSH.

Saw-​toothed glandular epithel​ium is seen in secretory ​phase. 3. Stratum compact‍um contains mainly the gl​ands and less stroma. 4. ​Pseudostratification is s​een in proliferative phas​e of menstrual cycle. Whi​ch of the statements give​n above are correct?
questions.raw_text:
Consider the following statements with respect to endometrial cycle:
1.	The basal zone is uninfluenced by any hormone.
2.	Saw-toothed glandular epithelium is seen in secretory phase.
3.	Stratum compactum contains mainly the glands and less stroma.
4.	Pseudostratification is seen in proliferative phase of menstrual cycle.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

  1. Basal zone is uninfluenced by hormones — Correct
    • The stratum basale is relatively unaffected by cyclical hormonal changes and remains after menstruation.
    • It serves as the source for regeneration of the functional layer.
  2. Saw-toothed glandular epithelium is seen in secretory phase — Correct
    • Under progesterone influence, endometrial glands become tortuous/coiled (“saw-toothed”) and begin secreting glycogen.
  3. Stratum compactum contains mainly glands and less stroma — Incorrect
    • The stratum compactum contains densely packed stromal cells and relatively fewer glands.
    • The stratum spongiosum contains more prominent, dilated glands.
  4. Pseudostratification is seen in proliferative phase — Correct
    • During the estrogen-driven proliferative phase, the endometrial glands are relatively straight and show pseudostratified columnar epithelium.

Which of the following are indications of endometrial sampling?

I. Endometrial tuberculosis
II. Endometrial polyp
III. Postmenopausal bleeding
IV. Abnormal uterine bleeding

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Endometrial sampling (endometrial biopsy) is a minimally invasive procedure used to obtain endometrial tissue for histopathological examination. It is primarily indicated to evaluate abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma, and diagnose specific endometrial diseases such as tuberculosis. The following are indications for endometrial sampling:

  • I. Endometrial tuberculosis: Endometrial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing genital tuberculosis, demonstrating granulomatous inflammation and allowing microbiological testing (AFB stain, culture, PCR). ⭐
  • III. Postmenopausal bleeding: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation for endometrial carcinoma, and endometrial sampling is indicated, especially when endometrial thickness is >4 mm or bleeding is recurrent. ⭐
  • IV. Abnormal uterine bleeding: Endometrial biopsy is recommended in:
    • Women ≥45 years with AUB
    • Women <45 years with persistent AUB, failed medical treatment, or risk factors for endometrial carcinoma.

Why is II incorrect?

  • II. Endometrial polyp: The preferred investigations are transvaginal ultrasound, saline infusion sonography, or hysteroscopy. Although a removed polyp is sent for histopathology, endometrial sampling alone is not the investigation of choice for diagnosing an endometrial polyp.

  • Irregularity of the tubal lumen
  • Peritubal adhesions
  • Tubal narrowing or obstruction

When contrast fills the tube during HSG, these thickened mucosal folds project into the lumen, creating the characteristic cogwheel appearance.

Chronic PID is an important cause of:

  • Tubal factor infertility
  • Chronic pelvic pain
  • Ectopic pregnancy

  • B. Asherman syndrome: Characterized by intrauterine adhesions, producing irregular filling defects within the uterine cavity, not changes in the fallopian tubes.
  • D. Ectopic pregnancy: Diagnosed primarily by transvaginal ultrasonography and serum β-hCG. HSG is contraindicated in suspected pregnancy and does not produce a cogwheel appearance.

If ovarian reserve decreases → ovaries respond poorly → FSH increases due to reduced negative feedback.

| --- | -------------- |
| >15 | Good reserve |
| 8–15 | Normal |
| <5 | Poor ovarian reserve |

Produced by: 
Granulosa cells of pre-antral and small antral follicles.

questions.correct_answer: A. I, II, III and IV
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II, III and IV

Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency in which the umbilical cord descends below or alongside the presenting part after rupture of membranes, leading to cord compression, acute fetal hypoxia, and fetal death if not managed promptly.

Cord prolapse is more likely whenever the presenting part is not well applied to the cervix, allowing the cord to slip past it. All the listed factors increase the risk of cord prolapse:

  • I. Malpresentations: Breech, transverse lie, compound presentation, and unstable lie prevent proper engagement of the presenting part, increasing the risk of cord prolapse.
  • II. Contracted pelvis: A contracted pelvis prevents engagement of the fetal head, leaving space for the umbilical cord to prolapse.
  • III. Stabilizing induction: During stabilizing induction (artificial rupture of membranes after external cephalic version or procedures to stabilize the presenting part), if the presenting part is not well engaged, the risk of cord prolapse increases.
  • IV. Prematurity: Premature fetuses have smaller presenting parts, which are less likely to engage, predisposing to cord prolapse.

Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency in which, after delivery of the fetal head, the anterior shoulder becomes impacted behind the maternal pubic symphysis (or less commonly, the posterior shoulder behind the sacral promontory), preventing delivery of the shoulders. It requires prompt recognition and a series of obstetric maneuvers to prevent fetal hypoxia and birth trauma. The following statements are true:

  • II. Anencephaly is a risk factor: Anencephalic fetuses have a small head with relatively normal-sized shoulders, increasing the risk of shoulder dystocia.
  • III. Turtle neck sign is present: The turtle sign is the classic clinical sign of shoulder dystocia, in which the delivered fetal head retracts against the maternal perineum after expulsion because the shoulders are impacted.
  • IV. Episiotomy should always be given: Although an episiotomy does not relieve the bony obstruction, it is commonly performed to provide additional space for internal maneuvers (e.g., Rubin or Woods screw maneuver). Hence, many traditional examination questions consider it appropriate.

  • I. It can be predicted during early labour: Shoulder dystocia is largely unpredictable. Although several risk factors are recognized, most cases occur without warning, and many women with risk factors deliver without shoulder dystocia.

Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL) is performed to prevent postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) by promoting uterine contraction and placental separation.

  • Administration of a uterotonic: Oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV within 1 minute after birth (preferred uterotonic).

  • Immediate cord clamping (<30 seconds) is no longer recommended in routine deliveries.

The Burns–Marshall maneuver is used for the delivery of the after-coming head in breech presentation.

The McRoberts maneuver is the first-line intervention for shoulder dystocia. It involves hyperflexion and abduction of the maternal hips, which straightens the lumbosacral angle, flattens the sacrum, and rotates the symphysis pubis cephalad. These changes improve alignment of the pelvis with the expulsive forces and help release the impacted anterior shoulder. It successfully resolves 40–60% of cases alone and up to 90% when combined with suprapubic pressure.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Rubin II maneuver – An internal rotational maneuver in which pressure is applied to the posterior aspect of the anterior shoulder to reduce the bisacromial diameter.
  • C. Woods screw maneuver – Internal rotation of the posterior shoulder to rotate the fetus and dislodge the impacted anterior shoulder.
  • D. Gaskin maneuver – The mother is repositioned onto all fours (hands-and-knees); used when initial maneuvers fail.

High-Yield Pearl:
HELPERR sequence for shoulder dystocia:

  • H – Help
  • E – Evaluate for episiotomy
  • L – Legs (McRoberts maneuver)
  • P – Suprapubic pressure
  • E – Enter maneuvers (Rubin II, Woods screw, Reverse Woods)
  • R – Remove posterior arm
  • R – Roll the patient onto all fours (Gaskin)

questions.correct_answer: B. Two finger breadths below umbilicus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Two finger breadths below umbilicus

Uterus is at the umbilicus after delivery and involutes \~1 fingerbreadth per day. Therefore, on day 2 it lies 2 fingerbreadths below.

| Postpartum Day | Fundal Position |
| -------------- | --------------- |
| Immediately after delivery | At the level of the umbilicus |
| Day 1 | 1 finger breadth below umbilicus |
| Day 2 | 2 finger breadths below umbilicus |
| Each subsequent day | Descends \~1 cm/day |
| 10–14 days | Not palpable abdominally |

The controversy:

  • The dispute is entirely about the day-counting convention, not the physiology. Both camps agree on \~1 FB/day. They disagree on when the clock starts.

The two models

| | Model A | Model B |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| Reckoning | Day of delivery = Day 0, fundus at umbilicus | Fundus static for first 24 h; descent begins on day 2 |
| Day 1 | 1 FB below | at umbilicus |
| Day 2 | 2 FB below ✅ | 1 FB below |
| Day 7 | 7 FB below | 6 FB below |
| Day 12–14 | \~12–13 FB below = pelvic organ ✅ | 13 FB below — overshoots |

Why Model A wins on internal consistency

  • Immediately postpartum, fundus ≈ 13.5 cm above symphysis (DC Dutta) — i.e., roughly umbilical level.
  • Involution rate = 1.25 cm (½ inch)/day ≈ 1 fingerbreadth/day.
  • Umbilicus → symphysis ≈ 12–13 cm.
  • 13.5 cm ÷ 1.25 cm/day ≈ day 11–12 → uterus reaches the pelvis.
  • This lands squarely on the universally-agreed endpoint: "pelvic organ by the end of the 2nd week."

The third stage of labour is the period from delivery of the baby to expulsion of the placenta. Proper management is crucial to prevent Postpartum Hemorrhage, the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide.

Delayed cord clamping means clamping the cord after 1–3 minutes.

  • Improves neonatal hemoglobin levels
  • Increases iron stores

It is used in management of postpartum hemorrhage, particularly when:

  • Uterine atony occurs
  • Bleeding persists despite uterotonics

Postpartum hemorrhage is defined as:

  • ≥500 mL blood loss after vaginal delivery
  • ≥1000 mL after cesarean section
  • Or any blood loss causing hemodynamic instability

Most common cause:
Uterine atony (≈70–80%)

| ----- | ----------- |
| Tone | Uterine atony (most common) |
| Trauma | Lacerations, uterine rupture |
| Tissue | Retained placenta |

| Step | Treatment |
| ---- | --------- |
| 1 | Uterine massage |
| 2 | Uterotonics (Oxytocin, Methylergometrine, Carboprost, Misoprostol) |
| 3 | Balloon tamponade |
| 4 | Surgical procedures |
| 5 | Hysterectomy |

When atonic PPH fails to respond to massage and first-line uterotonics, the next step is a mechanical tamponade—most commonly a Bakri balloon—as recommended in stepwise PPH algorithms. It provides rapid intrauterine pressure, buys time, and often avoids surgery. Correct answer: D. Serum Estradiol in the early follicular phase

Ovarian reserve tests reflect quantity of remaining follicles. Day-2/3 FSH, AMH, and Antral Follicle Count are validated markers. Ovarian reserve refers to the quantity and functional capacity of the remaining ovarian follicles and predicts response to ovarian stimulation in infertility treatment. Estradiol (E2), though measured in the early follicular phase, is not a reliable ovarian-reserve indicator—levels fluctuate and can even appear normal despite diminished reserve by suppressing FSH. Hence option D is not a true ovarian reserve test. 

1. Serum FSH (Day 2–3 of Cycle) 
Measured in the early follicular phase (Day 2–3).

Principle 
If ovarian reserve decreases → ovaries respond poorly → FSH increases due to reduced negative feedback.

| FSH Level | Interpretation |
| --------- | -------------- |
| <10 IU/L | Normal ovarian reserve |
| 10–15 IU/L | Reduced reserve |
| >15 IU/L | Poor reserve |

2. Antral Follicle Count (AFC) 
Number of 2–10 mm follicles seen in ovaries on transvaginal ultrasound.

| AFC | Interpretation |
| --- | -------------- |
| >15 | Good reserve |
| 8–15 | Normal |
| <5 | Poor ovarian reserve |

3. Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) 
Produced by: 
Granulosa cells of pre-antral and small antral follicles. 

Advantages

  • Most reliable ovarian reserve marker
  • Cycle independent
  • Declines with age

| AMH Level | Interpretation |
| --------- | -------------- |
| >3.5 ng/mL | High reserve / PCOS |
| 1–3.5 ng/mL | Normal |
| <1 ng/mL | Low ovarian reserve |

Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) categorizes the safety of contraceptive methods based on underlying medical conditions. The MEC classification system has four categories:
●        MEC 1: Method is absolutely safe for use
●        MEC 2: Safe for use but has certain limitations (benefits outweigh risks)
●        MEC 3: Relatively contraindicated (risks outweigh benefits)
●        MEC 4: Absolutely contraindicated (method should not be given)
HIV infection without complications is classified as MEC 1 for combined oral contraceptive pills.

For HIV-positive women:
COCs are MEC-1 (safe to use).

Reasons:

  • Do not worsen HIV disease progression
  • Do not significantly increase viral replication

Diabetes Mellitus - Often MEC-2 or MEC-3, especially with vascular complications.
Hyperlipidemia - COCs may increase lipid levels, so usually MEC-2 or MEC-3.
Hypertension - Estrogen-containing pills may increase thrombotic risk, so classified as MEC-3 or MEC-4 depending on severity.

| Regulates menstrual cycles | Reduces irregular bleeding |

questions.correct_answer: A. Folate supplements, from one month before conception to three months after

Folic acid supplementation before conception and during early pregnancy significantly reduces the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs) such as spina bifida and anencephaly. Since neural tube closure occurs by the 28th day after conception, folic acid should be started before pregnancy.

questions.raw_text:
Consider the following statements regarding non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS) for screening high-risk pregnancies for aneuploidies:
1.	It is carried out on maternal blood.
2.	It is done before 10 weeks gestation.
3.	It has a negative predictive value of about 98%.
4.	Invasive testing is needed for confirmation of a positive test.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Non-Invasive Prenatal Screening (NIPS), also known as cell-free fetal DNA (cfDNA) testing, is a screening test for common fetal aneuploidies such as Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome), and Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome). It analyzes cell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood, has very high sensitivity and negative predictive value, but a positive result must always be confirmed by invasive diagnostic testing.
Why is C correct?

  • 1. It is carried out on maternal blood. ✅
    • NIPS analyzes cell-free fetal DNA present in maternal plasma.
  • 2. It is done before 10 weeks gestation. ❌
    • NIPS is performed from 10 weeks of gestation onwards, when sufficient fetal DNA is present.
  • 3. It has a negative predictive value of about 98%. ✅
    • NIPS has an excellent negative predictive value (≈98–99% or higher), making it highly reliable for ruling out common aneuploidies.
  • 4. Invasive testing is needed for confirmation of a positive test. ✅
    • Since NIPS is a screening test, positive results require confirmation by chorionic villus sampling (CVS) or amniocentesis with fetal karyotyping or chromosomal microarray.

questions.raw_text: A 24-year-old woman with a history of generalized tonic-clonic epilepsy has been on long-term antiepileptic therapy for the past 2 years. She reports progressive weight gain, irregular menstrual periods, excessive facial hair, and acne. Examination reveals central obesity, and pelvic ultrasonography shows bilaterally enlarged ovaries with multiple small peripheral follicles, consistent with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Divalproex sodium

Valproate (divalproex sodium) is strongly associated with the development of PCOS, particularly in adolescent girls and women of reproductive age receiving long-term therapy.

Clinical features include:

  • Weight gain
  • Menstrual irregularities (oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea)
  • Hyperandrogenism (acne, hirsutism)
  • Polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography
  • Reduced fertility

The mechanism is thought to involve weight gain, insulin resistance, and altered ovarian steroidogenesis, leading to increased androgen production.

Because of these endocrine and reproductive adverse effects, along with its high teratogenic risk (e.g., neural tube defects and impaired neurodevelopment), valproate should generally be avoided in women of childbearing potential whenever suitable alternatives are available.

Why not the other options?

  • B. Lithium: Primarily used as a mood stabilizer in bipolar disorder. It commonly causes hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, tremor, and weight gain, but PCOS is not a typical adverse effect.
  • C. Lamotrigine: A preferred antiepileptic in women of reproductive age because it has minimal endocrine effects, causes little weight gain, and has a lower teratogenic risk than valproate.
  • D. Carbamazepine: May cause diplopia, ataxia, hyponatremia (SIADH), leukopenia, and hepatic enzyme induction, but PCOS is not classically associated with its use.

| Drug | Important adverse effects |
| ---- | ------------------------- |
| Valproate (Divalproex sodium) | Weight gain, PCOS, hyperandrogenism, teratogenicity, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis |
| Lamotrigine | Rash, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, relatively safe in pregnancy |
| Carbamazepine | Diplopia, ataxia, SIADH, agranulocytosis, enzyme induction |
| Lithium | Hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, tremor, Ebstein anomaly (in pregnancy) |

questions.raw_text: What is altered in thyroid profile throughout pregnancy? (NEET PG 2018)

Correct answer: C. Total T3 level

During pregnancy, estrogen increases hepatic production of thyroid-binding globulin (TBG), which increases the amount of protein-bound thyroid hormones in circulation. As a result:

  • Total T3 and Total T4 levels increase
  • Free T3 and Free T4 usually remain near normal
  • TSH may be slightly reduced in early pregnancy due to hCG stimulation of TSH receptors

Key physiologic changes:

  • ↑ Estrogen → ↑ TBG
  • ↑ Bound thyroid hormone
  • ↑ Total thyroid hormone levels

Despite elevated total thyroid hormone levels, pregnant women are usually euthyroid because free hormone levels remain relatively normal.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Continue pregnancy

Current evidence establishes that fetal risks — including malformations, growth restriction, and spontaneous abortion — are not significantly increased at radiation doses below 0.05 Gy (5 rads).

Importantly, diagnostic X-rays rarely deliver doses exceeding 0.1 Gy (10 rads). To put this into perspective, a dose of 0.1 Gy is equivalent to more than 1,000 chest X-rays — illustrating just how negligible the exposure from a single diagnostic study truly is.

Therefore, continuing the pregnancy is the most appropriate and reassuring advice for a woman who has undergone routine diagnostic imaging.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

  • Option B — Terminate Pregnancy: Termination is unwarranted. The radiation dose from a single chest X-ray falls far below the threshold associated with increased fetal risk, making termination both unnecessary and unjustified.
  • Option C — Pre-invasive Diagnostic Testing: Invasive diagnostic procedures carry their own procedural risks and are not indicated when the radiation exposure is this minimal.
  • Option D — Chromosome Screening: The radiation dose from a standard chest X-ray does not meaningfully elevate the risk of chromosomal abnormalities, rendering routine chromosome screening unnecessary in this context.

  • Parity: P1 (One previous pregnancy reaching viability, twins count as one para)

  • Reduced renal perfusion
  • Glomerular endotheliosis (swelling of glomerular endothelial cells)

  • D. Cordocentesis – Usually performed after 18 weeks and reserved for specific indications such as fetal anemia or rapid fetal karyotyping; it has the highest procedure-related risk.

  • NIPT is a screening test, not a diagnostic test.
  • A positive NIPT result must be confirmed with a diagnostic procedure such as amniocentesis or CVS before making irreversible clinical decisions.

  • NIPT: ≥10 weeks (screening)
  • Amniocentesis: ≥15 weeks, ideally 16–18 weeks (diagnostic)
  • Cordocentesis: ≥18 weeks (special indications)

Correct answer: D. Pansystolic murmur

A pansystolic murmur is not a normal finding in pregnancy. It suggests pathological regurgitation — mitral, tricuspid, or a ventricular septal defect — and warrants full cardiac evaluation.

Why the other three are normal:
A. Left axis deviation — as the uterus enlarges, the diaphragm is pushed upward, mechanically displacing the heart to the left and superiorly. This produces an average \~15° left axis shift on ECG, which is entirely physiological.
B. Mild ST changes in inferior leads — the same diaphragmatic elevation alters the heart's positional relationship to the chest wall, producing mild non-specific ST and T-wave changes in the inferior leads. These are positional, not ischaemic.
C. Atrial and ventricular premature contractions — the hyperdynamic circulation, increased sympathetic tone, and expanded plasma volume of pregnancy make ectopic beats relatively common and generally benign in structurally normal hearts.

| ------ | -------------- | --------- |
| Murmurs | Ejection systolic (aortic/pulmonary areas) | Increased cardiac output → flow murmur |
| Murmurs | Mammary soufflé (2nd–4th ICS, continuous) | Increased breast blood flow |
| Murmurs | Venous hum | Increased venous return |
| Heart sounds | Loud, widely split S1 | Increased flow + hyperdynamic state |
| Heart sounds | Increased P2, split S2 | Increased pulmonary flow |
| Apex beat | Shifted to 4th ICS, 2.5 cm lateral to MCL | Diaphragmatic elevation displacing heart |
| ECG | \~15° left axis deviation | Diaphragm elevation |

            ↓

Low resistance vessels

Failure of trophoblastic invasion
            ↓

High resistance blood flow
            ↓
Placental ischemia
            ↓
Release of antiangiogenic factors
            ↓
Maternal endothelial dysfunction
            ↓
Hypertension and proteinuria
Preeclampsia results from abnormal spiral artery remodeling.

Spiral arteries supply the placenta and intervillous space. Their remodeling is crucial for:

  • Adequate uteroplacental circulation
  • Proper fetal growth

Failure leads to:

  • Preeclampsia
  • Fetal growth restriction

A) Spiral artery by villous trophoblasts
Villous Trophoblast

  • Responsible for maternal–fetal exchange, not arterial invasion.

B) Radial artery by cytotrophoblasts

  • Radial arteries are not the primary vessels remodeled in pregnancy.

D) Arcuate artery by extravillous trophoblasts

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sodium valproate

Sodium valproate is the antiepileptic drug most strongly associated with neural tube defects (NTDs) when taken during early pregnancy. Valproate interferes with folate metabolism, which is essential for DNA synthesis and neural tube formation.

Mechanisms include:

  • Folate antagonism
  • Oxidative stress
  • Histone deacetylase inhibition

This results in failure of neural tube closure.
Valproate exposure in pregnancy increases risk of spina bifida by 10–20 times.
Neural tube defects occur due to failure of neural tube closure during early embryogenesis.

Timing
Neural tube closes between:

  • Day 21–28 of gestation

If closure fails, defects occur such as:

| Defect | Description |
| ------ | ----------- |
| Anencephaly | Absence of brain and skull |
| Spina bifida | Defect in vertebral arch |
| Meningomyelocele | Herniation of meninges and spinal cord |

High-dose folic acid supplementation reduces risk.

| Group | Folic acid dose |
| ----- | --------------- |
| Normal pregnancy | 400 µg/day |
| High-risk women | 4–5 mg/day |

High-risk groups include:

  • Previous NTD pregnancy
  • Women taking antiepileptic drugs like valproate.

| Drug | Congenital defect |
| ---- | ----------------- |
| Valproate | Neural tube defects |
| Isotretinoin | Craniofacial defects |
| Thalidomide | Limb defects (phocomelia) |

A first-trimester ultrasound (10–13+6 weeks) is the most important scan in twin pregnancy. It establishes the diagnosis of multiple gestation, accurately determines chorionicity and amnionicity, confirms fetal viability, dates the pregnancy, and screens for major fetal anomalies. Early determination of chorionicity is essential because it is the single most important predictor of pregnancy outcome in twin gestations.

All the listed objectives are achieved by ultrasound at 10–13 weeks:

  • I. Number of fetus: Confirms whether the pregnancy is singleton, twin, or higher-order multiple gestation. ⭐
  • II. Viability of fetus: Demonstrates cardiac activity in each fetus and confirms viability. ⭐
  • III. Chorionicity of twins: The most important purpose of the first-trimester scan is to determine chorionicity and amnionicity. This is best assessed between 11 and 13+6 weeks using:
    • Lambda (Twin Peak) sign → Dichorionic twins
    • T-sign → Monochorionic twins
  • IV. Malformation in either fetus: A first-trimester scan includes screening for major structural anomalies and nuchal translucency assessment.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Assisted breech delivery

When the first twin is delivered cephalically, vaginal delivery is appropriate regardless of the presentation of the second twin, provided there are no contraindications. If the second twin is breech, assisted breech delivery is the preferred technique. The breech is allowed to descend spontaneously until the umbilicus is visible ("hands off the breech"), after which maneuvers such as Lovset (for the arms) and Burns–Marshall or Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit (for the after-coming head) are used.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Lower segment cesarean section (LSCS ) – Not routinely required. Combined vaginal–cesarean delivery has higher maternal morbidity and is reserved for failed vaginal delivery or fetal compromise.
  • B. Internal podalic version (IPV) – Indicated for a transverse or oblique lie of the second twin, not for a fetus already presenting by the breech.
  • C. Breech extraction – Involves immediate traction on the fetal feet from the outset and is reserved for selected situations such as fetal distress or after internal podalic version, not for a spontaneously descending breech.

High-Yield Pearl:
Second twin breech with full cervical dilatation:

  • Assisted breech delivery = Wait, then assist.
  • Breech extraction = Pull from the start.

questions.text: The best time to identify ‌the type of twin pregnanc‍y on ultrasound is? (NEET​ PG 2018)
questions.raw_text: The best time to identify the type of twin pregnancy on ultrasound is? (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 11-14 weeks

The best time to determine chorionicity and amnionicity in twin pregnancy is during the first trimester, especially between 11–14 weeks of gestation.

Why this period is ideal:

  • Membranes and placental relationships are clearly visible
  • Lambda (twin peak) sign and T-sign can be identified accurately
  • Early diagnosis guides antenatal surveillance and management

Ultrasound findings:

  • Lambda (twin peak) sign → dichorionic twins
  • T-sign → monochorionic twins

Importance of determining chorionicity:

  • Monochorionic twins have higher risks of:
    • Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS)
    • Selective fetal growth restriction
    • Twin anemia-polycythemia sequence
    • Increased perinatal morbidity and mortality

Accuracy of chorionicity assessment decreases later in pregnancy as membranes become thinner and placentas may fuse.

questions.text: If division occurs on the ‌7th day during twin gesta‍tion, the result would be​: (NEET PG 2016)
questions.raw_text: If division occurs on the 7th day during twin gestation, the result would be: (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diamnionic, monochorionic

The timing of division of a monozygotic twin pregnancy determines chorionicity and amnionicity.

Timing of division:

  • 0–3 days → Diamniotic, dichorionic
  • 4–8 days → Diamniotic, monochorionic
  • 8–13 days → Monoamniotic, monochorionic
  • 13 days → Conjoined twins

Division on the 7th day occurs after formation of the chorion but before formation of the amnion, resulting in:

  • One chorion
  • Two amniotic sacs

Thus, the twins are diamniotic and monochorionic.

questions.raw_text:
A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 22 weeks of gestation presents to the maternal-fetal medicine clinic for a routine prenatal check-up. She is pregnant with monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA) twins. On ultrasound examination, the following findings are noted: 
•	Twin A: Normal amniotic fluid volume and fetal growth.
•	Twin B: Significant polyhydramnios (excessive amniotic fluid) and evidence of cardiomegaly.
What is the likely Quintero stage for the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II

Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS) occurs in monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA) twins due to placental vascular anastomoses, causing unequal blood flow between twins.

Quintero Staging of TTTS:

  • Stage I: Polyhydramnios in recipient + oligohydramnios in donor, donor bladder visible
  • Stage II: Donor bladder not visible on ultrasound
  • Stage III: Abnormal Doppler findings (umbilical artery, ductus venosus, or umbilical vein)
  • Stage IV: Hydrops fetalis in one or both twins
  • Stage V: Fetal demise

Key Concept:

  • Recipient twin: Polyhydramnios, cardiomegaly, cardiac overload
  • Donor twin: Oligohydramnios, growth restriction

In this case, the ultrasound findings are consistent with TTTS Stage II, characterized by absence of the donor twin bladder with fluid imbalance between twins.

questions.text: Which will you not see in ‌twin pregnancy?
questions.raw_text: Which will you not see in twin pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MADC (Monoamniotic Dichorionic)

Twin pregnancies are classified based on:

  • Chorionicity → number of placentas
  • Amnionicity → number of amniotic sacs

| Type | Chorion | Amnion | Frequency |
| ---- | ------- | ------ | --------- |
| Dichorionic diamniotic (DCDA) | 2 | 2 | Most common |
| Monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA) | 1 | 2 | Common in identical twins |
| Monochorionic monoamniotic (MCMA) | 1 | 1 | Rare |

MADC = Monoamniotic Dichorionic
This means:

  • Two placentas (dichorionic)
  • Only one amniotic sac (monoamniotic)

This is embryologically impossible because:

  • Each chorion normally develops its own amniotic sac.
  • If two chorions exist, there must be two amniotic sacs.

Thus monoamniotic dichorionic twins cannot exist.

questions.raw_text:
Which of the following are correct regarding pathology of stress urinary incontinence?

1.	Hypermobility of urethra
2.	Ascend of bladder neck and proximal urethra above pelvic diaphragm
3.	Lowered urethral pressure
4.	Increased detrusor activity

Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3

Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is the involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., coughing, sneezing, laughing, exercise).

  • 1. Hypermobility of urethra ✓
    • The most common mechanism of SUI is urethral hypermobility due to weakness of the pelvic floor and endopelvic fascia, resulting in loss of urethral support.
  • 2. Ascend of bladder neck and proximal urethra above pelvic diaphragm ✗
    • In SUI, the bladder neck and proximal urethra descend below the pelvic floor, not ascend.
  • 3. Lowered urethral pressure ✓
    • Intrinsic sphincter deficiency causes reduced urethral closing pressure, contributing to stress incontinence.
  • 4. Increased detrusor activity ✗
    • Detrusor overactivity is the hallmark of urge urinary incontinence, not stress urinary incontinence.

  • Tension-free vaginal tape (TVT)
  • Transobturator tape (TOT)

Advantages

  • Minimally invasive
  • High long-term cure rates
  • Effective in both urethral hypermobility and intrinsic sphincter deficiency
  • Short recovery period

  • Anterior colporrhaphy: Primarily repairs cystocele; inferior success rates for SUI.
  • Le Fort colpocleisis: Obliterative procedure for advanced prolapse in elderly women who no longer desire vaginal intercourse.
  • Posterior colpoperineorrhaphy: Used for rectocele and perineal defects, not stress incontinence.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Topical estrogen

Topical Estrogen in the Treatment of Atrophic Vaginitis

Atrophic vaginitis (vaginal atrophy) is a condition predominantly seen in postmenopausal women, arising from declining estrogen levels. It manifests as vaginal dryness, itching, and discomfort.

For the management of postmenopausal vaginal atrophy, local estrogen preparations are preferred over systemic hormone replacement therapy (HRT), as they act directly at the site of involvement while minimizing systemic exposure and associated side effects.

A standard regimen of conjugated estrogen cream 1 g applied intravaginally daily for 1–2 weeks is generally effective in providing symptomatic relief.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

  • Option A — Steroids: Steroids are not appropriate for atrophic vaginitis. While they may possess anti-inflammatory properties, they fail to address the root cause — estrogen deficiency.
  • Option C — Antihistamines alone: Antihistamines may offer transient relief from pruritus but do not correct the underlying hormonal deficiency responsible for the condition.
  • Option D — None of the above: This is incorrect, as topical estrogen is well-established as the treatment of choice.

Correct answer: C. Begin oxytocin infusion for augmentation of labor

This patient is in the active phase of labor and has demonstrated inadequate labor progress after epidural analgesia.
Active Labor Arrest Criteria

  • No cervical change despite:
    • ≥6 cm dilatation and
    • Adequate uterine contractions for ≥4 hours, or
    • Inadequate contractions despite oxytocin for ≥6 hours

This patient does not yet meet criteria for active-phase arrest because contractions are inadequate.
Interpretation:

  • Labor progress is inadequate due to hypotonic uterine contractions (power dysfunction)
  • There is no evidence of fetal distress or cephalopelvic disproportion

Management:

  • Oxytocin augmentation should be initiated to increase contraction frequency and strength
  • Continuous fetal and uterine monitoring should be maintained

Why other options are incorrect?

  • Proceed with cesarean delivery for arrest of active labor: Cesarean delivery is not indicated because active-phase arrest requires adequate contractions before diagnosing labor arrest
  • Continue expectant management for another 2 hours: Expectant management may unnecessarily prolong labor when contractions are inadequate
  • Administer intravaginal misoprostol for cervical ripening: Misoprostol is used for cervical ripening and labor induction, not for augmentation of established labor

●  Haultain method: used when the cervical ring is tight and replacement fails. It involves posterior incision of the constriction ring to allow reposition.

Postpartum endometritis is the most common cause of postpartum fever after cesarean delivery, especially in women with prolonged rupture of membranes and prolonged labor.

Risk factors:
• Cesarean delivery (most important risk factor)
• Prolonged rupture of membranes (>18 hours)
• Prolonged labor or multiple vaginal examinations
• Internal fetal monitoring

Clinical features:
• Fever, chills
• Lower abdominal pain
• Uterine fundal tenderness
• Foul-smelling lochia

Correct answer: C. Clamp the cord, cut it and unwind it from around the fetal neck

A nuchal cord occurs when the umbilical cord is wrapped around the fetal neck. It is a common finding during delivery.

Management depends on whether the cord is loose or tight:

1. Loose nuchal cord

  • Slip the cord over the fetal head before delivery of the shoulders.

2. Tight nuchal cord (cannot be slipped over the head)

  • Clamp the cord in two places and cut it
  • Then unwind the cord from around the neck
  • Proceed with delivery of the shoulders

A tight nuchal cord may compress the cord, impairing fetal blood flow and preventing further descent if not released.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Uterine rupture

Uterine rupture should be suspected in a laboring woman with a previous cesarean scar who suddenly develops:

  • Severe abdominal pain
  • Fetal distress (eg, recurrent late decelerations on fetal heart rate tracing)
  • Loss of fetal station (fetal head moves from 0 station to −3 station)
  • Vaginal bleeding
  • Arrest of labor progress

In this patient, the prior cesarean delivery is the key risk factor. During labor, the uterine scar can rupture, causing the fetus to move back into the abdominal cavity, which explains the sudden loss of fetal station and fetal distress. This is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate emergency laparotomy and cesarean delivery.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Fetal nuchal cord: Causes variable decelerations, not sudden loss of station.
  • B. Normal labor: Cervical dilation and fetal descent should progress.
  • D. Vasa previa: Painless bleeding after membrane rupture with fetal bradycardia, but no loss of fetal station or severe maternal pain.

| Day 1 | 1 FB below | at umbilicus |
| Day 2 | 2 FB below ✅ | 1 FB below |
| Day 7 | 7 FB below | 6 FB below |
| Day 12–14 | \~12–13 FB below = pelvic organ ✅ | 13 FB below — overshoots |

Correct answer: A. Testosterone levels are decreased due to dysgenetic Leydig cells

Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) should be suspected in a phenotypic female presenting with:

  • Primary amenorrhea
  • Normal breast development
  • Sparse or absent pubic/axillary hair
  • Absent uterus
  • 46,XY karyotype
  • Normal testes are present
  • Testosterone production is normal or increased
  • Mutation of the androgen receptor causes target tissues to be unresponsive to androgens

Explanation of Findings

  • Sertoli cells produce Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) → Müllerian duct regression → absent uterus, cervix, and fallopian tubes.
  • Leydig cells produce testosterone normally.
  • Testosterone is converted peripherally to estrogen → normal breast development.
  • Lack of androgen action results in scant pubic and axillary hair.

The defect is not dysgenetic Leydig cells. In CAIS:

  • Leydig cells are functional.
  • Testosterone levels are usually normal or elevated male-range levels.
  • The problem is androgen receptor resistance, not decreased androgen production.

• Müllerian agenesis (Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome, MRKH) → 46,XX karyotype, normal ovaries, absent uterus

Why other options do not require immediate karyotyping:

• Amenorrhea with hirsutism → more suggestive of PCOS or hyperandrogenism
• Amenorrhea with hyperprolactinemia → likely prolactinoma or endocrine cause
• Amenorrhea with normal secondary sexual characters and uterus present → often due to outflow tract obstruction (e.g., imperforate hymen) or endocrine causes

Correct answer: B. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism

The most likely diagnosis is: Pure gonadal dysgenesis (46,XY Swyer syndrome), which presents as hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

Why?

This patient has:

  • Primary amenorrhea
  • Absent breast development → estrogen deficiency
  • Absent pubic and axillary hair (can occur with severe hypogonadism)
  • Rudimentary uterus and fallopian tubes → Müllerian structures are present because there is no functional Sertoli cell secretion of AMH
  • Bilateral inguinal masses → likely dysgenetic gonads (streak gonads) located in the inguinal canal

Diagnosis

  • Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism due to gonadal dysgenesis (46,XY Swyer syndrome).

Expected hormonal profile

  • ↑ FSH
  • ↑ LH
  • ↓ Estradiol
  • Low testosterone

Why not Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS)?

AIS would have:

  • Absent uterus and fallopian tubes (AMH from testes causes Müllerian regression)
  • Normal breast development
  • Sparse/absent pubic hair
  • Testes in the inguinal canal or labia

The presence of a rudimentary uterus and fallopian tubes rules out AIS.

| Feature | Swyer syndrome (46,XY gonadal dysgenesis) | Complete AIS |
| ------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| Karyotype | 46,XY | 46,XY |
| Uterus | Present | Absent |
| Breasts | Absent/poorly developed | Well developed |
| Pubic hair | Reduced or absent | Sparse/absent |
| Gonads | Dysgenetic streak gonads | Testes (inguinal/labial) |
| Gonadotropins | ↑ FSH, ↑ LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) | Normal or mildly ↑ LH |

Endometrial polyps are the most common cause of persistent intermenstrual (between-period) bleeding in reproductive-aged women after pregnancy has been excluded (β-hCG negative). They are localized overgrowths of endometrial glands and stroma that bleed irregularly.

  • Best initial imaging: Transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS).
  • Most sensitive test: Saline infusion sonography (SIS).
  • Gold standard for diagnosis and treatment: Hysteroscopy with polypectomy.

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

  • A. PCOS: Typically causes oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea with irregular heavy bleeding due to anovulation, not persistent intermenstrual spotting.
  • C. Endometrial hyperplasia: Usually presents with abnormal heavy or prolonged uterine bleeding, especially in women with chronic unopposed estrogen exposure.
  • D. Submucosal fibroid: Commonly causes heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) and may cause intermenstrual bleeding, but persistent spotting is more characteristic of an endometrial polyp.

Transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS) is the initial investigation of choice for uterine fibroids. However, when a submucosal fibroid is suspected, Saline Infusion Sonography (SIS) is the investigation of choice, as instillation of sterile saline distends the endometrial cavity and clearly delineates intracavitary lesions. In early pregnancy, absence of fetal cardiac activity does not always indicate pregnancy failure. Diagnosis of nonviable pregnancy should be made only when strict ultrasound criteria are met.

Definitive diagnosis of pregnancy loss:

  • CRL ≥7 mm with no cardiac activity
  • Mean sac diameter (MSD) ≥25 mm with no embryo

Findings in This Case

  • Gestational sac present
  • Yolk sac present
  • Fetal pole present
  • CRL = 5 mm (<7 mm)

| ------------------- | -------------------- |
| Gestational sac | 4.5–5 weeks |
| Yolk sac | 5–5.5 weeks |
| Embryo / fetal pole | 5.5 weeks |
| Cardiac activity | \~6 weeks |

| Parameter | Important cutoff |
| --------- | ---------------- |
| MSD cutoff to visualize fetal pole | 25 mm |
| CRL cutoff for cardiac activity | 7 mm |
| β-hCG discriminatory zone for gestational sac on TVS | \~2000 IU |

Correct answer: B. Presenting visual acuity <3/60 in the better eye

NPCBVI defines blindness as:

  • Presenting distance visual acuity <3/60 in the better eye, or
  • Visual field restricted to <10° around fixation.

NPCBVI uses presenting visual acuity, not best-corrected acuity, for its operational/surveillance definition. This is deliberate — the programme is tracking the burden of avoidable blindness (uncorrected refractive error, cataract, etc.) in the population, not just uncorrectable/best-corrected blindness. This is why C and D (which specify "best corrected") are wrong — they don't match the programme's operational definition, even though they sound like standard clinical descriptions of blindness.

The cutoff is <3/60, not <6/60. This trips people up because the WHO's older definitions and some contexts use <6/60 as a "visual impairment" or "low vision" threshold, while <3/60 is the blindness threshold. Remember the tiered WHO/NPCBVI categories roughly as:

  • Normal/mild: 6/6 to 6/18
  • Moderate visual impairment (low vision): <6/18 to 6/60
  • Severe visual impairment: <6/60 to 3/60
  • Blindness: <3/60 (down to no light perception), or visual field <10° around fixation in the better eye

The field criterion (<10° around fixation) is the second, independent criterion — useful for conditions like advanced glaucoma or retinitis pigmentosa where central acuity may be preserved but the field is severely constricted.

Degenerative (pathologic) myopia is distinct from simple myopia in that it is progressive throughout life, not just during the school-age/adolescent growth years. This continued axial elongation is what drives its characteristic complications.

questions.raw_text: A patient has progressive bilateral corneal guttata with morning blurring of vision due to endothelial pump failure. Which corneal dystrophy is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fuchs corneal dystrophy

Fuchs dystrophy affects the Descemet membrane and corneal endothelium, causing guttata, stromal edema and reduced vision, especially on waking.

  • Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy is a primary disorder of the corneal endothelium — progressive loss and dysfunction of endothelial cells leads to corneal guttata (wart-like excrescences on Descemet's membrane, seen as a "beaten metal" appearance on specular reflection).
  • As endothelial pump function fails, the cornea can't stay deturgesced, leading to stromal and epithelial edema — classically worse on waking (morning blurring) because eyes are closed overnight, tears aren't evaporating, and stromal hydration peaks; it improves through the day as evaporation resumes. Advanced disease leads to painful bullous keratopathy.

The other three are all stromal dystrophies, not endothelial, so they don't fit the "endothelial pump failure" mechanism:

  • A. Lattice dystrophy — amyloid deposits in the stroma, branching linear/lattice pattern (TGFBI gene).
  • B. Granular dystrophy — hyaline/"breadcrumb" deposits in the stroma, sparing the periphery early on.
  • D. Reis-Bücklers dystrophy — actually a Bowman's layer dystrophy (anterior), causing recurrent erosions and superficial reticular scarring — again not endothelial.

    • Avoids the retina (which could be injured if the injection is too posterior, especially since the retina thins out but the pars plana corresponds roughly to the area overlying the peripheral retina/ora serrata region)
