questions.raw_text: Following clubfoot surgery, which of the following is the commonest residual deformity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Forefoot adduction.

In clubfoot (CTEV) the deformity components are remembered by CAVE:

  • C → Cavus
  • A → Adduction (forefoot)
  • V → Varus (hindfoot)
  • E → Equinus

After clubfoot surgery (posteromedial release / Turco procedure) some deformities may persist or recur.

Most Common Residual Deformity

The most common residual deformity after clubfoot correction is:
➡ Forefoot adduction
Reason:

  • Medial soft tissues remain tight
  • Incomplete correction of midfoot adduction
❌B. Internal tibial torsion
  • May be associated with clubfoot
  • But not the most common residual deformity
❌C. Forefoot supination
  • Can occur due to tibialis anterior overpull
  • But still less common than adduction
❌D. Equinus
  • Usually well corrected surgically by Achilles tendon lengthening

So persistent equinus is less common.

Synovial chondromatosis is a benign metaplastic disorder of the synovium in which the synovial membrane forms multiple cartilaginous nodules that may detach as multiple intra-articular loose bodies.   • C. Synovial sarcoma: A malignant soft tissue tumor presenting as a painful enlarging mass, not multiple calcified intra-articular loose bodies.
  • D. Secondary osteoarthritis with loose bodies: Loose bodies arise from degenerative cartilage, but the presence of numerous similar-sized calcified bodies with synovial metaplasia favors primary synovial chondromatosis.

Correct answer: A. Increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine

Physiological neonatal jaundice is caused by increased bilirubin production (high RBC turnover), reduced hepatic UDP-glucuronyl transferase activity, and increased enterohepatic circulation. This results in unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia. Since unconjugated bilirubin is water-insoluble, it cannot be filtered by the kidneys, so urine bilirubin is absent. However, the increased bilirubin reaching the intestine is converted by gut bacteria to urobilinogen, leading to increased urinary urobilinogen. The jaundice typically appears after 24 hours, peaks on day 3–5 in term infants, and resolves by 7–10 days.

The VSD transiently closes‌ during the spell, elimin​ating the murmur; no acut‍e intervention is require‌d

questions.correct_answer: B. Worsening infundibular spasm reduces flow across the right ventricular outflow tract, softening the murmur; place the child in knee-chest position and give oxygen and morphine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Worsening infundibular spasm reduces flow across the right ventricular outflow tract, softening the murmur; place the child in knee-chest position and give oxygen and morphine

  • This is a hypercyanotic ("Tet") spell — precipitated by crying/agitation, which triggers infundibular (subpulmonic) muscular spasm, acutely worsening right ventricular outflow tract obstruction.
  • As outflow obstruction worsens, less blood crosses the stenotic infundibulum into the pulmonary artery, causing the murmur (generated by flow through the stenotic RVOT) to become softer or even disappear.
  • Simultaneously, obstructed right ventricular outflow diverts more blood right-to-left across the VSD, bypassing the lungs entirely — worsening systemic hypoxemia and cyanosis despite the softer murmur.
  • Immediate management targets reducing right-to-left shunting and relieving infundibular spasm:
    • Knee-chest position (or squatting in older children) — increases systemic vascular resistance, reducing right-to-left shunt and improving pulmonary flow.
    • Oxygen supplementation.
    • Morphine — sedates and reduces the hyperpnea/catecholamine drive.
    • NaHCO₃ for correction of metabolic acidosis.
    • IV propranolol (β-blocker) — relieves infundibular spasm directly.

questions.raw_text: A full-term neonate develops tachypnea and central cyanosis within a few hours of birth. Pulse oximetry reveals an oxygen saturation of 96% in the right hand and 84% in the left foot. Femoral pulses are palpable with no brachiofemoral delay. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart but markedly elevated pulmonary artery pressures. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Persistent pulmonary hyper‌tension of the newborn (P​PHN)

questions.correct_answer: C. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)

In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), the normal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) after birth fails to occur. As a result:

  • Pulmonary artery pressure remains abnormally high.
  • Blood is shunted right-to-left through the patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and/or foramen ovale.
  • The right upper limb (preductal) receives blood before it mixes with deoxygenated blood at the ductus, resulting in a higher oxygen saturation than the lower limbs (postductal).

This produces the characteristic finding of: Preductal SpO₂ > Postductal SpO₂

The presence of a structurally normal heart with elevated pulmonary pressures strongly supports the diagnosis of PPHN.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Coarctation of the aorta: Typically presents with weak femoral pulses and radiofemoral/brachiofemoral delay, which are absent in this infant.
  • B. Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR): Causes cyanosis but echocardiography would demonstrate anomalous pulmonary venous drainage rather than a structurally normal heart.
  • D. Eisenmenger syndrome: Develops over years as a consequence of long-standing congenital left-to-right shunts and does not occur in the neonatal period.

questions.raw_text: A 3-year-old boy is brought with bluish discoloration of the lips and nail beds present since late infancy. CXR is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tetralogy of Fallot

Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease beyond the neonatal period. The classic chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) due to right ventricular hypertrophy with an uplifted apex, concavity of the main pulmonary artery segment (pulmonary bay), and decreased pulmonary vascular markings (pulmonary oligemia) due to reduced pulmonary blood flow. Clinical features include cyanosis, ejection systolic murmur, and hypercyanotic ("Tet") spells. Definitive treatment is complete intracardiac repair, while severe cyanotic spells require urgent management with oxygen, knee-chest position, morphine, and β-blockers.

High-Yield

  • Most common cyanotic CHD after the neonatal period: Tetralogy of Fallot.
  • CXR: Boot-shaped heart + pulmonary oligemia + pulmonary bay.
  • Four components: VSD, overriding aorta, RV outflow tract obstruction (pulmonary stenosis), right ventricular hypertrophy.
  • Hypercyanotic ("Tet") spells improve with squatting/knee-chest position by increasing systemic vascular resistance and reducing the right-to-left shunt.

Correct answer: B. Pulmonary veins connect abnormally to the systemic venous circulation

Supracardiac TAPVC
The snowman (figure-of-eight) sign on chest X-ray is characteristic of supracardiac Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC). In TAPVC, all pulmonary veins drain into the systemic venous circulation instead of the left atrium, so oxygenated pulmonary venous blood mixes completely with systemic venous blood before reaching the heart. As a result, oxygen saturation is nearly identical in all four cardiac chambers, a classic catheterization finding. Survival depends on the presence of an atrial septal defect (ASD), which allows mixed blood to reach the left heart and systemic circulation. Definitive treatment is early surgical repair by connecting the pulmonary venous confluence to the left atrium.
High-Yield

  • Snowman sign → Supracardiac TAPVC
  • Pulmonary veins drain into systemic veins, not the left atrium
  • Uniform oxygen saturation in all cardiac chambers due to complete mixing
  • ASD is essential for survival
  • Treatment: Early surgical correction

Correct answer: D. Parallel pulmonary and systemic circuits

A term neonate with severe cyanosis immediately after birth that does not improve with 100% oxygen suggests a cyanotic congenital heart disease, most classically transposition of the great arteries (TGA). In TGA, the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, creating parallel pulmonary and systemic circulations instead of the normal series circulation.
Key features:

  • Profound cyanosis within hours of birth
  • Minimal response to oxygen therapy (“hyperoxia test” negative)
  • Survival depends on mixing through a PDA, ASD, or VSD
  • Chest x-ray may show the classic “egg-on-a-string” appearance

Initial management includes:

  • Prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductus arteriosus patency
  • Balloon atrial septostomy if needed
  • Definitive treatment with arterial switch surgery.

  • Hyperglycemia (glucose 450 mg/dL)

  • Urinary potassium loss
  • Shift of potassium from intracellular to extracellular space during acidosis

Correct answer: C. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)

In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), the normal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) after birth fails to occur. As a result:

  • Pulmonary artery pressure remains abnormally high.
  • Blood is shunted right-to-left through the patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and/or foramen ovale.
  • The right upper limb (preductal) receives blood before it mixes with deoxygenated blood at the ductus, resulting in a higher oxygen saturation than the lower limbs (postductal).

This produces the characteristic finding of: Preductal SpO₂ > Postductal SpO₂

The presence of a structurally normal heart with elevated pulmonary pressures strongly supports the diagnosis of PPHN.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Coarctation of the aorta: Typically presents with weak femoral pulses and radiofemoral/brachiofemoral delay, which are absent in this infant.
  • B. Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR): Causes cyanosis but echocardiography would demonstrate anomalous pulmonary venous drainage rather than a structurally normal heart.
  • D. Eisenmenger syndrome: Develops over years as a consequence of long-standing congenital left-to-right shunts and does not occur in the neonatal period.

questions.raw_text: A teenage boy presents with gradually progressive weakness involving the shoulder and calf muscles, along with difficulty climbing stairs. He also has cardiac conduction defects and contractures of the elbows and knees. His elder brother had similar complaints and died at an early age. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Emery-Dreifuss Muscular Dystrophy

Recognize Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD) by its characteristic triad of early joint contractures, slowly progressive humeroperoneal muscle weakness, and cardiac conduction defects. Cardiac involvement is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, making early diagnosis and regular cardiac surveillance essential.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Duchenne muscular dystrophy – Early childhood onset, rapidly progressive proximal muscle weakness, Gowers’ sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, dilated cardiomyopathy; contractures and conduction defects are not the hallmark early features.
  • B. Becker muscular dystrophy – Similar to Duchenne but milder with later onset; contractures and prominent cardiac conduction abnormalities are less characteristic.
  • D. Myotonic dystrophy – Characterized by myotonia (delayed muscle relaxation), distal muscle weakness, cataracts, frontal balding, and endocrine abnormalities rather than humeroperoneal weakness with early contractures.

Exam pearls:

  • Classic triad of EDMD:
    • Early elbow, Achilles tendon, and neck contractures
    • Humeroperoneal muscle weakness (shoulders, upper arms, and calves)
    • Cardiac conduction defects (heart block, arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death)
  • Inheritance: Most commonly X-linked due to EMD (emerin) gene mutation; autosomal dominant/recessive forms occur due to LMNA (lamin A/C) mutations.
  • CK levels: Normal or mildly elevated.
  • Management: Regular ECG/Holter monitoring; pacemaker or ICD may be lifesaving.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cephalohaematoma

Cephalohematoma is a subperiosteal hemorrhage caused by rupture of blood vessels between the pericranium (periosteum) and the skull bone, most commonly following instrumental deliveries (forceps or vacuum). Since the periosteum is firmly attached at the suture lines, the swelling is limited by sutures and does not cross them.

Why are the other options incorrect?

  • A.  Caput succedaneum:
    • Edema of the scalp (subcutaneous tissue) caused by pressure during labour.
    • Crosses suture lines and is present at birth.
  • B. Intraventricular haemorrhage: Bleeding into the ventricular system of the brain, seen mainly in preterm infants; it does not present as an external scalp swelling.
  • D. Subgaleal haemorrhage:
    • Bleeding between the galea aponeurotica and periosteum.
    • Crosses suture lines, can involve the entire scalp, and may lead to massive blood loss and shock, especially after vacuum-assisted delivery.

| Feature | Caput Succedaneum | Cephalohematoma | Subgaleal Hemorrhage |
| ------- | ----------------- | --------------- | -------------------- |
| Plane | Subcutaneous tissue | Subperiosteal | Subaponeurotic (beneath galea) |
| Crosses sutures | Yes | No | Yes |
| Present at birth | Yes | Usually appears hours after birth | May appear soon after birth |
| Common cause | Prolonged labour | Forceps/Vacuum delivery | Vacuum extraction |
| Risk | Benign | Hyperbilirubinemia, skull fracture | Massive hemorrhage, shock |

WT1 (Wilms Tumor 1) is a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 11p13 that plays a crucial role in the development of the kidneys and gonads. Mutations in the WT1 gene can cause focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) associated with abnormal genital development, Wilms tumor, and intellectual disability, classically seen in Denys-Drash syndrome and WAGR syndrome.

WT1 mutations are associated with:

  • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) or diffuse mesangial sclerosis ⭐
  • Wilms tumor
  • Disorders of sexual development (abnormal genitalia)
  • In some syndromes (e.g., WAGR syndrome), intellectual disability may also be present.

  • B. INF2: Causes autosomal dominant FSGS, sometimes associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, but not Wilms tumor or genital abnormalities.
  • C. LMX1B: Mutated in Nail-Patella syndrome, characterized by nail dysplasia, absent/hypoplastic patellae, and nephropathy.
  • D. APOL1: Risk variants are associated with FSGS and HIV-associated nephropathy, particularly in individuals of African ancestry, but not with Wilms tumor or genital abnormalities.

Correct answer: C. No further investigations

In a child >3 years with a first febrile UTI who responds well to treatment and has a normal ultrasonography (USG KUB), no further imaging is recommended according to current pediatric UTI guidelines. Micturating cystourethrogram (MCU/VCUG) is reserved for recurrent febrile UTIs, abnormal USG findings, atypical/non-E. coli infections, or suspected vesicoureteric reflux (VUR). A DMSA scan is not performed routinely after the first UTI; it is indicated 4–6 months later only when there is concern for renal scarring, such as after recurrent or atypical infections.

  • MCU (VCUG): Recurrent UTI, abnormal USG, atypical/non-E. coli UTI, suspected VUR
  • DMSA scan: 4–6 months after infection to detect renal scarring, not acute pyelonephritis routinely.

3.	Kernicterus most commonly affects the globus pallidus and subthalamic nuclei

Consider the following statements regarding the management of trachea-esophageal fistula in neonates:

1.	The baby should be nursed in prone position.
2.	The neonate should be kept nil per orally and started on intravenous fluids.
3.	The neonate needs continuous oral suction using a slow suction device.
4.	Surgery should be planned once the neonate attains 2.5 kg weight.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 3 only

  • Statement 1. The baby should be nursed in prone position: incorrect. The neonate should be nursed propped-up (head elevated 30–40°), not prone. This position reduces reflux of gastric contents through the distal fistula into the tracheobronchial tree and minimizes pooling/aspiration of secretions from the proximal esophageal pouch.
  • Statement 2. The neonate should be kept nil per orally and started on intravenous fluids: Correct. Oral feeding is withheld to prevent aspiration through the fistula/proximal pouch, and hydration is maintained intravenously pending surgery.
  • Statement 3. The neonate needs continuous oral suction using a slow suction device: Correct. A Replogle tube (double-lumen) is placed in the proximal pouch on continuous gentle/low suction to clear pooled saliva and secretions, preventing overflow aspiration into the airway.
  • Statement 4. Surgery should be planned once the neonate attains 2.5 kg weight: Incorrect. This reflects outdated teaching. Modern management does not mandate delaying surgery until a specific weight threshold; timing is guided by the infant's overall clinical stability, associated anomalies, and type of TEF rather than a fixed weight cutoff. Even low-birth-weight neonates are managed early (with staged approaches if unstable), not simply held until 2.5 kg.

The cornerstone of treatment for mild to moderate dehydration due to acute diarrhea is oral rehydration solution (ORS) along with continued breastfeeding or age-appropriate feeding.

  • Give ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours
  • Reassess hydration status after 4 hours
  • Replace ongoing stool losses with additional ORS
  • Continue breastfeeding throughout treatment
  • Add zinc supplementation for 14 days

Intravenous fluids (Ringer lactate or normal saline) are reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or when the child cannot tolerate oral fluids (persistent vomiting, ileus, altered consciousness).

  • B. Ringer lactate: Preferred IV fluid for severe dehydration (WHO Plan C), but unnecessary if ORS can be given.
  • C. Normal saline in 5% dextrose: Not recommended for initial rehydration in acute diarrheal dehydration.

Correct answer: C. Emery-Dreifuss Muscular Dystrophy

Recognize Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD) by its characteristic triad of early joint contractures, slowly progressive humeroperoneal muscle weakness, and cardiac conduction defects. Cardiac involvement is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, making early diagnosis and regular cardiac surveillance essential.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Duchenne muscular dystrophy – Early childhood onset, rapidly progressive proximal muscle weakness, Gowers’ sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, dilated cardiomyopathy; contractures and conduction defects are not the hallmark early features.
  • B. Becker muscular dystrophy – Similar to Duchenne but milder with later onset; contractures and prominent cardiac conduction abnormalities are less characteristic.
  • D. Myotonic dystrophy – Characterized by myotonia (delayed muscle relaxation), distal muscle weakness, cataracts, frontal balding, and endocrine abnormalities rather than humeroperoneal weakness with early contractures.

Exam pearls:

  • Classic triad of EDMD:
    • Early elbow, Achilles tendon, and neck contractures
    • Humeroperoneal muscle weakness (shoulders, upper arms, and calves)
    • Cardiac conduction defects (heart block, arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death)
  • Inheritance: Most commonly X-linked due to EMD (emerin) gene mutation; autosomal dominant/recessive forms occur due to LMNA (lamin A/C) mutations.
  • CK levels: Normal or mildly elevated.
  • Management: Regular ECG/Holter monitoring; pacemaker or ICD may be lifesaving.

Cephalohematoma is a subperiosteal hemorrhage caused by rupture of blood vessels between the pericranium (periosteum) and the skull bone, most commonly following instrumental deliveries (forceps or vacuum). Since the periosteum is firmly attached at the suture lines, the swelling is limited by sutures and does not cross them.

    • Edema of the scalp (subcutaneous tissue) caused by pressure during labour.

  • B. Intraventricular haemorrhage: Bleeding into the ventricular system of the brain, seen mainly in preterm infants; it does not present as an external scalp swelling.
  • D. Subgaleal haemorrhage:
    • Bleeding between the galea aponeurotica and periosteum.
    • Crosses suture lines, can involve the entire scalp, and may lead to massive blood loss and shock, especially after vacuum-assisted delivery.

Consider the following statements regarding Eisenmenger Syndrome:
1.	In patients with severe and prolonged pulmonary hypertension, the right-to-left shunt gets reversed to a left-to-right shunt.
2.	There is marked cyanosis, which may be more apparent in the feet and toes than in the upper part of the body.
3.	Antihypertensives which cause peripheral vasodilatation can exacerbate the shunting and worsen the symptoms.

Correct answer: D. 2 and 3

  • 1. Right-to-left shunt reverses to left-to-right: Incorrect
    • The sequence is the opposite.
    • Initially, a congenital left-to-right shunt causes increased pulmonary blood flow.
    • Prolonged pulmonary hypertension increases pulmonary vascular resistance until it exceeds systemic resistance, causing the shunt to reverse from left-to-right → right-to-left.
    • This is Eisenmenger syndrome.
  • 2. Cyanosis may be more prominent in the feet and toes: Correct
    • This is differential cyanosis, classically seen when Eisenmenger syndrome develops due to a PDA.
    • Deoxygenated blood enters the descending aorta distal to the branches supplying the upper limbs → lower limbs become more cyanotic than upper limbs.
  • 3. Peripheral vasodilators can worsen shunting: Correct
    • Systemic vasodilation decreases systemic vascular resistance (SVR).
    • This favors right-to-left shunting, increasing the amount of deoxygenated blood entering systemic circulation and worsening cyanosis.

questions.raw_text: A full-term neonate develops tachypnea and central cyanosis within a few hours of birth. Pulse oximetry reveals an oxygen saturation of 96% in the right hand and 84% in the left foot. Femoral pulses are palpable with no brachiofemoral delay. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart but markedly elevated pulmonary artery pressures. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Persistent pulmonary hyper‌tension of the newborn (P​PHN)

questions.correct_answer: C. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)

In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), the normal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) after birth fails to occur. As a result:

  • Pulmonary artery pressure remains abnormally high.
  • Blood is shunted right-to-left through the patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and/or foramen ovale.
  • The right upper limb (preductal) receives blood before it mixes with deoxygenated blood at the ductus, resulting in a higher oxygen saturation than the lower limbs (postductal).

This produces the characteristic finding of: Preductal SpO₂ > Postductal SpO₂

The presence of a structurally normal heart with elevated pulmonary pressures strongly supports the diagnosis of PPHN.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Coarctation of the aorta: Typically presents with weak femoral pulses and radiofemoral/brachiofemoral delay, which are absent in this infant.
  • B. Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR): Causes cyanosis but echocardiography would demonstrate anomalous pulmonary venous drainage rather than a structurally normal heart.
  • D. Eisenmenger syndrome: Develops over years as a consequence of long-standing congenital left-to-right shunts and does not occur in the neonatal period.

Correct answer: B. Large Patent Ductus Arteriosus

Differential cyanosis (cyanosis of the lower extremities with pink upper extremities) is a classic finding in large Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) with Eisenmenger syndrome. Progressive pulmonary hypertension causes reversal of the shunt (right-to-left) across the PDA, allowing deoxygenated blood to enter the descending aorta distal to the origin of the subclavian arteries, thereby affecting the lower limbs while sparing the upper limbs.

  • In a large PDA with Eisenmenger physiology:
    • Initial shunt: Left → Right
    • With pulmonary hypertension: Right → Left
    • Deoxygenated blood enters the descending aorta distal to the branches supplying the upper limbs.
    • Upper extremities remain pink, while the lower extremities become cyanotic (differential cyanosis).

Why not the other options?

  • A. Severe peripheral vascular disease: Causes ischemia but does not produce differential cyanosis.
  • C. Atrioventricular septal defect: Eisenmenger syndrome causes central cyanosis, not differential cyanosis.
  • D. Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome: Causes hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with recurrent epistaxis and AVMs, not differential cyanosis.

questions.raw_text:
Consider the following statements regarding the management of trachea-esophageal fistula in neonates:

1.	The baby should be nursed in prone position.
2.	The neonate should be kept nil per orally and started on intravenous fluids.
3.	The neonate needs continuous oral suction using a slow suction device.
4.	Surgery should be planned once the neonate attains 2.5 kg weight.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 3 only

  • Statement 1. The baby should be nursed in prone position: incorrect. The neonate should be nursed propped-up (head elevated 30–40°), not prone. This position reduces reflux of gastric contents through the distal fistula into the tracheobronchial tree and minimizes pooling/aspiration of secretions from the proximal esophageal pouch.
  • Statement 2. The neonate should be kept nil per orally and started on intravenous fluids: Correct. Oral feeding is withheld to prevent aspiration through the fistula/proximal pouch, and hydration is maintained intravenously pending surgery.
  • Statement 3. The neonate needs continuous oral suction using a slow suction device: Correct. A Replogle tube (double-lumen) is placed in the proximal pouch on continuous gentle/low suction to clear pooled saliva and secretions, preventing overflow aspiration into the airway.
  • Statement 4. Surgery should be planned once the neonate attains 2.5 kg weight: Incorrect. This reflects outdated teaching. Modern management does not mandate delaying surgery until a specific weight threshold; timing is guided by the infant's overall clinical stability, associated anomalies, and type of TEF rather than a fixed weight cutoff. Even low-birth-weight neonates are managed early (with staged approaches if unstable), not simply held until 2.5 kg.

questions.explanation:

  • ReSoMal (Rehydration Solution for Malnutrition) is specially formulated for children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM).
  • Children with SAM have excess total body sodium but marked intracellular potassium deficiency.
  • Therefore, ReSoMal contains:
    • Lower sodium (45 mmol/L vs 75 mmol/L in low-osmolar ORS)
    • Higher potassium (40 mmol/L vs 20 mmol/L)
  • It also contains more glucose and added magnesium, zinc, copper, and other micronutrients.
  • ReSoMal helps prevent sodium overload while correcting potassium depletion.
  • Exception: In SAM with profuse watery diarrhea or suspected cholera, standard low-osmolarity ORS is preferred because ReSoMal may not adequately replace sodium losses.
  • Rehydration should be slow and carefully monitored to avoid heart failure.

High-yield values

| Component | ReSoMal | Low-osmolar ORS |
| --------- | ------- | --------------- |
| Sodium | 45 mmol/L | 75 mmol/L |
| Potassium | 40 mmol/L | 20 mmol/L |

questions.text: Which of the following sta‌tements is not true regar​ding Zero-Based Budgeting​ (ZBB)?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following statements is not true regarding Zero-Based Budgeting (ZBB)?

options.text: It is a priority-based bud‌geting system
It proceeds from resources‌ to targets
It does not depend on data‌ from the previous budget​
Every line item of the bud‌get must be justified and​ approved

questions.correct_answer: B. It proceeds from resources to targets
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It proceeds from resources to targets

Distractor-by-distractor analysis:

  • A. It is a priority-based budgeting system: True. ZBB is inherently a priority-based system. Managers prepare "decision packages" for every activity, which are then ranked in order of priority, and resources are allocated down that ranking until funds are exhausted.
  • B. It proceeds from resources to targets: False. ZBB proceeds from targets to resources, not the other way around. You first define objectives/activities, justify them from a zero base, and then work out what resources they require. Proceeding from resources to targets — letting the existing resource envelope dictate what gets done — is the hallmark of conventional/incremental budgeting.
  • C. It does not depend on data from the previous budget: True. The defining feature of ZBB: each budgeting cycle starts from a "zero base" with no reference to the previous year's allocations. Last year's budget carries no automatic legitimacy.
  • D. Every line item of the budget must be justified and approved: True. Every line item and every activity must be justified afresh and approved on its own merits — nothing is carried forward by default.

High-yield contrast table:

| Feature | Incremental (traditional) budgeting | Zero-Based Budgeting |
| ------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| Starting point | Previous year's budget ± increment | Zero base every cycle |
| Direction | Resources → targets | Targets → resources |
| Justification | Only the increment is justified | Every item justified |
| Basis of allocation | Historical precedent | Priority-ranked decision packages |
| Effort/cost | Low | High (time- and paper-intensive) |

Exam pearl: ZBB was popularized by Peter Pyhrr (Texas Instruments, 1970s) and is asked in PSM under health planning and management. The "targets → resources" direction is the classic trap — it mirrors the planning cycle itself, where objectives are set first and resources mobilized to meet them.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Confounding by socioeconomic status

The key clue is that the crude association between poor diet and hypertension disappears after stratification by socioeconomic status (SES), and it disappears in every stratum. This pattern is classic for confounding.

Confounding occurs when a third variable is:

  • Associated with the exposure (poor diet is more common in certain SES groups).
  • Independently associated with the outcome (hypertension risk differs by SES through access to healthcare, stress, obesity patterns, salt intake, physical activity, etc).
  • Not on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome.

When SES is a confounder, the crude estimate is distorted. After stratification, if the exposure–outcome association becomes null in all strata, it implies that the original association was largely due to differences in SES distribution between exposed and unexposed groups rather than a true causal effect of diet.

In Rothman’s model:

  • A “sufficient cause” is represented by a whole pie, meaning a complete set of causal components that, together, inevitably produce the disease.
  • Each slice is a “component cause.”

questions.explanation:

  • In this scenario, the progressive decrease in blood pressure over time, regardless of whether the participant is receiving Drug X or Drug Y, suggests a period effect.
  • This could be due to factors such as lifestyle modifications, increased adherence to study protocols, or other time-related influences that affect blood pressure.

Other Options:
Option A. Carryover effect: This occurs when the effects of the first treatment persist into the period when the second treatment is administered. The presence of a washout period is intended to minimize this effect. In this case, the consistent decline over time does not align with a carryover effect.

Option C. Regression to the mean: This statistical phenomenon occurs when extreme measurements tend to move closer to the average upon subsequent testing. It does not adequately explain a continuous downward trend over the study period.

Option D. Sequence effect: This refers to differences in outcomes depending on the order in which treatments are administered. The observed trend is independent of treatment sequence, making this explanation less likely.

Maternal IgG antibodies are actively transferred across the placenta during the third trimester and provide passive protection against several toxin-mediated and viral infections, including tetanus, diphtheria, and measles during the first few months of life.   • Does not provide reliable protection: Polio (especially mucosal infection).

  • Maximum transplacental antibody transfer occurs during the third trimester, making preterm infants more susceptible to infections.

A public health team is evaluating the effectiveness of the National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (NIDDCP) in a mountainous district with historically high endemic goitre prevalence. During assessment, investigators collect household salt samples, neonatal screening data, and urinary iodine measurements from school-going children. The team wishes to identify:

2.	The most appropriate indicator for assessing population-level iodine sufficiency in neonates
3.	The minimum recommended iodine concentration in household salt at the point of consumption

options.text: Urinary iodine excretion |‌ Neonatal TSH | 15 ppm

questions.correct_answer: B. Urinary iodine excretion | Neonatal TSH | 15 ppm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urinary iodine excretion | Neonatal TSH | 15 ppm

  • Urinary iodine excretion (UIE) is the best epidemiological indicator and the best marker of recent iodine intake, as >90% of ingested iodine is excreted in urine.
  • Neonatal TSH is considered the best indicator for assessing population iodine sufficiency, especially in neonatal screening programs.
  • Under public health recommendations, iodine content of household salt should be at least 15 ppm at the consumer level.
  • Daily iodine requirement:
    • Adults: 150 µg/day
    • Pregnancy/lactation: 250 µg/day.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mass chemoprophylaxis is generally not recommended

In cholera outbreaks, routine public health practice prioritizes rapid case management and WASH measures rather than giving antibiotics to all contacts. Mass chemoprophylaxis is generally discouraged because it has limited impact on outbreak control, promotes antimicrobial resistance, can cause adverse drug effects, and diverts resources from interventions that actually reduce transmission.

Core outbreak control pillars are:

  • Early detection and prompt rehydration (ORS for most, IV Ringer lactate for severe dehydration).
  • Antibiotics for moderate to severe cholera to shorten duration and reduce stool volume, used for cases rather than mass contacts.
  • Safe water, sanitation, and hygiene including chlorination, safe storage, hand hygiene, and safe food practices.
  • Risk communication, surveillance, and in some settings, oral cholera vaccine as an adjunct.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nitrates

A 4-month-old infant with cyanosis, irritability, and feeding difficulty after consuming formula prepared with shallow well water is a classic presentation of methemoglobinemia (Blue Baby Syndrome).

  • Nitrates in well water (from agricultural runoff, sewage contamination) are converted to nitrites in the infant gut.
  • Nitrites oxidize hemoglobin (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺) → methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen → cyanosis.
  • Infants <6 months are especially vulnerable due to:
    o    Low gastric acidity
    o    Immature methemoglobin reductase enzyme system

The probability that a person with a positive test actually has the disease is called the Positive Predictive Value (PPV). PPV depends on:

  • Sensitivity = 85%

  • Specificity = 95%
    • True negatives = 95% of 950 = 902.5
    • False positives = 47.5

Now:

  • PPV =  42.5 / ( 42.5 + 47.5) =  42.5 / 90 = approx 47%
  • In low-prevalence diseases, even highly specific tests can have a relatively low PPV due to increased false positives. Increasing prevalence increases PPV and decreases NPV.

questions.raw_text: A study finds that a poor diet is associated with hypertension. After stratifying by socioeconomic status, the association disappears in every stratum. Which best explains this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Confounding by socioeconomic status

The key clue is that the crude association between poor diet and hypertension disappears after stratification by socioeconomic status (SES), and it disappears in every stratum. This pattern is classic for confounding.

Confounding occurs when a third variable is:

  • Associated with the exposure (poor diet is more common in certain SES groups).
  • Independently associated with the outcome (hypertension risk differs by SES through access to healthcare, stress, obesity patterns, salt intake, physical activity, etc).
  • Not on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome.

When SES is a confounder, the crude estimate is distorted. After stratification, if the exposure–outcome association becomes null in all strata, it implies that the original association was largely due to differences in SES distribution between exposed and unexposed groups rather than a true causal effect of diet.

Correct answer: B. Rothman causal pie model

The stem explicitly describes the idea of a necessary component cause that is not sufficient alone, and it asks for the model in which multiple component causes together form a sufficient cause. This is the core idea of the Rothman causal pie model.

In Rothman’s model:

  • A “sufficient cause” is represented by a whole pie, meaning a complete set of causal components that, together, inevitably produce the disease.
  • Each slice is a “component cause.”
  • A component can be necessary in a particular causal pathway if it appears in every sufficient cause for that disease in that population, but it is still not sufficient by itself.
  • Removing 1 component cause can prevent disease in those individuals whose sufficient cause required that component. It will not prevent all disease if there are alternative pies that do not include that component.

This fits the occupational cluster description where asbestos might be one crucial piece among several, such as co-exposures, smoking, genetic susceptibility, intensity-duration, and other workplace factors.

Hill’s criteria for disease causation include:
(1) Strength of association, where a higher relative risk or odds ratio suggests a stronger likelihood of causality;

(3) Specificity, in which a single exposure leads to a specific disease (though this is the weakest criterion and lack of specificity does not exclude causation);
(4) Temporality, the most important and mandatory criterion, which states that the exposure must precede the disease;

(7) Coherence, whereby the observed association does not contradict known facts about the natural history and biology of the disease;

(9) Analogy, where similar exposures are known to cause similar effects.

Sensitivity is a measure of a diagnostic test’s ability to detect disease and is not included among the Bradford Hill causal criteria.

questions.text: An ASHA (Accredited Social​ Health Activist) mobiliz‍es pregnant women for ant​enatal check-ups, encoura​ges families to attend Vi​llage Health, Sanitation ‌and Nutrition Day (VHSND)‌ sessions, promotes immun​ization, and conducts hea​lth education within the ​community. questions.raw_text: An ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) mobilizes pregnant women for antenatal check-ups, encourages families to attend Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Day (VHSND) sessions, promotes immunization, and conducts health education within the community. These activities primarily reflect which principle of Primary Health Care (PHC)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Community participation

Community participation is one of the four fundamental principles of Primary Health Care (PHC) as outlined in the Alma-Ata Declaration (1978). It emphasizes the active involvement of individuals, families, and the community in planning, implementing, and utilizing health services.

ASHA workers are community-based health activists who:

  • Mobilize people to attend Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Day (VHSND) sessions
  • Promote antenatal care and institutional deliveries
  • Encourage childhood immunization
  • Provide health education on nutrition, sanitation, and family planning
  • Serve as a link between the community and the health system

These responsibilities primarily foster community ownership and participation, making community participation the best answer.

Why not the other options?

  • B. Equitable distribution: Refers to ensuring equal access to essential health services for all sections of the population, especially underserved groups. Although ASHAs help improve access, their defining role in VHSNDs is community mobilization.
  • C. Intersectoral coordination: Involves collaboration between sectors such as health, education, sanitation, nutrition, agriculture, and rural development. While VHSNDs involve multiple sectors, the ASHA's primary function is to engage the community.
  • D. Appropriate technology: Refers to the use of simple, scientifically sound, affordable, and locally acceptable technologies, such as ORS, home-based newborn care, and rapid diagnostic tests.

High-yield pearl
Four principles of Primary Health Care (Alma-Ata):

  1. Equitable distribution – Health care for all, with emphasis on underserved populations.
  2. Community participation – Active involvement of the community in health programs.
  3. Intersectoral coordination – Collaboration among health and non-health sectors.
  4. Appropriate technology – Affordable, practical, evidence-based interventions.

questions.text: A public health officer wa​nts to assess environment‍al iodine deficiency in a​ district. Which indicato​r should be used?
questions.raw_text: A public health officer wants to assess environmental iodine deficiency in a district. Which indicator should be used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neonatal hypothyroidism prevalence

Park lists four criteria for assessing Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD) in a community: goitre prevalence, urinary iodine excretion, neonatal hypothyroidism, and thyroid function tests (T4/TSH). Among these, neonatal hypothyroidism is specifically described as the indicator of "environmental iodine deficiency" — because the neonatal thyroid has minimal iodine reserve, it is the most sensitive tissue to a deficient environment, and neonatal TSH reflects iodine status at the time of birth rather than years of past exposure. The cut-off: if >3% of neonates have TSH >5 mIU/L on cord/heel-prick blood, environmental iodine deficiency exists in that population. It also carries a direct public-health meaning — risk of brain damage in the community.

Other options:

  • A. Serum thyroxine → an individual diagnostic test, poor sensitivity for community surveys; often normal in mild deficiency.
  • B. Goitre prevalence → indicator of chronic/past iodine deficiency; goitre persists for years even after iodine repletion ("goitre lags"). Used for grading endemicity (>5% in 6–12 yr children = endemic).
  • D. Urinary iodine excretion → best indicator of current dietary iodine intake / recent nutritional status (median <100 µg/L = deficiency). Reflects intake, not the disease burden of environmental deficiency.

Pearl:

  • Goitre = past deficiency
  • Urinary iodine = present intake
  • Neonatal hypothyroidism = environmental deficiency + brain damage risk.

The Bhore Committee (Health Survey and Development Committee, 1946) was the first committee in India to recommend the concept of comprehensive health services. It emphasized that preventive, promotive, curative, and rehabilitative services should be integrated and made available to all individuals irrespective of their ability to pay.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 6 departments

The Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy is structured around 6×6×6 framework, which includes 6 target beneficiary groups, 6 interventions, and 6 institutional mechanisms.

The 6 Beneficiary Groups

The program targets populations most vulnerable to anemia:

  1. Children (6–59 months)
  2. Children (5–9 years)
  3. Adolescents (10–19 years)
  4. Women of reproductive age (15–49 years)
  5. Pregnant women
  6. Lactating mothers

The 6 Interventions of Anemia Mukt Bharat:

  1. Prophylactic Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) Supplementation: Age-appropriate dosage for children (6-59 months), children (5-9 years), adolescents (10-19 years), women of reproductive age (15-49 years), pregnant women, and lactating women.
  2. Periodic Deworming: Administering anthelmintic drugs (Albendazole) to children, adolescents, and pregnant women to eliminate parasitic worms.
  3. Intensified Year-Round Behaviour Change Communication (BCC) Campaign: Promoting healthy eating habits (Solid Body, Smart Mind), including iron-rich foods and delayed cord clamping (by 3 minutes) at birth.
  4. Testing and Treatment of Anemia: Using digital, non-invasive methods (digital haemoglobinometer) for testing and point-of-care treatment.
  5. Mandatory Provision of Iron & Folic Acid Fortified Foods: Ensuring IFA-fortified foods are available in all government-funded public health programs.
  6. Addressing Non-Nutritional Causes of Anemia: Targeting anemia in endemic areas caused by malaria, hemoglobinopathies, and fluorosis.
The 6 Institutional Mechanisms

These ensure proper implementation and monitoring:

  1. Inter-ministerial coordination
  2. National Anaemia Mukt Bharat Unit
  3. Convergence with other programs
  4. Supply chain management
  5. Digital monitoring
  6. Capacity building and training

Understanding the structural pillars of AMB helps distinguish program design elements from implementation personnel.

Distractor-by-distractor analysis:

  • A. It is a priority-based budgeting system: True. ZBB is inherently a priority-based system. Managers prepare "decision packages" for every activity, which are then ranked in order of priority, and resources are allocated down that ranking until funds are exhausted.
  • B. It proceeds from resources to targets: False. ZBB proceeds from targets to resources, not the other way around. You first define objectives/activities, justify them from a zero base, and then work out what resources they require. Proceeding from resources to targets — letting the existing resource envelope dictate what gets done — is the hallmark of conventional/incremental budgeting.
  • C. It does not depend on data from the previous budget: True. The defining feature of ZBB: each budgeting cycle starts from a "zero base" with no reference to the previous year's allocations. Last year's budget carries no automatic legitimacy.
  • D. Every line item of the budget must be justified and approved: True. Every line item and every activity must be justified afresh and approved on its own merits — nothing is carried forward by default.

High-yield contrast table:

| Feature | Incremental (traditional) budgeting | Zero-Based Budgeting |
| ------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| Starting point | Previous year's budget ± increment | Zero base every cycle |
| Direction | Resources → targets | Targets → resources |
| Justification | Only the increment is justified | Every item justified |
| Basis of allocation | Historical precedent | Priority-ranked decision packages |
| Effort/cost | Low | High (time- and paper-intensive) |

Exam pearl: ZBB was popularized by Peter Pyhrr (Texas Instruments, 1970s) and is asked in PSM under health planning and management. The "targets → resources" direction is the classic trap — it mirrors the planning cycle itself, where objectives are set first and resources mobilized to meet them.

•	Statement 2- Precontemplation – A person is considering starting morning walks and the benefits to their health

Correct answer: A. Statement 1 and 3 are correct

The Stages of Change (Transtheoretical Model):
A behavioral change framework (Prochaska & DiClemente) describing readiness to change across sequential stages.

Stages of Change

  • Precontemplation
    • No intention to change
    • Unaware / denial / resistance
    • Example: “Smoking isn’t a problem for me.”
  • Contemplation
    • Aware of problem, thinking about change
    • Ambivalence present
    • Example: “I should quit, but it’s hard.”
  • Preparation
    • Intends to act soon
    • Small initial steps taken
    • Example: “I’ll quit next month; I’ve reduced cigarettes.”
  • Action
    • Active behavior change
    • High effort and risk of relapse
    • Example: Recently stopped smoking
  • Maintenance
    • Sustained change (>6 months)
    • Focus on preventing relapse
    • Example: Abstinent for months, avoiding triggers
  • Relapse
    • Return to old behavior
    • Common and part of the cycle

Contemplation involves awareness and thinking about change (Statement 1 correct), while precontemplation reflects lack of intent to change; considering health benefits fits early contemplation rather than denial. (hence statement 2 is incorrect)
Maintenance refers to sustained behaviour change for >6 months, as in quitting smoking for one year (Statement 3 correct).
The action phase involves active behaviour change; expressing helplessness reflects precontemplation, making Statement 4 incorrect.

questions.raw_text: Which one of the following most appropriately describes the “tracking” phenomenon of blood pressure?

options.text: Continuous monitoring of b‌lood pressure on any indi‍vidual to keep a track of‍ blood pressure for early​ diagnosis of hypertensio‌n
Persistence of rank order ‌of blood pressure in indi‍viduals as they grow olde‍r

questions.correct_answer: B. Persistence of rank order of blood pressure in individuals as they grow older
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Persistence of rank order of blood pressure in individuals as they grow older

  • "Tracking" in epidemiology refers to the phenomenon whereby an individual's relative position (rank/percentile) within a population distribution of a measurement tends to persist over time as the population as a whole ages. In the context of blood pressure, this means that a child or adolescent whose BP is in the higher percentile of their peer group tends to remain in a similarly high percentile as they grow into adulthood — even as the absolute BP values of everyone in the cohort rise with age.
  • Significance:
    • Tracking underlies the rationale for early identification of children/adolescents with high-normal or elevated BP, since those with higher BP early in life are more likely to become hypertensive adults.
    • It's a key concept in longitudinal/cohort studies of chronic disease risk factors (also applies to BMI, cholesterol, and other continuous variables).

Why not the other options?

  • A. Continuous monitoring of blood pressure on any individual to keep a track of blood pressure for early diagnosis of hypertension: Describes serial/continuous BP monitoring for diagnosis — not "tracking" in the epidemiological sense; this is simply longitudinal measurement.
  • C. Keeping a track of the prevalence of hypertension in a community: Describes surveillance of hypertension prevalence at a population level — a public health monitoring activity, not "tracking" of individual rank.
  • D. Tracking of twins for change in blood pressure to see the effect of genetic makeup: Describes a twin study design used to estimate heritability — a different research methodology, not the tracking phenomenon.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Community participation

Community participation is one of the four fundamental principles of Primary Health Care (PHC) as outlined in the Alma-Ata Declaration (1978). It emphasizes the active involvement of individuals, families, and the community in planning, implementing, and utilizing health services.

ASHA workers are community-based health activists who:

  • Mobilize people to attend Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Day (VHSND) sessions
  • Promote antenatal care and institutional deliveries
  • Encourage childhood immunization
  • Provide health education on nutrition, sanitation, and family planning
  • Serve as a link between the community and the health system

These responsibilities primarily foster community ownership and participation, making community participation the best answer.

Why not the other options?

  • B. Equitable distribution: Refers to ensuring equal access to essential health services for all sections of the population, especially underserved groups. Although ASHAs help improve access, their defining role in VHSNDs is community mobilization.
  • C. Intersectoral coordination: Involves collaboration between sectors such as health, education, sanitation, nutrition, agriculture, and rural development. While VHSNDs involve multiple sectors, the ASHA's primary function is to engage the community.
  • D. Appropriate technology: Refers to the use of simple, scientifically sound, affordable, and locally acceptable technologies, such as ORS, home-based newborn care, and rapid diagnostic tests.

High-yield pearl
Four principles of Primary Health Care (Alma-Ata):

  1. Equitable distribution – Health care for all, with emphasis on underserved populations.
  2. Community participation – Active involvement of the community in health programs.
  3. Intersectoral coordination – Collaboration among health and non-health sectors.
  4. Appropriate technology – Affordable, practical, evidence-based interventions.

questions.text: A public health officer wa‌nts to assess environment‍al iodine deficiency in a‍ district. Which indicato​r should be used?
questions.raw_text: A public health officer wants to assess environmental iodine deficiency in a district. Which indicator should be used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neonatal hypothyroidism prevalence

Park lists four criteria for assessing Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD) in a community: goitre prevalence, urinary iodine excretion, neonatal hypothyroidism, and thyroid function tests (T4/TSH). Among these, neonatal hypothyroidism is specifically described as the indicator of "environmental iodine deficiency" — because the neonatal thyroid has minimal iodine reserve, it is the most sensitive tissue to a deficient environment, and neonatal TSH reflects iodine status at the time of birth rather than years of past exposure. The cut-off: if >3% of neonates have TSH >5 mIU/L on cord/heel-prick blood, environmental iodine deficiency exists in that population. It also carries a direct public-health meaning — risk of brain damage in the community.

Other options:

  • A. Serum thyroxine → an individual diagnostic test, poor sensitivity for community surveys; often normal in mild deficiency.
  • B. Goitre prevalence → indicator of chronic/past iodine deficiency; goitre persists for years even after iodine repletion ("goitre lags"). Used for grading endemicity (>5% in 6–12 yr children = endemic).
  • D. Urinary iodine excretion → best indicator of current dietary iodine intake / recent nutritional status (median <100 µg/L = deficiency). Reflects intake, not the disease burden of environmental deficiency.

Pearl:

  • Goitre = past deficiency
  • Urinary iodine = present intake
  • Neonatal hypothyroidism = environmental deficiency + brain damage risk.

The program targets populations most vulnerable to anemia:

  4. Women of reproductive age (15–49 years)
  5. Pregnant women
  6. Lactating mothers

The 6 Interventions of Anemia Mukt Bharat:

  1. Prophylactic Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) Supplementation: Age-appropriate dosage for children (6-59 months), children (5-9 years), adolescents (10-19 years), women of reproductive age (15-49 years), pregnant women, and lactating women.

  3. Intensified Year-Round Behaviour Change Communication (BCC) Campaign: Promoting healthy eating habits (Solid Body, Smart Mind), including iron-rich foods and delayed cord clamping (by 3 minutes) at birth.
  4. Testing and Treatment of Anemia: Using digital, non-invasive methods (digital haemoglobinometer) for testing and point-of-care treatment.
  5. Mandatory Provision of Iron & Folic Acid Fortified Foods: Ensuring IFA-fortified foods are available in all government-funded public health programs.
  6. Addressing Non-Nutritional Causes of Anemia: Targeting anemia in endemic areas caused by malaria, hemoglobinopathies, and fluorosis.
The 6 Institutional Mechanisms

These ensure proper implementation and monitoring:

  1. Inter-ministerial coordination
  2. National Anaemia Mukt Bharat Unit
  3. Convergence with other programs
  4. Supply chain management
  5. Digital monitoring
  6. Capacity building and training

options.text: It is a priority-based bud‍geting system
It proceeds from resources‍ to targets

Every line item of the bud‍get must be justified and​ approved

questions.correct_answer: B. It proceeds from resources to targets
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It proceeds from resources to targets

Distractor-by-distractor analysis:

  • A. It is a priority-based budgeting system: True. ZBB is inherently a priority-based system. Managers prepare "decision packages" for every activity, which are then ranked in order of priority, and resources are allocated down that ranking until funds are exhausted.
  • B. It proceeds from resources to targets: False. ZBB proceeds from targets to resources, not the other way around. You first define objectives/activities, justify them from a zero base, and then work out what resources they require. Proceeding from resources to targets — letting the existing resource envelope dictate what gets done — is the hallmark of conventional/incremental budgeting.
  • C. It does not depend on data from the previous budget: True. The defining feature of ZBB: each budgeting cycle starts from a "zero base" with no reference to the previous year's allocations. Last year's budget carries no automatic legitimacy.
  • D. Every line item of the budget must be justified and approved: True. Every line item and every activity must be justified afresh and approved on its own merits — nothing is carried forward by default.

High-yield contrast table:

| Feature | Incremental (traditional) budgeting | Zero-Based Budgeting |
| ------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| Starting point | Previous year's budget ± increment | Zero base every cycle |
| Direction | Resources → targets | Targets → resources |
| Justification | Only the increment is justified | Every item justified |
| Basis of allocation | Historical precedent | Priority-ranked decision packages |
| Effort/cost | Low | High (time- and paper-intensive) |

Exam pearl: ZBB was popularized by Peter Pyhrr (Texas Instruments, 1970s) and is asked in PSM under health planning and management. The "targets → resources" direction is the classic trap — it mirrors the planning cycle itself, where objectives are set first and resources mobilized to meet them.

Hill’s criteria for disease causation include:

(3) Specificity, in which a single exposure leads to a specific disease (though this is the weakest criterion and lack of specificity does not exclude causation);
(4) Temporality, the most important and mandatory criterion, which states that the exposure must precede the disease;
(5) Biological gradient (dose–response relationship), where increasing exposure results in increasing disease risk;
(6) Biological plausibility, indicating that the association is biologically reasonable based on existing knowledge;
(7) Coherence, whereby the observed association does not contradict known facts about the natural history and biology of the disease;

(9) Analogy, where similar exposures are known to cause similar effects.

questions.raw_text: Which one of the following most appropriately describes the “tracking” phenomenon of blood pressure?

options.text: Continuous monitoring of b‍lood pressure on any indi​vidual to keep a track of​ blood pressure for early​ diagnosis of hypertensio​n
Persistence of rank order ‍of blood pressure in indi​viduals as they grow olde​r
Keeping a track of the pre‍valence of hypertension i​n a community
Tracking of twins for chan‍ge in blood pressure to s​ee the effect of genetic ​makeup

questions.correct_answer: B. Persistence of rank order of blood pressure in individuals as they grow older
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Persistence of rank order of blood pressure in individuals as they grow older

  • "Tracking" in epidemiology refers to the phenomenon whereby an individual's relative position (rank/percentile) within a population distribution of a measurement tends to persist over time as the population as a whole ages. In the context of blood pressure, this means that a child or adolescent whose BP is in the higher percentile of their peer group tends to remain in a similarly high percentile as they grow into adulthood — even as the absolute BP values of everyone in the cohort rise with age.
  • Significance:
    • Tracking underlies the rationale for early identification of children/adolescents with high-normal or elevated BP, since those with higher BP early in life are more likely to become hypertensive adults.
    • It's a key concept in longitudinal/cohort studies of chronic disease risk factors (also applies to BMI, cholesterol, and other continuous variables).

Why not the other options?

  • A. Continuous monitoring of blood pressure on any individual to keep a track of blood pressure for early diagnosis of hypertension: Describes serial/continuous BP monitoring for diagnosis — not "tracking" in the epidemiological sense; this is simply longitudinal measurement.
  • C. Keeping a track of the prevalence of hypertension in a community: Describes surveillance of hypertension prevalence at a population level — a public health monitoring activity, not "tracking" of individual rank.
  • D. Tracking of twins for change in blood pressure to see the effect of genetic makeup: Describes a twin study design used to estimate heritability — a different research methodology, not the tracking phenomenon.

  5. Mandatory Provision of Iron & Folic Acid Fortified Foods: Ensuring IFA-fortified foods are available in all government-funded public health programs.
  6. Addressing Non-Nutritional Causes of Anemia: Targeting anemia in endemic areas caused by malaria, hemoglobinopathies, and fluorosis.
The 6 Institutional Mechanisms

These ensure proper implementation and monitoring:

  1. Inter-ministerial coordination
  2. National Anaemia Mukt Bharat Unit
  3. Convergence with other programs
  4. Supply chain management
  5. Digital monitoring

2.	It is primarily a disorder of memory

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 5

Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness caused by an underlying medical condition and is typically reversible if the cause is treated.

  • Core deficit: Impaired attention (most important distinguishing feature)
  • Clinical features:
    • Acute onset with fluctuating course
    • Altered level of consciousness
    • Visual hallucinations common
    • Sleep–wake cycle disturbance
  • Subtypes:
    • Hyperactive (agitation)
    • Hypoactive (lethargy, often missed)
    • Mixed
  • Investigations: EEG → generalized slowing
  • Management principle:
    • Always identify and treat underlying cause
    • Benzodiazepines → only in withdrawal delirium

questions.text: A 42-year-old woman with s​evere major depressive di​sorder and suicidal ideat​ion is planned for electr​oconvulsive therapy (ECT)​. She has been taking clo​nazepam regularly for ins​omnia. Which of the follo‍wing medication adjustmen‌ts should be made before ‌ECT?
questions.raw_text: A 42-year-old woman with severe major depressive disorder and suicidal ideation is planned for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). She has been taking clonazepam regularly for insomnia. Which of the following medication adjustments should be made before ECT?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Discontinue clonazepam before ECT

ECT works by inducing a generalized seizure of adequate duration and quality. The therapeutic effect depends on achieving a robust, adequately prolonged seizure (roughly ≥15–20 seconds of motor activity / ≥25 seconds on EEG). Anything that raises the seizure threshold or shortens seizure duration undermines efficacy. Benzodiazepines are potent anticonvulsants, so they directly oppose what ECT is trying to achieve.

Mechanism — why clonazepam interferes
Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators at the GABA_A receptor. They increase the frequency of chloride channel opening → hyperpolarization → raised seizure threshold and reduced neuronal excitability. In the ECT context this translates to:

  • Higher seizure threshold → may need higher electrical charge, sometimes failure to elicit a seizure at all
  • Shortened seizure duration → subtherapeutic/abortive seizures
  • Reduced treatment efficacy → poorer clinical response, more sessions needed

Clonazepam is particularly problematic because of its long half-life (\~30–40 hours), so its anticonvulsant effect lingers across treatment sessions rather than washing out between them.

Why the other options are wrong:

| Option | Why incorrect |
| ------ | ------------- |
| A. Increase clonazepam | Worsens the problem — greater GABAergic anticonvulsant effect, higher threshold, shorter/abortive seizures. Directly antitherapeutic. |
| B. Continue unchanged | Ongoing anticonvulsant load compromises seizure adequacy and efficacy. Not acceptable when a good seizure is the goal. |
| D. Replace with phenobarbital | Phenobarbital is a barbiturate — also a GABA_A modulator (increases duration of chloride channel opening) and an even more potent, longer-acting anticonvulsant. Swapping one anticonvulsant sedative for a stronger one is counterproductive. |

Practical/clinical nuances (exam-relevant):

  • Ideally taper/discontinue benzodiazepines before starting an ECT course. Abrupt withdrawal risks rebound insomnia, anxiety, and (with high doses/long use) withdrawal seizures — so a planned taper is preferred over sudden cessation where feasible.
  • If a benzodiazepine genuinely cannot be stopped (e.g., dependence, severe agitation), flumazenil (a benzodiazepine antagonist) can be given immediately before the stimulus to transiently reverse the anticonvulsant effect and allow an adequate seizure. This is the standard workaround.
  • For insomnia in a patient heading into ECT, a non-benzodiazepine agent with minimal anticonvulsant/threshold-raising effect is preferred as a substitute.

He has racing thoughts and speaks rapidly. The patient has stopped going to his job having decided to stay home and "unravel the secrets of the universe." He has been drawing shapes and equations on the walls, and he has accused his wife of working for the police and trying to steal his secrets. Prior to examination, the patient becomes increasingly agitated and is hospitalized against his will. He is prescribed multiple medications to address his symptoms. Five days later, the patient is calm but has difficulty moving spontaneously or getting out of bed. He does not respond appropriately to questions and appears newly disoriented and confused. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), blood pressure is 162/98 mmHg, pulse is 98/min, and respirations are 20/min. Dysregulation of which of the following neurotransmitters is most likely to be the primary cause of this patient's new symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dopamine

This patient’s fever, rigidity, confusion, and autonomic instability after antipsychotic treatment are consistent with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), a life-threatening reaction caused by dopamine (D₂) receptor blockade.

  • Marked dopamine deficiency in the central nervous system
  • Hypothalamic dopamine blockade → hyperthermia and autonomic instability
  • Nigrostriatal blockade → severe rigidity and bradykinesia
  • Altered mental status and elevated CK from muscle breakdown

Management:

  • Stop antipsychotic immediately
  • Supportive care (fluids, cooling)
  • Dantrolene or bromocriptine if severe

The patient's last menstrual period was 4 months ago; her menses tend to be erratic, occurring every 30-60 days and lasting 4-8 days. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for this patient's infertility?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Risperidone

Risperidone commonly causes hyperprolactinemia due to dopamine D₂ receptor blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, which normally inhibits prolactin release from the anterior pituitary. Increased prolactin suppresses GnRH secretion, leading to decreased LH and FSH, resulting in menstrual irregularities, anovulation, and infertility.

Clinical effects of antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia:

  • Amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea
  • Infertility
  • Galactorrhea
  • Decreased libido
  • Gynecomastia in men

Among antipsychotics, risperidone and typical antipsychotics have the highest risk of hyperprolactinemia, whereas aripiprazole (partial dopamine agonist) has minimal or may reduce prolactin levels.

Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose (eg, amitriptyline) causes a characteristic triad of anticholinergic effects, seizures, and cardiotoxicity due to sodium channel blockade.

  • Hypotension and coma in severe cases

  • Anticholinergic and antihistaminic effects → delirium and autonomic symptoms
  • GABA antagonism → seizures

Caffeine causes release of​ chemicals from locus coe​ruleus that causes awaken​ing
Caffeine has histaminic ac​tion in the brain that le​ads to awakening
Caffeine inhibits adenosin​e receptors, thus leading​ to awakening

questions.correct_answer: D. Caffeine inhibits adenosine receptors, thus leading to awakening
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Caffeine inhibits adenosine receptors, thus leading to awakening

The neurochemical basis of sleep–wake regulation, specifically the role of adenosine and caffeine.

  • Adenosine:
    • Builds up during wakefulness
    • Promotes sleep by inhibiting neuronal activity
  • Caffeine mechanism:
    • Adenosine receptor antagonist (A1, A2A)
    • Blocks sleep-promoting effects → increases alertness and wakefulness
  • Clinical correlation:
    • Consumption close to bedtime → delayed sleep onset (insomnia)
    • Common cause of lifestyle-related sleep disturbance
  • High-yield differentiation:
    • Locus coeruleus → norepinephrine (arousal system) but not caffeine’s primary mechanism
    • Histamine → wakefulness (via hypothalamus), but not caffeine action

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypnogram

A hypnogram is a graphical representation of sleep architecture that shows the cyclical pattern of sleep stages (NREM stages N1, N2, N3 and REM sleep) across the night. Helps evaluate sleep disorders like insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnea, and parasomnias by analyzing sleep stage distribution and fragmentation.

Other Options:
B. Electroencephalogram (EEG)

  • EEG shows brain wave patterns (alpha, beta, theta, delta waves) as electrical tracings.
  • It does not show sleep stages across time in a staged graph format.

C. Polysomnogram
Polysomnography is a comprehensive sleep study that records multiple parameters:

  • EEG (brain activity)
  • EOG (eye movements)
  • EMG (muscle activity)
  • ECG, airflow, oxygen saturation

D. Epworth Sleepiness Scale

  • A questionnaire used to assess daytime sleepiness.
  • It is not a graphical sleep-stage diagram.

questions.raw_text:
A 44-year-old woman has fear of contamination leading to her repeated hand-washing. With regard to her management, consider the following statements:
1.	Diagnosis is made on the basis of history.
2.	The disorder responds to antidepressant drugs.
3.	Patients may be subjected to cognitive behavioural therapy.
4.	Admission to a psychiatry ward is mandatory.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The patient has obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), characterized here by contamination obsessions and repetitive hand-washing compulsions.

  1. Diagnosis is made on the basis of history: Correct
    • OCD is primarily a clinical diagnosis, based on the presence of obsessions and/or compulsions that are time-consuming or cause significant distress/functional impairment.
  2. Responds to antidepressant drugs: Correct
    • SSRIs such as fluoxetine, sertraline, fluvoxamine, paroxetine and escitalopram are first-line pharmacological treatments.
    • Clomipramine, a TCA with strong serotonergic activity, is also effective.
  3. Cognitive behavioural therapy: Correct
    • CBT, particularly exposure and response prevention (ERP), is a first-line treatment.
  4. Psychiatric admission is mandatory: Incorrect
    • Most patients are treated on an outpatient basis. Hospitalization is reserved for severe cases, significant functional impairment, suicidality, or inability to care for oneself.

  • Not implicated in OCD pathogenesis.

  • Significant distress or impairment in social and occupational functioning.

  • Cognitive restructuring

Despite repeated reassurance that all reports are normal, he remains convinced that he has a serious illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypochondriasis

Illness Anxiety Disorder (formerly called Hypochondriasis) is characterized by a persistent fear or conviction of having a serious medical illness despite minimal or no physical symptoms, normal examination findings, and repeated medical reassurance. The anxiety persists for at least 6 months and leads to repeated doctor visits, investigations, or excessive health-related behaviors.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Somatic Symptom Disorder: Characterized by distressing physical symptoms with excessive thoughts or behaviors related to those symptoms. In this case, the primary problem is fear of disease, not significant physical symptoms.
  • C. Delusional disorder, somatic type: The belief is fixed and unshakeable (delusional) despite overwhelming contrary evidence. Patients generally lack insight. In illness anxiety disorder, some insight is usually preserved.
  • D. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD): Involves excessive anxiety about multiple aspects of life (work, family, finances), not specifically about having a serious illness.

| Disorder | Key Feature |
| -------- | ----------- |
| Illness Anxiety Disorder (Hypochondriasis) | Fear of serious illness with minimal or no physical symptoms |
| Somatic Symptom Disorder | Prominent physical symptoms with excessive concern |
| Delusional Disorder (Somatic Type) | Fixed false belief of having a disease despite evidence |
| Generalized Anxiety Disorder | Excessive worry about multiple life domains |

Correct answer: C. Pathological doubt

Pathological doubt is one of the hallmark symptoms of adult OCD. Patients experience persistent uncertainty about whether routine tasks have been completed correctly (eg, locking doors, turning off appliances). This leads to repetitive checking compulsions aimed at reducing anxiety.

Although aggressive, sexual, and symmetry-related obsessions are well-recognized manifestations of OCD, pathological doubt with checking rituals is among the most characteristic and frequently encountered clinical presentations.

Educational Objective:

  • In adults with OCD, the most common obsession is contamination, typically associated with washing compulsions.
  • Pathological doubt is the second most common obsession and is classically associated with checking compulsions.

This question emphasizes the ability to differentiate anxiety disorders from organic medical causes, particularly hyperthyroidism presenting with psychiatric symptoms.

options.text: Association of conditioned‌ stimulus with conditione​d response

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Conditioned stimulus provokes conditioned response after learning

Classical conditioning is a form of associative learning in which a previously neutral stimulus (conditioned stimulus), after repeated pairing with an unconditioned stimulus, acquires the ability to elicit a conditioned response on its own. Thus, after learning, the conditioned stimulus alone provokes the conditioned response.

  • The defining feature of classical conditioning is that the conditioned stimulus (CS) elicits the conditioned response (CR) after repeated association with the unconditioned stimulus (US).

Why not the other options?

  • A. Association of conditioned stimulus with conditioned response: Describes the final association but does not define the learning process.
  • B. Association of unconditioned stimulus with unconditioned response: This is an innate reflex, not learned behavior.
  • C. Unconditioned stimulus produces conditioned response after learning: The unconditioned stimulus always elicits the unconditioned response (UR); it does not produce a conditioned response.

  • Exhaustion stage – Prolonged stress leads to depletion of resources, resulting in fatigue, illness, and decreased stress tolerance.

  • Resistance → adaptation with sustained cortisol
  • Exhaustion → burnout and failure of adaptation.

Statement 2: Precontemplation – A person is considering starting morning walk considering its benefits to health.

Correct answer: A. Classical conditioning

Classical conditioning is a form of associative learning in which a neutral stimulus becomes capable of eliciting a physiologic or emotional response after being repeatedly paired with a stimulus that naturally produces that response. Classical conditioning involves automatic, involuntary responses (eg, fear, salivation, autonomic symptoms) produced by learned associations between stimuli — unlike operant conditioning, which involves voluntary behaviors shaped by reinforcement or punishment.

In this case, prior painful or anxiety-provoking medical experiences (unconditioned stimulus) produced fear/anxiety (unconditioned response). Now the stethoscope alone (conditioned stimulus) triggers anxiety, sweating, and tachycardia (conditioned response).
