questions.text: A 42-year-old woman with s​evere major depressive di‍sorder and suicidal ideat​ion is planned for electr‍oconvulsive therapy (ECT)​. She has been taking clo​nazepam regularly for ins‌omnia. Which of the follo‌wing medication adjustmen​ts should be made before ‌ECT?
questions.raw_text: A 42-year-old woman with severe major depressive disorder and suicidal ideation is planned for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). She has been taking clonazepam regularly for insomnia. Which of the following medication adjustments should be made before ECT?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Discontinue clonazepam before ECT

ECT works by inducing a generalized seizure of adequate duration and quality. The therapeutic effect depends on achieving a robust, adequately prolonged seizure (roughly ≥15–20 seconds of motor activity / ≥25 seconds on EEG). Anything that raises the seizure threshold or shortens seizure duration undermines efficacy. Benzodiazepines are potent anticonvulsants, so they directly oppose what ECT is trying to achieve.

Mechanism — why clonazepam interferes
Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators at the GABA_A receptor. They increase the frequency of chloride channel opening → hyperpolarization → raised seizure threshold and reduced neuronal excitability. In the ECT context this translates to:

  • Higher seizure threshold → may need higher electrical charge, sometimes failure to elicit a seizure at all
  • Shortened seizure duration → subtherapeutic/abortive seizures
  • Reduced treatment efficacy → poorer clinical response, more sessions needed

Clonazepam is particularly problematic because of its long half-life (\~30–40 hours), so its anticonvulsant effect lingers across treatment sessions rather than washing out between them.

Why the other options are wrong:

| Option | Why incorrect |
| ------ | ------------- |
| A. Increase clonazepam | Worsens the problem — greater GABAergic anticonvulsant effect, higher threshold, shorter/abortive seizures. Directly antitherapeutic. |
| B. Continue unchanged | Ongoing anticonvulsant load compromises seizure adequacy and efficacy. Not acceptable when a good seizure is the goal. |
| D. Replace with phenobarbital | Phenobarbital is a barbiturate — also a GABA_A modulator (increases duration of chloride channel opening) and an even more potent, longer-acting anticonvulsant. Swapping one anticonvulsant sedative for a stronger one is counterproductive. |

Practical/clinical nuances (exam-relevant):

  • Ideally taper/discontinue benzodiazepines before starting an ECT course. Abrupt withdrawal risks rebound insomnia, anxiety, and (with high doses/long use) withdrawal seizures — so a planned taper is preferred over sudden cessation where feasible.
  • If a benzodiazepine genuinely cannot be stopped (e.g., dependence, severe agitation), flumazenil (a benzodiazepine antagonist) can be given immediately before the stimulus to transiently reverse the anticonvulsant effect and allow an adequate seizure. This is the standard workaround.
  • For insomnia in a patient heading into ECT, a non-benzodiazepine agent with minimal anticonvulsant/threshold-raising effect is preferred as a substitute.

Correct answer: D. Conditioned stimulus provokes conditioned response after learning

Classical conditioning is a form of associative learning in which a previously neutral stimulus (conditioned stimulus), after repeated pairing with an unconditioned stimulus, acquires the ability to elicit a conditioned response on its own. Thus, after learning, the conditioned stimulus alone provokes the conditioned response.

  • The defining feature of classical conditioning is that the conditioned stimulus (CS) elicits the conditioned response (CR) after repeated association with the unconditioned stimulus (US).

Why not the other options?

  • A. Association of conditioned stimulus with conditioned response: Describes the final association but does not define the learning process.
  • B. Association of unconditioned stimulus with unconditioned response: This is an innate reflex, not learned behavior.
  • C. Unconditioned stimulus produces conditioned response after learning: The unconditioned stimulus always elicits the unconditioned response (UR); it does not produce a conditioned response.

In CT imaging, pitch refers to table movement per gantry rotation relative to beam width.
Imagine CT scan table is like a moving conveyor belt.

  • Low pitch → Table moves slowly
  • High pitch → Table moves fast

When the table moves slowly:

  • X-rays overlap more
  • Patient gets more radiation

When the table moves faster (high pitch):

  • X-rays overlap less
  • Patient gets less radiation

So:

  • High pitch = Faster scan = Less overlap = Less radiation dose
  • That’s why option D is wrong.

Simple rule to remember:
📌 Higher pitch → lower dose → slightly lower image quality
Thus:

  • Higher pitch → faster scan, lower radiation dose, slightly lower image quality
  • Lower pitch → slower scan, higher radiation dose, better image quality

Correct answer: C. Mammography uses Bremsstrahlung radiation for better tissue contrast

Normal radiography (X-ray):

  • Uses Tungsten target
  • Uses Aluminum filter
  • More Bremsstrahlung radiation
  • Higher energy X-rays (Needs to penetrate bone, chest, abdomen etc.)
  • Think of it like a “powerful beam” that has to go through thick structures.

Mammography:

  • Uses Molybdenum (or Rhodium) target
  • Uses Molybdenum filter (molybdenum produces X-rays at ideal energy (17–19 keV)
    Lower energy X-rays (for soft tissue contrast)
  • Breast is a soft tissue organ, so we need to see tiny differences (like microcalcifications)
  • So we use low energy X-rays
  • Uses more characteristic radiation, not mainly bremsstrahlung.
  • Think of it like a “gentle, precise beam” made specially for soft tissue contrast.

Bremsstrahlung radiation?

  • Bremsstrahlung = wide range of X-ray energies (mixed spectrum).
  • Good for general X-rays, not for fine soft tissue contrast.

Characteristic radiation?

  • Very specific energy peaks.
  • In mammography, molybdenum produces X-rays at ideal energy
  • This gives excellent breast tissue contrast.

Option-wise:
A) Radiography uses tungsten, mammography uses molybdenum
✔ Correct
B) Beryllium is used as exit window in mammography
✔ Correct (allows low-energy X-rays to pass)
C) Mammography uses Bremsstrahlung radiation for better tissue contrast
❌ Wrong. Mammography mainly uses characteristic radiation from molybdenum (17–19 keV) for better breast tissue contrast.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leptomeningeal cyst

  • A leptomeningeal cyst (growing skull fracture) is a late complication of skull fracture in infants and young children.
  • It occurs when Skull fracture leads to a dural tear allows CSF pulsations and herniation of leptomeninges/brain tissue through the fracture site, leading to progressive enlargement of the bony defect and scalp swelling.
  • It typically presents months to years after head trauma as a painful, enlarging cranial swelling,

most commonly in the parietal region.

Why not other options:
A. Growing scalp hematoma: Resolves over weeks; does not progressively enlarge 1 year later or cause bony defect.
C. Subdural hygroma: CSF collection in subdural space causing neurological signs, not localized skull swelling.
D. Chronic abscess: Shows infection signs (fever, redness, systemic toxicity), not gradual post-traumatic bony expansion.

TAKEAWAY:
Why are growing skull fracture seen in children?

  • The dura sticks firmly to the inner table of skull
  • So when a fracture happens, dura tears along with bone

While In adults:

  • Dura is less tightly attached ,stays intact even if bone fractures
  • No dural tear = no leptomeningeal cyst.

Bremsstrahlung (“braking”) radiation is the principal mechanism of X-ray production. It occurs when high-speed electrons from the cathode are decelerated or deflected by the electric field of the tungsten target nucleus (anode), causing loss of kinetic energy that is emitted as X-ray photons. It accounts for approximately 85–90% of diagnostic X-rays.
The remaining 10–15% of X-rays are produced by characteristic radiation, which results from electron transitions between atomic shells after inner-shell ionization.

  • B. Compton effect: Scattering of X-rays by outer-shell electrons; a major source of image degradation and radiation exposure, not production.
  • C. Pair production: Occurs only with high-energy photons (>1.02 MeV) and is not involved in diagnostic X-ray generation.

questions.correct_answer: D. The higher the pitch, the higher will be the radiation dose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The higher the pitch, the higher will be the radiation dose

In CT imaging, pitch refers to table movement per gantry rotation relative to beam width.
Imagine CT scan table is like a moving conveyor belt.

  • Low pitch → Table moves slowly
  • High pitch → Table moves fast

When the table moves slowly:

  • X-rays overlap more
  • Patient gets more radiation

When the table moves faster (high pitch):

  • X-rays overlap less
  • Patient gets less radiation

So:

  • High pitch = Faster scan = Less overlap = Less radiation dose
  • That’s why option D is wrong.

Simple rule to remember:
📌 Higher pitch → lower dose → slightly lower image quality
Thus:

  • Higher pitch → faster scan, lower radiation dose, slightly lower image quality
  • Lower pitch → slower scan, higher radiation dose, better image quality
    Multidetector CT (MDCT) enables rapid acquisition and superior 3D reconstruction compared with conventional CT.

questions.raw_text: All of the following are correct differences between normal radiography and mammography, except:

options.text: Radiography uses tungsten ‌as the target, while mamm​ography uses molybdenum
Beryllium is used as the e‌xit window in mammography​

questions.correct_answer: C. Mammography uses Bremsstrahlung radiation for better tissue contrast
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mammography uses Bremsstrahlung radiation for better tissue contrast

Normal radiography (X-ray):

  • Uses Tungsten target
  • Uses Aluminum filter
  • More Bremsstrahlung radiation
  • Higher energy X-rays (Needs to penetrate bone, chest, abdomen etc.)
  • Think of it like a “powerful beam” that has to go through thick structures.

Mammography:

  • Uses Molybdenum (or Rhodium) target
  • Uses Molybdenum filter (molybdenum produces X-rays at ideal energy (17–19 keV)
    Lower energy X-rays (for soft tissue contrast)
  • Breast is a soft tissue organ, so we need to see tiny differences (like microcalcifications)
  • So we use low energy X-rays
  • Uses more characteristic radiation, not mainly bremsstrahlung.
  • Think of it like a “gentle, precise beam” made specially for soft tissue contrast.

Bremsstrahlung radiation?

  • Bremsstrahlung = wide range of X-ray energies (mixed spectrum).
  • Good for general X-rays, not for fine soft tissue contrast.

Characteristic radiation?

  • Very specific energy peaks.
  • In mammography, molybdenum produces X-rays at ideal energy
  • This gives excellent breast tissue contrast.

Option-wise:
A) Radiography uses tungsten, mammography uses molybdenum
✔ Correct
B) Beryllium is used as exit window in mammography
✔ Correct (allows low-energy X-rays to pass)
C) Mammography uses Bremsstrahlung radiation for better tissue contrast
❌ Wrong. Mammography mainly uses characteristic radiation from molybdenum (17–19 keV) for better breast tissue contrast.
D) Aluminum filter in radiography, molybdenum filter in mammography
✔ Correct

Achalasia cardia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax and absence of normal esophageal peristalsis, resulting from degeneration of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus.

Characteristic barium swallow findings:

    • Increased LES resting pressure
    • Absent peristalsis
  • Upper GI endoscopy: Performed to exclude pseudoachalasia (e.g., malignancy).

Why not the other options?

  • A. Diffuse esophageal spasm: Barium swallow shows corkscrew (rosary bead) esophagus.
  • B. Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus: Produces an irregular, shouldered narrowing, not a smooth bird’s beak appearance.
  • D. Barrett’s esophagus: Diagnosed endoscopically by specialized intestinal metaplasia, not by a bird’s beak deformity.

Educational Objective:
Different imaging modalities are used to evaluate the hepatobiliary and pancreatic system, each with distinct indications and techniques.

  • ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography) is an endoscopic fluoroscopic procedure used for both diagnosis and therapy (stone extraction, sphincterotomy, biliary stenting).
  • MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) is a non-invasive MRI technique that provides excellent visualization of the biliary and pancreatic ducts without contrast injection or radiation.
  • HIDA (Hepatobiliary Iminodiacetic Acid) scan is a nuclear medicine study that evaluates gallbladder function and biliary patency.
  • Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTC) is an invasive fluoroscopic procedure in which contrast is injected directly into the intrahepatic bile ducts through a percutaneous transhepatic needle, commonly used when ERCP is not feasible.

options.text: Portal vein diameter &gt;1​3 mm on grey-scale ultras​ound
Free fluid in the hepatore​nal pouch and pelvis
A patent tubular structure​ in the falciform ligamen​t with hepatofugal flow o​n Doppler

questions.correct_answer: D. A patent tubular structure in the falciform ligament with hepatofugal flow on Doppler
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A patent tubular structure in the falciform ligament with hepatofugal flow on Doppler

This describes a recanalized paraumbilical vein (umbilical vein recanalisation) — the most specific sonographic sign of portal hypertension.

The umbilical vein normally closes at birth and becomes the ligamentum teres. When portal pressure rises significantly, this vessel reopens to shunt blood from the left portal vein → paraumbilical vein → umbilical region → systemic veins. On Doppler, flow is hepatofugal (away from the liver), confirming portosystemic shunting. This is a direct pathophysiological consequence of raised portal pressure and does not occur in any other condition — making it highly specific.

Why the other options lack specificity:

| Finding | Seen in Portal HTN? | Problem with Specificity |
| ------- | ------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Portal vein >13 mm (A) | Yes | Varies with respiration, body habitus, meals; absent in \~30% of confirmed cases |
| Splenomegaly (B) | Yes | Also seen in haematological malignancy, infections, infiltrative disorders |
| Ascites (C) | Yes | Also seen in CCF, hypoalbuminaemia, nephrotic syndrome, peritoneal malignancy |
| Recanalized umbilical vein (D) | Yes | Unique to portal hypertension — pathognomonic |

Doppler findings in portal hypertension to know:

  • Hepatofugal flow in the portal vein — reversal of normal direction; indicates severe portal hypertension
  • Recanalized paraumbilical vein — most specific sign
  • Reduced portal vein velocity (<16 cm/s) — sensitive but non-specific
  • Spontaneous splenorenal or gastrorenal collaterals — seen in advanced disease

High-yield pearl: The clinical correlate of a recanalized umbilical vein on ultrasound is caput medusae on examination — both represent the same portosystemic collateral pathway made visible by different means. questions.raw_text: What is the best imaging study for diagnosis of cerebral infarct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diffusion weighted MRI

Diffusion-weighted MRI is the most sensitive investigation for diagnosis of cerebral ischemia.  It is particularly useful for identifying acute ischemic changes in the brain due to its ability to detect diffusion restriction of water molecules in the brain tissue.
Diffusion restriction: hyperintense on DWI and hypointense on ADC.
●       Diffusion restriction is seen with:
1.     Acute stroke
2.     Hypercellular tumors
3.     Abscess
4.     Epidermoid cyst
5.     Keratin-Craniopharyngioma/ Cholesteatoma
Other Options:
Option A: FLAIR MRI: Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) MRI is useful for identifying older infarcts and chronic changes but is less sensitive in the acute phase of a stroke.
Option B: Non-contrast CT: While commonly used for initial assessment due to its availability and speed, it is less sensitive in the early stages of a stroke, often not showing changes until several hours post-onset.
Option D: СECT (Contrast-Enhanced CT): Typically used to assess for complications or other causes of symptoms but not as sensitive as DWI for early detection of cerebral infarcts.
Educational Objective
Diffusion-weighted MRI is the optimal choice for early detection of cerebral infarcts, making it an indispensable tool in acute stroke management. Its ability to show diffusion restriction provides critical information that can influence therapeutic decisions.

questions.text: Which of the following mec​hanism is involved in X-r‌ay production?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following mechanism is involved in X-ray production?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bremsstrahlung radiation

Bremsstrahlung (“braking”) radiation is the principal mechanism of X-ray production. It occurs when high-speed electrons from the cathode are decelerated or deflected by the electric field of the tungsten target nucleus (anode), causing loss of kinetic energy that is emitted as X-ray photons. It accounts for approximately 85–90% of diagnostic X-rays.
The remaining 10–15% of X-rays are produced by characteristic radiation, which results from electron transitions between atomic shells after inner-shell ionization.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Photoelectric effect: Interaction of X-rays with matter causing complete absorption of the photon; responsible for image contrast, not X-ray production.
  • B. Compton effect: Scattering of X-rays by outer-shell electrons; a major source of image degradation and radiation exposure, not production.
  • C. Pair production: Occurs only with high-energy photons (>1.02 MeV) and is not involved in diagnostic X-ray generation.

ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) is the fundamental principle of radiation protection, which states that radiation exposure should be kept as low as reasonably achievable while obtaining the necessary diagnostic or therapeutic benefit.   • Achieving this by balancing clinical benefit against radiation risk

options.text: Portal vein diameter &gt;1​3 mm on grey-scale ultras‌ound

questions.correct_answer: D. A patent tubular structure in the falciform ligament with hepatofugal flow on Doppler
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A patent tubular structure in the falciform ligament with hepatofugal flow on Doppler

This describes a recanalized paraumbilical vein (umbilical vein recanalisation) — the most specific sonographic sign of portal hypertension.

The umbilical vein normally closes at birth and becomes the ligamentum teres. When portal pressure rises significantly, this vessel reopens to shunt blood from the left portal vein → paraumbilical vein → umbilical region → systemic veins. On Doppler, flow is hepatofugal (away from the liver), confirming portosystemic shunting. This is a direct pathophysiological consequence of raised portal pressure and does not occur in any other condition — making it highly specific.

Why the other options lack specificity:

| Finding | Seen in Portal HTN? | Problem with Specificity |
| ------- | ------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Portal vein >13 mm (A) | Yes | Varies with respiration, body habitus, meals; absent in \~30% of confirmed cases |
| Splenomegaly (B) | Yes | Also seen in haematological malignancy, infections, infiltrative disorders |
| Ascites (C) | Yes | Also seen in CCF, hypoalbuminaemia, nephrotic syndrome, peritoneal malignancy |
| Recanalized umbilical vein (D) | Yes | Unique to portal hypertension — pathognomonic |

Doppler findings in portal hypertension to know:

  • Hepatofugal flow in the portal vein — reversal of normal direction; indicates severe portal hypertension
  • Recanalized paraumbilical vein — most specific sign
  • Reduced portal vein velocity (<16 cm/s) — sensitive but non-specific
  • Spontaneous splenorenal or gastrorenal collaterals — seen in advanced disease

High-yield pearl: The clinical correlate of a recanalized umbilical vein on ultrasound is caput medusae on examination — both represent the same portosystemic collateral pathway made visible by different means. Caput medusae radiates from the umbilicus; a Cruveilhier–Baumgarten murmur (venous hum at the umbilicus) may also be audible.

Correct answer: B. Kartagener syndrome

Kartagener syndrome is a subtype of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective dynein arms of motile cilia. Impaired ciliary motility leads to defective mucociliary clearance and abnormal embryonic left-right axis determination.

The classic triad consists of:

  • Chronic sinusitis
  • Bronchiectasis
  • Situs inversus (or dextrocardia)

Other features include:

  • Recurrent otitis media
  • Chronic productive cough
  • Male infertility (immotile sperm)
  • Female subfertility/ectopic pregnancy due to impaired fallopian tube cilia

Why not the other options?

  • A. Cystic fibrosis: Also causes recurrent respiratory infections and bronchiectasis, but is associated with pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, elevated sweat chloride, and does not cause situs inversus.
  • C. Young syndrome: Characterized by bronchiectasis with obstructive azoospermia, but ciliary function is normal and situs inversus is absent.
  • D. Primary immunodeficiency: May cause recurrent sinopulmonary infections but does not produce the characteristic combination of bronchiectasis with situs inversus.

| -------- | ---------- | ----------------------- |
| Kartagener syndrome (PCD) | Defective dynein arms → impaired ciliary motility | Sinusitis + bronchiectasis + situs inversus |
| Cystic fibrosis | CFTR mutation | Bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, ↑ sweat chloride |
| Young syndrome | Unknown cause | Bronchiectasis + obstructive azoospermia; no situs inversus |
| Primary immunodeficiency | Immune defect | Recurrent infections without laterality defects |

questions.raw_text: What is the earliest indicator of left atrial enlargement in cases of mitral stenosis? (NEET PG 2015)

options.text: Elevation of the right mai​n bronchus
Enlargement of the left at​rial appendage

questions.correct_answer: B. Enlargement of the left atrial appendage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enlargement of the left atrial appendage

In mitral stenosis, left atrial enlargement follows a predictable radiographic sequence. The left atrial appendage (left auricle) forms part of the normal left heart border between the pulmonary trunk and the left ventricle. It is the first structure to enlarge, producing straightening — or even bulging — of the left heart border, obliterating the normal concavity. This is the earliest and most sensitive plain film sign.

The sequence of progressive left atrial enlargement on CXR is:

| Stage | Radiographic Sign |
| ----- | ----------------- |
| Earliest | Straightening of left heart border (LAA prominence) |
| Intermediate | Splaying of carina (>70°), double density sign |
| Late | Elevation of left main bronchus, posterior oesophageal displacement |

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Elevation of the right main bronchus (A) — not a feature of LA enlargement; it is the left main bronchus that is elevated and splayed as the LA expands superiorly
  • Widening of the carina (C) — occurs after significant LA enlargement; an intermediate sign, not the earliest
  • Oesophageal displacement (D) — seen on barium swallow or lateral CXR only after substantial posterior LA enlargement; a late sign

High-yield pearl: The four classic signs of LA enlargement in mitral stenosis on PA CXR in order — left heart border straightening → double density sign → left main bronchus elevation → splayed carina. Oesophageal displacement is best seen on lateral view with barium.

Which of the following statements are correct regarding a brain abscess?

I. Abscesses arise when the brain is exposed directly as a result of fracture or infection of air sinus.
II. Presenting features include low grade fever, confusion, seizures and focal deficits.
III. MRI with contrast is the initial imaging modality of choice.
IV. The aetiological agents include bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses.

Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

A brain abscess is a focal intracerebral infection consisting of a collection of pus surrounded by a vascularized capsule. It usually develops due to direct spread from adjacent infections, hematogenous dissemination, or penetrating cranial trauma/neurosurgery.

The following statements are true:

  • I. Abscesses arise when the brain is exposed directly as a result of fracture or infection of air sinus: Brain abscesses commonly result from:
    • Direct extension from otitis media, mastoiditis, sinusitis
    • Penetrating skull fractures or neurosurgery
    • Hematogenous spread from distant infections
  • II. Presenting features include low-grade fever, confusion, seizures and focal deficits: Common clinical features include:
    • Headache (most common symptom)
    • Fever (may be absent)
    • Altered mental status/confusion
    • Focal neurological deficits
    • Seizures
    • Features of raised intracranial pressure
  • IV. The etiological agents include bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses: Although bacteria are the most common cause, brain abscess-like lesions can also occur due to:
    • Fungi (Aspergillus, Candida)
    • Protozoa (Toxoplasma gondii, especially in AIDS)
    • Rarely viral infections can produce focal necrotizing lesions, though classic brain abscesses are predominantly bacterial.

Why is III incorrect?

  • III. MRI with contrast is the initial imaging modality of choice: Contrast-enhanced CT scan is usually the initial imaging investigation because it is rapid, widely available, and useful in emergency settings.

Correct answer: C. Diffusion weighted MRI

Diffusion-weighted MRI is the most sensitive investigation for diagnosis of cerebral ischemia.  It is particularly useful for identifying acute ischemic changes in the brain due to its ability to detect diffusion restriction of water molecules in the brain tissue.
Diffusion restriction: hyperintense on DWI and hypointense on ADC.
●       Diffusion restriction is seen with:
1.     Acute stroke
2.     Hypercellular tumors
3.     Abscess
4.     Epidermoid cyst
5.     Keratin-Craniopharyngioma/ Cholesteatoma
Other Options:
Option A: FLAIR MRI: Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) MRI is useful for identifying older infarcts and chronic changes but is less sensitive in the acute phase of a stroke.
Option B: Non-contrast CT: While commonly used for initial assessment due to its availability and speed, it is less sensitive in the early stages of a stroke, often not showing changes until several hours post-onset.
Option D: СECT (Contrast-Enhanced CT): Typically used to assess for complications or other causes of symptoms but not as sensitive as DWI for early detection of cerebral infarcts.
Educational Objective
Diffusion-weighted MRI is the optimal choice for early detection of cerebral infarcts, making it an indispensable tool in acute stroke management. Its ability to show diffusion restriction provides critical information that can influence therapeutic decisions.

questions.correct_answer: B. Determines tracer distribution using time-of-flight coincidence detection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Determines tracer distribution using time-of-flight coincidence detection

  • Positron emission tomography (PET) detects pairs of 511 keV gamma photons produced when a positron emitted from a radionuclide annihilates with an electron.
  • These photons travel in opposite directions and are detected simultaneously by opposing detectors (coincidence detection).
  • This simultaneous detection allows accurate localization of the radiotracer using time-of-flight and coincidence principles, enabling reconstruction of tracer distribution and generation of functional metabolic images.
  • PET does not directly detect positrons or measure radionuclide half-life; instead, it maps tissue metabolism based on coincident gamma photon detection.

High-resolution CT of the chest shows bronchiectasis, and a chest radiograph demonstrates dextrocardia with complete situs inversus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kartagener syndrome

Kartagener syndrome is a subtype of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective dynein arms of motile cilia. Impaired ciliary motility leads to defective mucociliary clearance and abnormal embryonic left-right axis determination.

The classic triad consists of:

  • Chronic sinusitis
  • Bronchiectasis
  • Situs inversus (or dextrocardia)

Other features include:

  • Recurrent otitis media
  • Chronic productive cough
  • Male infertility (immotile sperm)
  • Female subfertility/ectopic pregnancy due to impaired fallopian tube cilia

Why not the other options?

  • A. Cystic fibrosis: Also causes recurrent respiratory infections and bronchiectasis, but is associated with pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, elevated sweat chloride, and does not cause situs inversus.
  • C. Young syndrome: Characterized by bronchiectasis with obstructive azoospermia, but ciliary function is normal and situs inversus is absent.
  • D. Primary immunodeficiency: May cause recurrent sinopulmonary infections but does not produce the characteristic combination of bronchiectasis with situs inversus.

| -------- | ---------- | ----------------------- |
| Kartagener syndrome (PCD) | Defective dynein arms → impaired ciliary motility | Sinusitis + bronchiectasis + situs inversus |
| Cystic fibrosis | CFTR mutation | Bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, ↑ sweat chloride |
| Young syndrome | Unknown cause | Bronchiectasis + obstructive azoospermia; no situs inversus |
| Primary immunodeficiency | Immune defect | Recurrent infections without laterality defects |

options.text: Elevation of the right mai‌n bronchus

questions.correct_answer: B. Enlargement of the left atrial appendage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enlargement of the left atrial appendage

In mitral stenosis, left atrial enlargement follows a predictable radiographic sequence. The left atrial appendage (left auricle) forms part of the normal left heart border between the pulmonary trunk and the left ventricle. It is the first structure to enlarge, producing straightening — or even bulging — of the left heart border, obliterating the normal concavity. This is the earliest and most sensitive plain film sign.

The sequence of progressive left atrial enlargement on CXR is:

| Stage | Radiographic Sign |
| ----- | ----------------- |
| Earliest | Straightening of left heart border (LAA prominence) |
| Intermediate | Splaying of carina (>70°), double density sign |
| Late | Elevation of left main bronchus, posterior oesophageal displacement |

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Elevation of the right main bronchus (A) — not a feature of LA enlargement; it is the left main bronchus that is elevated and splayed as the LA expands superiorly
  • Widening of the carina (C) — occurs after significant LA enlargement; an intermediate sign, not the earliest
  • Oesophageal displacement (D) — seen on barium swallow or lateral CXR only after substantial posterior LA enlargement; a late sign

High-yield pearl: The four classic signs of LA enlargement in mitral stenosis on PA CXR in order — left heart border straightening → double density sign → left main bronchus elevation → splayed carina. Oesophageal displacement is best seen on lateral view with barium.

questions.text: Which of the following mec‌hanism is involved in X-r​ay production?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following mechanism is involved in X-ray production?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bremsstrahlung radiation

Bremsstrahlung (“braking”) radiation is the principal mechanism of X-ray production. It occurs when high-speed electrons from the cathode are decelerated or deflected by the electric field of the tungsten target nucleus (anode), causing loss of kinetic energy that is emitted as X-ray photons. It accounts for approximately 85–90% of diagnostic X-rays.
The remaining 10–15% of X-rays are produced by characteristic radiation, which results from electron transitions between atomic shells after inner-shell ionization.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Photoelectric effect: Interaction of X-rays with matter causing complete absorption of the photon; responsible for image contrast, not X-ray production.
  • B. Compton effect: Scattering of X-rays by outer-shell electrons; a major source of image degradation and radiation exposure, not production.
  • C. Pair production: Occurs only with high-energy photons (>1.02 MeV) and is not involved in diagnostic X-ray generation.

Correct answer: B. As Low As Reasonably Achievable

ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) is the fundamental principle of radiation protection, which states that radiation exposure should be kept as low as reasonably achievable while obtaining the necessary diagnostic or therapeutic benefit. It is based on the assumption that there is no completely safe dose of ionizing radiation, and therefore unnecessary exposure should always be minimized.

The ALARA principle emphasizes:

  • Minimizing radiation exposure to patients, healthcare workers, and the public
  • Achieving this by balancing clinical benefit against radiation risk
  • Applying practical measures without compromising diagnostic quality or treatment efficacy

Why not the other options?

  • A. As Long As Radiation Allows – Incorrect expansion.
  • C. As Little As Radiation Accepted – Not the accepted terminology.
  • D. As Low As Required for Assessment – Incorrect expansion; the standard term is Reasonably Achievable.

  • This gives excellent breast tissue contrast.

questions.raw_text: What is the best imaging study for diagnosis of cerebral infarct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diffusion weighted MRI

Diffusion-weighted MRI is the most sensitive investigation for diagnosis of cerebral ischemia.  It is particularly useful for identifying acute ischemic changes in the brain due to its ability to detect diffusion restriction of water molecules in the brain tissue.
Diffusion restriction: hyperintense on DWI and hypointense on ADC.
●       Diffusion restriction is seen with:
1.     Acute stroke
2.     Hypercellular tumors
3.     Abscess
4.     Epidermoid cyst
5.     Keratin-Craniopharyngioma/ Cholesteatoma
Other Options:
Option A: FLAIR MRI: Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) MRI is useful for identifying older infarcts and chronic changes but is less sensitive in the acute phase of a stroke.
Option B: Non-contrast CT: While commonly used for initial assessment due to its availability and speed, it is less sensitive in the early stages of a stroke, often not showing changes until several hours post-onset.
Option D: СECT (Contrast-Enhanced CT): Typically used to assess for complications or other causes of symptoms but not as sensitive as DWI for early detection of cerebral infarcts.
Educational Objective
Diffusion-weighted MRI is the optimal choice for early detection of cerebral infarcts, making it an indispensable tool in acute stroke management. Its ability to show diffusion restriction provides critical information that can influence therapeutic decisions.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leptomeningeal cyst

  • A leptomeningeal cyst (growing skull fracture) is a late complication of skull fracture in infants and young children.
  • It occurs when Skull fracture leads to a dural tear allows CSF pulsations and herniation of leptomeninges/brain tissue through the fracture site, leading to progressive enlargement of the bony defect and scalp swelling.
  • It typically presents months to years after head trauma as a painful, enlarging cranial swelling,

most commonly in the parietal region.

Why not other options:
A. Growing scalp hematoma: Resolves over weeks; does not progressively enlarge 1 year later or cause bony defect.
C. Subdural hygroma: CSF collection in subdural space causing neurological signs, not localized skull swelling.
D. Chronic abscess: Shows infection signs (fever, redness, systemic toxicity), not gradual post-traumatic bony expansion.

TAKEAWAY:
Why are growing skull fracture seen in children?

  • The dura sticks firmly to the inner table of skull
  • So when a fracture happens, dura tears along with bone

While In adults:

  • Dura is less tightly attached ,stays intact even if bone fractures
  • No dural tear = no leptomeningeal cyst.

2.	Lung cancer
3.	Breast cancer

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Ionizing radiation is a well-established carcinogen that causes DNA damage through direct strand breaks and free radical formation. The risk of malignancy depends on the radiation dose, age at exposure, and tissue radiosensitivity. Hematopoietic tissues and rapidly dividing cells are particularly susceptible.

  • 3. Breast cancer ✅
    • Exposure to ionizing radiation, particularly during childhood or adolescence, significantly increases the risk of breast cancer.
  • 4. Lymphoma ✅
    • Ionizing radiation is associated with an increased risk of lymphomas, especially non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.raw_text: Which of the following terms describes nuclides that have identical atomic mass numbers but different atomic numbers? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Isobars

Isobars are nuclides that have the same mass number (A) but different atomic numbers (Z). This means they have the same total number of protons and neutrons, but the distribution between protons and neutrons differs.
Other Options:
Option A. Isotopes - Isotopes are different forms of the same element (same atomic number/Z) with different numbers of neutrons\, resulting in different mass numbers (A). Isotopes have identical chemical properties but different physical properties due to their different masses.
Option C. Isotones - Isotones are nuclides that have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons. This results in different elements with different mass numbers but the same neutron count.
Option D. Isomers - Isomers are nuclides with identical atomic numbers (Z) and mass numbers (A)\, but different nuclear energy states. An example is Technetium-99m\, where the "m" denotes a metastable state with higher energy than the ground state Technetium-99.
Educational Objective:
Isobars are different elements with the same mass number but different atomic numbers, representing nuclides with the same total number of nucleons but different proton-to-neutron ratios.

Respiratory gating is used in thoracic radiotherapy to compensate for tumor movement caused by breathing. B. Fractionation: Dividing total radiation dose into multiple sessions to reduce toxicity; unrelated to breathing movement.

Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) depends on Starling forces across the glomerular membrane.

Thus, changes in hydrostatic and oncotic pressures across the glomerulus directly influence GFR.

  • ↓ Renin secretion

Vasopressin (ADH) concentrates urine not only by increasing water permeability in the collecting ducts but also by enhancing urea reabsorption in the inner medullary collecting duct (IMCD). Reabsorbed urea accumulates in the renal medulla, contributing significantly to medullary hypertonicity, which is essential for producing maximally concentrated urine during dehydration.

  • During water deprivation, ADH levels rise markedly.
  • ADH increases the expression of urea transporters (UT-A1 and UT-A3) in the medullary collecting duct.
  • Urea is reabsorbed into the medullary interstitium, strengthening the corticomedullary osmotic gradient.
  • This hyperosmotic medulla promotes water reabsorption and allows urine osmolality to reach 1000–1200 mOsm/kg.

  • A. Thin ascending limb → Involved in passive NaCl handling but not the principal ADH-responsive site for urea reabsorption.
  • B. Cortical collecting duct → ADH increases water permeability here, but it does not significantly contribute to medullary hypertonicity via urea transport.
  • C. Proximal tubule → Reabsorbs water and solutes isosmotically; largely independent of ADH.
  • E. Early distal tubule → Diluting segment; relatively impermeable to water and not involved in ADH-mediated urea recycling.

Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that is freely filtered at the glomerulus but not reabsorbed, leading to an increase in tubular fluid osmolality.   • Increased tubular fluid osmolality
  • Decreased serum sodium (dilutional hyponatremia initially)

The earliest functional change in diabetic nephropathy is glomerular hyperfiltration, characterized by an increased GFR despite normal serum creatinine and absence of albuminuria. This occurs due to afferent arteriolar dilation mediated by altered tubuloglomerular feedback: increased proximal glucose and sodium reabsorption reduces sodium delivery to the macula densa, leading to decreased afferent arteriolar resistance and increased intraglomerular capillary pressure.

This phase precedes structural damage and is potentially reversible. Persistent hyperfiltration, however, leads to glomerular injury, basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and eventual microalbuminuria, marking progression of disease.

questions.text: Which transport mechanism ‌is primarily responsible ​for bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) r​eabsorption in the proxim​al convoluted tubule (PCT​)?
questions.raw_text: Which transport mechanism is primarily responsible for bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sodium–hydrogen antiporter

In the proximal convoluted tubule, bicarbonate reabsorption occurs indirectly via the Na⁺–H⁺ antiporter (NHE).

  • H⁺ is secreted into the tubular lumen in exchange for Na⁺.
  • Secreted H⁺ combines with filtered HCO₃⁻ → forms CO₂ and H₂O (via carbonic anhydrase).
  • CO₂ diffuses into tubular cells and is converted back to HCO₃⁻, which enters blood.

Thus, Na⁺–H⁺ antiporter is the primary mechanism driving bicarbonate reabsorption in PCT.

options.text: Thick ascending limb of lo‌op of Henle

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medullary collecting duct

Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) promotes natriuresis primarily by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the medullary collecting duct.

Why Medullary Collecting Duct Specifically?

The medullary collecting duct (MCD) is the primary site of ANP action because:

| Feature | Detail |
| ------- | ------ |
| Receptor density | Highest concentration of NPR-A receptors in the entire nephron |
| Transport target | Inhibits ENaC (Epithelial Sodium Channels) on luminal side |
| Net effect | ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption → Na⁺ stays in tubule → osmotic water retention in lumen → natriuresis + diuresis |
| Aldosterone antagonism | ANP opposes aldosterone action at this same segment |

ANP Actions Across the Nephron

| Site | Action | Significance |
| ---- | ------ | ------------ |
| Medullary Collecting Duct ⭐ | ↓ ENaC → ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption | Primary natriuretic effect |
| Glomerulus | ↑ GFR (dilates afferent, constricts efferent arteriole) | ↑ filtered Na⁺ load |
| Proximal tubule | Mild ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption | Minor contribution |
| Inner medullary CD | ↓ Urea transporters | Reduces medullary tonicity → impairs concentrating ability |
| Adrenal gland | ↓ Aldosterone secretion | Indirect natriuresis |
| Vasculature | Vasodilation | ↓ BP, ↓ venous return |

Correct answer: B. Anion gap metabolic acidosis plus metabolic alkalosis

Step 1: Calculate the Anion Gap
Normal AG is \~12 (±2). An AG of 40 confirms a high anion gap metabolic acidosis — this is common to all four options, so it doesn't discriminate between them yet.

Step 2: Check respiratory compensation (rule out a primary respiratory disorder)
Use Winter's formula to predict the expected PaCO2 for a purely metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation:
Expected range: 24–28 mmHg
Actual PaCO2: 25 mmHg → falls within the expected range.
This means the respiratory system is compensating appropriately for the metabolic acidosis — there is no additional primary respiratory acid-base disorder. This eliminates:

  • A (mixed respiratory alkalosis) — would require PaCO2 lower than predicted
  • D (mixed respiratory acidosis) — would require PaCO2 higher than predicted

Step 3: Use the Delta-Delta (ΔAG/ΔHCO3) ratio to check for a second metabolic process

Interpretation of delta ratio:

| Ratio | Interpretation |
| ----- | -------------- |
| < 1 | Concurrent normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis |
| 1–2 | Pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis |
| > 2 | Concurrent metabolic alkalosis (HCO3 is "too high" relative to the rise in AG — something is propping the bicarbonate up) |

A ratio of 2.33 (>2) tells you the bicarbonate has not fallen as much as expected given the severity of the anion gap rise. If this were a pure AG metabolic acidosis, HCO3 should have dropped much lower (by roughly the same amount the AG rose, i.e., HCO3 ≈ 24 − 28 = deeply negative — clearly impossible, reinforcing that something is buffering/raising the HCO3). This "extra" bicarbonate points to a superimposed metabolic alkalosis — hence eliminating C (which would require ratio <1, not >2) and confirming B.

Correct answer: C. Increased secretion of antidiuretic hormone

Severe diarrhea causes extrarenal loss of sodium and water, leading to hypovolemia. The resulting decrease in effective circulating volume stimulates non-osmotic release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). ADH promotes water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, causing retention of free water that exceeds sodium retention, thereby producing dilutional hyponatremia.
Although the kidneys conserve sodium by activating the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), the marked increase in ADH-mediated water retention is the primary mechanism responsible for the low serum sodium concentration.

  • A. Decreased reabsorption of sodium from kidney – Incorrect. In hypovolemia, the kidneys increase sodium reabsorption under the influence of aldosterone.
  • B. Decreased absorption of sodium from the gut – Incorrect. Diarrhea causes sodium loss, not impaired intestinal absorption.
  • D. Decreased secretion of aldosterone – Incorrect. Hypovolemia stimulates increased, not decreased, aldosterone secretion.

| ---- | ------------------- |

•	Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc): 18 mmHg
•	Capillary oncotic pressure (πc): 27 mmHg
•	Interstitial oncotic pressure (πi): 7 mmHg

  • Pi = interstitial hydrostatic pressure (pushes fluid IN)
  • πc = capillary oncotic pressure (pulls fluid IN)
  • πi = interstitial oncotic pressure (pulls fluid OUT)

| Force | Direction | Function |
| ----- | --------- | -------- |
| Pc | Outward | Filtration |
| Pi | Inward (if positive) | Opposes filtration |
| πc | Inward | Reabsorption |
| πi | Outward | Filtration |

Net filtration pressure (NFP) = (Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi).
Given no net filtration, NFP = 0 ⇒ (18 − Pi) − (27 − 7) = 0.

questions.text: A patient with severe cent​ral diabetes insipidus ha‍s markedly reduced secret​ion of ADH. At which of t​he following nephron segm‌ents would the tubular fl​uid attain its lowest osm‌olality?
questions.raw_text: A patient with severe central diabetes insipidus has markedly reduced secretion of ADH. At which of the following nephron segments would the tubular fluid attain its lowest osmolality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. D

In central diabetes insipidus (DI), there is deficient secretion of ADH (vasopressin). Consequently, the late distal tubule and collecting ducts have markedly reduced water permeability due to failure of aquaporin-2 (AQP2) insertion into the luminal membrane.

The tubular fluid reaching these segments is already dilute because solute has been reabsorbed without water in the thick ascending limb and early distal tubule. In the absence of ADH, further solute reabsorption can occur without proportionate water reabsorption, allowing the tubular fluid to become maximally dilute.

Thus, the lowest tubular fluid osmolality is found in the late distal tubule/collecting duct and ultimately in the final urine.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Proximal convoluted tubule: Water and solutes are reabsorbed proportionately, so tubular fluid remains nearly iso-osmotic (\~300 mOsm/kg).
  • B. Descending limb: Highly permeable to water; water leaves the tubule as it enters the hyperosmotic medulla, making tubular fluid progressively hyperosmotic.
  • C. Thick ascending limb: Known as the diluting segment because Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻ are reabsorbed via NKCC2 while the segment is impermeable to water. However, further dilution can occur downstream when ADH is absent.
  • D. Late distal tubule and collecting duct: In severe ADH deficiency, water permeability remains very low, resulting in maximally dilute tubular fluid and urine.

The tubular fluid reaching these segments is already dilute because solute has been reabsorbed without water in the thick ascending limb and early distal tubule. In the absence of ADH, further solute reabsorption can occur without proportionate water reabsorption, allowing the tubular fluid to become maximally dilute.

  • B. Descending limb: Highly permeable to water; water leaves the tubule as it enters the hyperosmotic medulla, making tubular fluid progressively hyperosmotic.
  • C. Thick ascending limb: Known as the diluting segment because Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻ are reabsorbed via NKCC2 while the segment is impermeable to water. However, further dilution can occur downstream when ADH is absent.
  • D. Late distal tubule and collecting duct: In severe ADH deficiency, water permeability remains very low, resulting in maximally dilute tubular fluid and urine.

CT scan of the head reveals a right basal ganglia hemorrhage with midline shift. The patient is intubated, and intravenous mannitol is administered to reduce intracranial pressure. Which of the following acute renal effects is most likely to occur following administration of this medication?

options.text: Decreased serum sodium, in‌creased tubular flow, inc‌reased tubular fluid osmo‍lality
No change in serum sodium,‌ decreased tubular flow, ‌increased tubular fluid o‍smolality
Increased serum sodium, no‌ change in tubular flow, ‌increased tubular fluid o‍smolality
Decreased serum sodium, no‌ change in tubular flow, ‌decreased tubular fluid o‍smolality

questions.correct_answer: A. Decreased serum sodium, increased tubular flow, increased tubular fluid osmolality
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased serum sodium, increased tubular flow, increased tubular fluid osmolality

Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that is freely filtered at the glomerulus but not reabsorbed, leading to an increase in tubular fluid osmolality. This prevents water reabsorption in the proximal tubule and descending limb of the loop of Henle, resulting in osmotic diuresis with increased tubular flow.

In the acute setting, mannitol increases plasma osmolality, drawing water from intracellular to extracellular compartments, including from brain parenchyma—thereby reducing intracranial pressure. This initial water shift into the intravascular space causes dilutional hyponatremia, even before diuresis becomes prominent.

Thus, the key acute renal effects are:

  • Increased tubular flow due to osmotic diuresis
  • Increased tubular fluid osmolality
  • Decreased serum sodium (dilutional hyponatremia initially)

questions.raw_text: 45-year-old man with a 2-year history of prediabetes presents for routine evaluation. He has gained weight over the past year and has a strong family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. His BMI is 32 kg/m², and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Laboratory evaluation shows fasting plasma glucose of 157 mg/dL and HbA1c of 7.4%. Serum creatinine is normal, and urine testing shows no detectable albuminuria. Which of the following renal changes is most likely present at this stage of disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased glomerular filtration rate

The earliest functional change in diabetic nephropathy is glomerular hyperfiltration, characterized by an increased GFR despite normal serum creatinine and absence of albuminuria. This occurs due to afferent arteriolar dilation mediated by altered tubuloglomerular feedback: increased proximal glucose and sodium reabsorption reduces sodium delivery to the macula densa, leading to decreased afferent arteriolar resistance and increased intraglomerular capillary pressure.

This phase precedes structural damage and is potentially reversible. Persistent hyperfiltration, however, leads to glomerular injury, basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and eventual microalbuminuria, marking progression of disease.

Why not other options?
A. Decreased intraglomerular capillary pressure → Incorrect; early diabetic nephropathy involves increased, not decreased pressure
B. Decreased peritubular capillary oncotic pressure → Not a defining feature of early diabetic kidney disease
C. Glomerular atrophy → Occurs in late-stage CKD, not early disease
D. Increased oncotic pressure in Bowman space → Seen when significant protein leaks into filtrate (i.e., later stages with proteinuria)

A patient has the following Starling forces at a capillary bed: 

•	Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc): 18 mmHg

•	Interstitial oncotic pressure (πi): 7 mmHg

Correct answer: D. -2 mmHg

The Starling equation for net filtration pressure (NFP) is: NFP = (Pc - Pi) - (πc - πi)
Where:

  • Pc = capillary hydrostatic pressure (pushes fluid OUT)
  • Pi = interstitial hydrostatic pressure (pushes fluid IN)
  • πc = capillary oncotic pressure (pulls fluid IN)
  • πi = interstitial oncotic pressure (pulls fluid OUT)

| Force | Direction | Function |
| ----- | --------- | -------- |
| Pc | Outward | Filtration |
| Pi | Inward (if positive) | Opposes filtration |
| πc | Inward | Reabsorption |
| πi | Outward | Filtration |

Net filtration pressure (NFP) = (Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi).
Given no net filtration, NFP = 0 ⇒ (18 − Pi) − (27 − 7) = 0.
So, 18 − Pi − 20 = 0 ⇒ Pi = −2 mmHg, making option D correct.

options.text: Thick ascending limb of lo​op of Henle

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medullary collecting duct

Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) promotes natriuresis primarily by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the medullary collecting duct.

Why Medullary Collecting Duct Specifically?

The medullary collecting duct (MCD) is the primary site of ANP action because:

| Feature | Detail |
| ------- | ------ |
| Receptor density | Highest concentration of NPR-A receptors in the entire nephron |
| Transport target | Inhibits ENaC (Epithelial Sodium Channels) on luminal side |
| Net effect | ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption → Na⁺ stays in tubule → osmotic water retention in lumen → natriuresis + diuresis |
| Aldosterone antagonism | ANP opposes aldosterone action at this same segment |

ANP Actions Across the Nephron

| Site | Action | Significance |
| ---- | ------ | ------------ |
| Medullary Collecting Duct ⭐ | ↓ ENaC → ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption | Primary natriuretic effect |
| Glomerulus | ↑ GFR (dilates afferent, constricts efferent arteriole) | ↑ filtered Na⁺ load |
| Proximal tubule | Mild ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption | Minor contribution |
| Inner medullary CD | ↓ Urea transporters | Reduces medullary tonicity → impairs concentrating ability |
| Adrenal gland | ↓ Aldosterone secretion | Indirect natriuresis |
| Vasculature | Vasodilation | ↓ BP, ↓ venous return |

•	PaCO₂: 53 mmHg 
•	HCO₃⁻: 33 mEq/L 
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

This patient has Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS), also known as Pickwickian syndrome.

The diagnosis is based on the triad of:

  • Obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²)
  • Awake daytime hypercapnia (PaCO₂ >45 mmHg)
  • Chronic hypoxemia without another cause of hypoventilation

The elevated HCO₃⁻ (33 mEq/L) indicates renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis, confirming long-standing hypoventilation rather than an acute event.

Patients commonly present with:

  • Excessive daytime sleepiness
  • Cognitive impairment
  • Loud snoring
  • Systemic hypertension
  • Morning headaches
  • Signs of chronic hypoventilation

Why the other options are incorrect?

  • B. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) – OSA causes recurrent nocturnal airway obstruction but awake ABG is usually normal. Persistent daytime hypercapnia suggests OHS rather than isolated OSA.
  • C. Central sleep apnea – Characterized by reduced respiratory drive during sleep and is commonly associated with heart failure, stroke, or opioid use. Severe obesity with chronic daytime hypercapnia favors OHS.
  • D. Narcolepsy – Causes excessive daytime sleepiness but does not produce hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or elevated bicarbonate.

High-yield pearl
Differentiate OHS from OSA:

| Feature | OSA | OHS |
| ------- | --- | --- |
| Obesity | Common | Almost always present |
| Daytime PaCO₂ | Usually normal | >45 mmHg ✅ |
| Serum HCO₃⁻ | Normal | Elevated (chronic compensation) |
| Daytime hypoxemia | Uncommon | Common |
| Treatment | CPAP | Weight loss + CPAP/BiPAP (BiPAP often required if hypercapnia persists) |

  • An obese patient with daytime hypercapnia (PaCO₂ >45 mmHg) and elevated bicarbonate should be diagnosed with Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome, even if obstructive sleep apnea is also present.

| --------- | ------ |

| Positive response criteria | ↓mPAP ≥10 mmHg to an absolute value ≤40 mmHg, with unchanged/increased cardiac output |
| Responders (\~10% of idiopathic PAH) | Trial of high-dose oral CCB; reassess response at 3–6 months |
| Non-responders (\~90%) | PAH-specific therapy: ERA, PDE-5 inhibitor/sGC stimulator, prostacyclin pathway agents (often combination therapy) |

| Long-term CCB success | Even among initial responders, only about half maintain sustained benefit long-term — requires reassessment |

questions.raw_text:
Consider the following statements regarding Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS):

1.	Exudative phase lasts from day 7 to day 21 after exposure to a precipitating risk factor.
2.	Proliferative phase is characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes.
3.	Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg body weight) has significantly lower mortality compared to high tidal volume ventilation (12 mL/kg body weight).
4.	PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤100 mm Hg is classified as severe ARDS.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4

  • Statement 1. Exudative phase lasts from day 7 to day 21 after exposure to a precipitating risk factor: Incorrect. The exudative phase actually lasts from day 1 to day 7 after the precipitating insult (characterized by diffuse alveolar damage, hyaline membrane formation, and neutrophil-rich edema). The timeframe of day 7–21 actually corresponds to the proliferative phase, not the exudative phase.
  • Statement 2. Proliferative phase is characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes: Correct. The proliferative phase (roughly days 7–21) is marked by proliferation of type II pneumocytes (which attempt to repair the damaged alveolar epithelium), fibroblast proliferation, and organization of the exudate.
  • Statement 3. Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg body weight) has significantly lower mortality compared to high tidal volume ventilation (12 mL/kg body weight): Correct. This is based on the landmark ARDSNet (ARMA) trial, which showed that a lung-protective ventilation strategy using low tidal volumes (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) significantly reduced mortality compared to traditional higher tidal volumes (12 mL/kg), along with plateau pressure limitation (<30 cm H₂O).
  • Statement 4. PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤100 mm Hg is classified as severe ARDS: Correct. As per the Berlin Definition of ARDS (2012), severity is graded by the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio (with PEEP ≥5 cm H₂O):
    • Mild: 200–300 mm Hg
    • Moderate: 100–200 mm Hg
    • Severe: ≤100 mm Hg

Alveolus Y would empty its​ air into Alveolus X beca‌use it has the higher col‍lapsing pressure
Both alveoli would remain ​stable since surface tens‌ion is identical

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alveolus Y would empty its air into Alveolus X because it has the higher collapsing pressure

According to the Law of Laplace for alveoli (P = 2T/r), the collapsing pressure (P) is directly proportional to surface tension (T) and inversely proportional to the radius (r). When two alveoli have the same surface tension, the smaller alveolus generates a higher collapsing pressure.
In this case, Alveolus Y (radius 25 μm) has a higher collapsing pressure than Alveolus X (radius 50 μm), causing air to flow from the smaller alveolus into the larger one. As a result, the smaller alveolus tends to collapse (atelectasis) in the absence of surfactant.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Alveolus X would collapse into Alveolus Y because larger alveoli always have higher collapsing pressure: Larger alveoli have lower, not higher, collapsing pressure.
  • C. Both alveoli would remain stable since surface tension is identical: Equal surface tension does not ensure stability when alveolar radii differ.
  • D. Alveolus X would empty into Alveolus Y due to lower resistance in larger airways: Air movement is determined by pressure gradients, not airway resistance in this scenario.

A pulmonary embolism (PE) causes an abrupt increase in pulmonary vascular resistance, resulting in acute right ventricular (RV) pressure overload (RV strain). On echocardiography or cardiac imaging, a GIF demonstrating RV strain typically shows characteristic dynamic changes.

The GIF demonstrates RV strain in acute PE, the following findings are expected:

  • Dilated right ventricle
    • The RV becomes enlarged because it suddenly has to pump against an obstructed pulmonary circulation.
    • Normally, the RV is smaller than the LV; in severe PE, the RV may equal or exceed the LV in size (RV/LV ratio >1).
  • Flattening or bowing of the interventricular septum
    • Increased RV pressure pushes the septum toward the LV.
    • In the parasternal short-axis view, the normally circular LV appears D-shaped ("D-sign").
  • Reduced RV free-wall motion
    • The RV free wall appears hypokinetic due to acute pressure overload.
  • McConnell sign (if present)
    • Akinesis of the RV free wall with preserved apical contraction.
    • Although classically associated with acute PE, it is not specific and can also occur in RV infarction.
  • Dilated right atrium
    • Elevated right-sided pressures lead to enlargement of the right atrium.
  • Tricuspid regurgitation
    • RV dilatation stretches the tricuspid annulus, causing functional tricuspid regurgitation.
  • Dilated inferior vena cava (IVC) with reduced inspiratory collapse
    • Reflects elevated right atrial pressure.

| Non-responders (\~90%) | PAH-specific therapy: ERA, PDE-5 inhibitor/sGC stimulator, prostacyclin pathway agents (often combination therapy) |
| Caution | CCBs should NOT be given empirically without testing — risk of hypotension/right heart decompensation in non-responders |
| Long-term CCB success | Even among initial responders, only about half maintain sustained benefit long-term — requires reassessment |

questions.text: A 25-year-old healthy man ‍performs high-intensity a​erobic exercise on a trea​dmill. His cardiac output‌ increases markedly, resu​lting in increased pulmon​ary blood flow. questions.raw_text: A 25-year-old healthy man performs high-intensity aerobic exercise on a treadmill. His cardiac output increases markedly, resulting in increased pulmonary blood flow. Compared with the resting state, which West lung zone demonstrates the greatest increase in pulmonary perfusion?

options.text: No significant change in p‍erfusion in any zone

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zone 1

At rest, West's zones exist because of the relationship between alveolar pressure (P_A), arterial pressure (P_a), and venous pressure (P_v):

  • Zone 1 (apex): P_A > P_a > P_v → capillaries are squashed shut by alveolar pressure → little to no perfusion
  • Zone 2 (middle): P_a > P_A > P_v → intermittent perfusion
  • Zone 3 (base): P_a > P_v > P_A → continuous, highest perfusion at rest

What happens with exercise:
Cardiac output rises sharply, so pulmonary artery pressure rises throughout the lung. This does two things:

  1. Distends vessels that are already open (mainly zone 3)
  2. Recruits vessels that were previously collapsed because P_a now exceeds P_A (mainly zone 1)

Zone 1 starts from a baseline of almost zero perfusion. When arterial pressure rises enough to overcome alveolar pressure, previously unperfused capillaries suddenly open up. That's a huge relative increase — in the extreme, zone 1 physiology can essentially disappear, and the whole lung starts behaving like zone 3.

Zone 3, by contrast, is already near-maximal perfusion at rest (Pa > Pv > PA already). It can only increase further through distension of already-open vessels — a smaller proportional change.

So the answer is Zone 1 (C) because it shows the greatest increase (largest relative jump — from minimal to substantial flow via recruitment), even though zone 3 still has the highest absolute flow overall.

| West's Zone | Pressure relationship | Perfusion |
| ----------- | --------------------- | --------- |
| Zone 1 | PA > Pa > Pv | Minimal or absent (normally not present) |
| Zone 2 | Pa > PA > Pv | Moderate, flow depends on Pa − PA |
| Zone 3 | Pa > Pv > PA | Maximum perfusion |

Consider the following statements regarding Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS):

1.	Exudative phase lasts from day 7 to day 21 after exposure to a precipitating risk factor.
2.	Proliferative phase is characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes.
3.	Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg body weight) has significantly lower mortality compared to high tidal volume ventilation (12 mL/kg body weight).

Which of the statements given above are correct?

Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4

  • Statement 1. Exudative phase lasts from day 7 to day 21 after exposure to a precipitating risk factor: Incorrect. The exudative phase actually lasts from day 1 to day 7 after the precipitating insult (characterized by diffuse alveolar damage, hyaline membrane formation, and neutrophil-rich edema). The timeframe of day 7–21 actually corresponds to the proliferative phase, not the exudative phase.
  • Statement 2. Proliferative phase is characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes: Correct. The proliferative phase (roughly days 7–21) is marked by proliferation of type II pneumocytes (which attempt to repair the damaged alveolar epithelium), fibroblast proliferation, and organization of the exudate.

This is based on the landmark ARDSNet (ARMA) trial, which showed that a lung-protective ventilation strategy using low tidal volumes (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) significantly reduced mortality compared to traditional higher tidal volumes (12 mL/kg), along with plateau pressure limitation (<30 cm H₂O).

    • Mild: 200–300 mm Hg
    • Moderate: 100–200 mm Hg
    • Severe: ≤100 mm Hg

  • B. Peroxidase: Enzyme involved in microbial killing by neutrophils; it does not cause alveolar destruction.

questions.text: A 25-year-old healthy man ​performs high-intensity a​erobic exercise on a trea​dmill. His cardiac output‌ increases markedly, resu‍lting in increased pulmon​ary blood flow. questions.raw_text: A 25-year-old healthy man performs high-intensity aerobic exercise on a treadmill. His cardiac output increases markedly, resulting in increased pulmonary blood flow. Compared with the resting state, which West lung zone demonstrates the greatest increase in pulmonary perfusion?

options.text: No significant change in p​erfusion in any zone

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zone 1

At rest, West's zones exist because of the relationship between alveolar pressure (P_A), arterial pressure (P_a), and venous pressure (P_v):

  • Zone 1 (apex): P_A > P_a > P_v → capillaries are squashed shut by alveolar pressure → little to no perfusion
  • Zone 2 (middle): P_a > P_A > P_v → intermittent perfusion
  • Zone 3 (base): P_a > P_v > P_A → continuous, highest perfusion at rest

What happens with exercise:
Cardiac output rises sharply, so pulmonary artery pressure rises throughout the lung. This does two things:

  1. Distends vessels that are already open (mainly zone 3)
  2. Recruits vessels that were previously collapsed because P_a now exceeds P_A (mainly zone 1)

Zone 1 starts from a baseline of almost zero perfusion. When arterial pressure rises enough to overcome alveolar pressure, previously unperfused capillaries suddenly open up. That's a huge relative increase — in the extreme, zone 1 physiology can essentially disappear, and the whole lung starts behaving like zone 3.

Zone 3, by contrast, is already near-maximal perfusion at rest (Pa > Pv > PA already). It can only increase further through distension of already-open vessels — a smaller proportional change.

So the answer is Zone 1 (C) because it shows the greatest increase (largest relative jump — from minimal to substantial flow via recruitment), even though zone 3 still has the highest absolute flow overall.

| West's Zone | Pressure relationship | Perfusion |
| ----------- | --------------------- | --------- |
| Zone 1 | PA > Pa > Pv | Minimal or absent (normally not present) |
| Zone 2 | Pa > PA > Pv | Moderate, flow depends on Pa − PA |
| Zone 3 | Pa > Pv > PA | Maximum perfusion |

Compared with the resting state, which West lung zone demonstrates the greatest increase in pulmonary perfusion?

options.text: No significant change in p‌erfusion in any zone

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zone 1

At rest, West's zones exist because of the relationship between alveolar pressure (P_A), arterial pressure (P_a), and venous pressure (P_v):

  • Zone 1 (apex): P_A > P_a > P_v → capillaries are squashed shut by alveolar pressure → little to no perfusion
  • Zone 2 (middle): P_a > P_A > P_v → intermittent perfusion
  • Zone 3 (base): P_a > P_v > P_A → continuous, highest perfusion at rest

What happens with exercise:
Cardiac output rises sharply, so pulmonary artery pressure rises throughout the lung. This does two things:

  1. Distends vessels that are already open (mainly zone 3)
  2. Recruits vessels that were previously collapsed because P_a now exceeds P_A (mainly zone 1)

Zone 1 starts from a baseline of almost zero perfusion. When arterial pressure rises enough to overcome alveolar pressure, previously unperfused capillaries suddenly open up. That's a huge relative increase — in the extreme, zone 1 physiology can essentially disappear, and the whole lung starts behaving like zone 3.

Zone 3, by contrast, is already near-maximal perfusion at rest (Pa > Pv > PA already). It can only increase further through distension of already-open vessels — a smaller proportional change.

So the answer is Zone 1 (C) because it shows the greatest increase (largest relative jump — from minimal to substantial flow via recruitment), even though zone 3 still has the highest absolute flow overall.

| West's Zone | Pressure relationship | Perfusion |
| ----------- | --------------------- | --------- |
| Zone 1 | PA > Pa > Pv | Minimal or absent (normally not present) |
| Zone 2 | Pa > PA > Pv | Moderate, flow depends on Pa − PA |
| Zone 3 | Pa > Pv > PA | Maximum perfusion |

1.	Exudative phase lasts from day 7 to day 21 after exposure to a precipitating risk factor.

3.	Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg body weight) has significantly lower mortality compared to high tidal volume ventilation (12 mL/kg body weight).

  • Statement 2. Proliferative phase is characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes: Correct.   • D. Alveolus X would empty into Alveolus Y due to lower resistance in larger airways: Air movement is determined by pressure gradients, not airway resistance in this scenario.

    • The RV becomes enlarged because it suddenly has to pump against an obstructed pulmonary circulation.

  • Flattening or bowing of the interventricular septum
    • Increased RV pressure pushes the septum toward the LV.

  • Dilated inferior vena cava (IVC) with reduced inspiratory collapse

Correct answer: A. High-dose oral calcium channel blocker (e.g., nifedipine or diltiazem)

Rationale: A positive acute vasoreactivity test — defined as a fall in mean pulmonary artery pressure of ≥10 mmHg to an absolute value ≤40 mmHg, with maintained or increased cardiac output — identifies a small subset (\~10%) of idiopathic PAH patients who respond favorably to long-term high-dose oral calcium channel blockers (typically nifedipine, diltiazem, or amlodipine), which can produce sustained hemodynamic and symptomatic improvement in true responders. Endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors, and prostacyclin analogs (B, C, D) are PAH-specific therapies used in vasoreactivity-negative patients (the majority), targeting the endothelin, nitric oxide, and prostacyclin pathways respectively — they are not the first-line choice in a confirmed acute responder.

| Parameter | Detail |
| --------- | ------ |
| Agents used for testing | Inhaled nitric oxide (preferred), IV epoprostenol, IV adenosine |
| Positive response criteria | ↓mPAP ≥10 mmHg to an absolute value ≤40 mmHg, with unchanged/increased cardiac output |
| Responders (\~10% of idiopathic PAH) | Trial of high-dose oral CCB; reassess response at 3–6 months |
| Non-responders (\~90%) | PAH-specific therapy: ERA, PDE-5 inhibitor/sGC stimulator, prostacyclin pathway agents (often combination therapy) |
| Caution | CCBs should NOT be given empirically without testing — risk of hypotension/right heart decompensation in non-responders |
| Long-term CCB success | Even among initial responders, only about half maintain sustained benefit long-term — requires reassessment |

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methotrexate

Methotrexate works primarily by inhibiting AICAR transformylase and thymidylate synthetase.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methotrexate

Methotrexate works primarily by inhibiting AICAR transformylase and thymidylate synthetase.

Option D. Hydroxychloroquine: Hydroxychloroquine is thought to exert its anti-inflammatory effects by interfering with lysosomal activity and autophagy in immune cells, and by modulating the activity of toll-like receptors (TLRs). It does not increase extracellular adenosine.

Correct answer: D. Sjögren syndrome

Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune exocrinopathy characterized by lymphocytic destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands, leading to keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) and xerostomia (dry mouth). It may occur as a primary disorder or secondary to another autoimmune disease, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis.

  • Autoantibodies: Anti-SSA (Ro) and Anti-SSB (La) are highly characteristic; ANA and RF are frequently positive.
  • Diagnosis: Positive Schirmer test (↓ tear production), ocular surface staining, and minor salivary gland (lip) biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.
  • Complications: Dental caries, oral candidiasis, parotid gland enlargement, corneal damage, and a markedly increased risk of MALT (marginal zone B-cell) lymphoma.
  • Treatment: Artificial tears, saliva substitutes, muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine, cevimeline), and immunomodulatory therapy for systemic disease.

Why not the other options?

  • A. SLE: Typically presents with photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, nephritis, serositis, and hematologic abnormalities; sicca symptoms may occur but are not the predominant feature.
  • B. Systemic sclerosis: Characterized by skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ fibrosis rather than isolated sicca symptoms.
  • C. Rheumatoid arthritis: Causes symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis but does not cause prominent dry eyes and dry mouth unless associated with secondary Sjögren syndrome.

  • Low CEA rules against all mucinous entities (MCN/IPMN).

The Nyhus classification is an anatomic system used to categorize inguinal hernias based on the status of the internal ring and the presence/extent of posterior wall weakness, and it helps guide operative repair.

A pantaloon hernia refers to the coexistence of:

  • a direct inguinal hernia (medial to inferior epigastric vessels), and
  • an indirect inguinal hernia (lateral to inferior epigastric vessels)

with two separate sacs straddling the inferior epigastric vessels, resembling a “pantaloon.”

In the Nyhus classification:

  • Type III = posterior wall defect (large hernias)
    • IIIa = direct hernia
    • IIIb = indirect hernia with posterior wall weakness (often large/scrotal) and includes combined/direct-indirect patterns such as pantaloon
  • Type IV = recurrent hernia

Therefore, a pantaloon hernia is classified as Nyhus Type IIIb (Option C).

Correct answer: C. Athletic pubalgia

Chronic deep groin pain in athletes that worsens with sprinting, twisting, kicking, and sit-ups in the absence of a visible/palpable groin bulge is most consistent with athletic pubalgia (sports hernia). Despite the term “hernia,” this condition is not a true hernia; instead it is caused by strain or tearing of the musculotendinous structures of the lower abdominal wall and groin, most commonly involving the rectus abdominis insertion, conjoint tendon, and/or posterior inguinal wall near the pubic tubercle. Key features supporting athletic pubalgia in this case:

  • Gradual progressive deep groin pain over months
  • Pain provoked by sit-ups (abdominal contraction) and sprinting
  • Tenderness over pubic tubercle
  • No cough impulse / no bulge → argues against inguinal hernia
  • Normal hip ROM and negative FADIR → rules out femoroacetabular impingement

Differentiation:

  • Occult inguinal hernia: may have cough impulse/bulge or pain with raised intra-abdominal pressure; imaging may show hernia.
  • Osteitis pubis: inflammatory pain at pubic symphysis, often midline with pain on adductor squeeze; imaging shows symphyseal changes.
  • Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI): hip pathology with reduced hip ROM and positive FADIR.

Thus, the most likely diagnosis is athletic pubalgia (sports hernia).
