questions.raw_text:
58-year-old, previously healthy man is evaluated due to a 2-month history of early satiety, postprandial epigastric pain and vomiting and unintended weight loss. Physical examination shows cachexia and palpable epigastric mass. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals a large prepyloric mass causing gastric outlet obstruction; biopsy of the mass is consistent with poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Abdominal CT scan reveals thickening of the gastric wall with adjacent fat infiltration, enlarged lymph nodes, and multiple hepatic metastatic lesions. The disease is considered unresectable, and the patient undergoes laparoscopic gastrojejunostomy for palliation of gastric outlet obstruction. Postoperatively, he tolerates tube feeding but experiences worsening weakness. The patient also has frequent episodes of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. Laboratory results are as follows:
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's worsening condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nutritional replenishment

A severely malnourished patient (eg, cancer cachexia) who is restarted on enteral feeds/TPN --> can develop refeeding syndrome.

  • a dangerous metabolic state caused by --> sudden switching from a catabolic to an anabolic insulin-driven state.

Key trigger
Restarting nutrition (especially carbohydrate-rich feeds) after prolonged starvation/malnutrition.

Laboratory findings:-
Hypophosphatemia (most characteristic + most life-threatening)
Associated with :
• Hypokalemia
• Hypomagnesemia
• Hyperglycemia
• Fluid retention → edema/heart failure

***Clinical consequences ***

• Muscle weakness , Respiratory failure (diaphragm weakness)
• Arrhythmias (VT/VF) due to ↓ATP + electrolyte derangements
• Hemolysis, rhabdomyolysis , Neurologic dysfunction

Prevention
• Start feeds slowly (low kcal initially)
• Give thiamine before feeding
• Replace PO₄/K/Mg aggressively
• Monitor electrolytes daily (or more frequently)

Therefore, the worsening weakness + VT with hypophosphatemia after tube feeding is due to nutritional replenishment (refeeding syndrome).

Correct answer: B. 2, 3, 4

Transillumination is a clinical test used to identify swellings that contain clear fluid (cystic lesions).

  • When a light is placed behind such a swelling in a dark room, the swelling glows-->indicating fluid content.

Swellings that transilluminate (fluid-filled)
✅ Spermatocoele – cystic swelling arising from epididymis, filled with fluid/sperm
✅ Ranula – mucus retention cyst in the floor of mouth (salivary origin)
✅ Cystic hygroma – congenital lymphatic malformation, multiloculated fluid-filled swelling
So: 2, 3, 4 are correct.

Swellings that do NOT transilluminate
❌ Meningomyelocele – contains neural tissue/CSF but has thick coverings and solid elements; not classically transilluminant in exam setting
❌ Lipoma – solid fat tumor, does not transilluminate

Correct answer: A. Collapse of the lung using double-lumen endotracheal intubation

Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) requires a clear operative field within the pleural cavity, which is only possible if the ipsilateral lung is collapsed. Therefore, the first essential step in standard VATS preparation is establishing one-lung ventilation (OLV), most commonly achieved with a double-lumen endotracheal tube (DLT) (or bronchial blocker when DLT is not feasible).

Collapsing the operative lung:

  • Improves visualization of pleura, lung, mediastinum
  • Reduces risk of lung injury during port placement
  • Facilitates safe manipulation and dissection

Only after confirming effective lung isolation and collapse should the team proceed with lateral decubitus positioning and subsequent port/camera insertion. Thus, lung collapse using double-lumen intubation is the first essential step before port insertion in VATS.

questions.raw_text: I-VITROS in relation to minimally invasive surgery refers to:

options.text: Incise, View, Identify, Ti​e, Repair, Observe, Seal
Incise, Visualise, Insuffu​late, Triangulate, Retrac‌t, Operate, Seal
Insuffulate, Visualise, In​cise, Triangulate, Repair‌, Operate, Seal

Correct answer: D. Insuffulate, Visualise, Identify, Triangulate, Retract, Operate, Seal

Minimally invasive surgery (MIS)/laparoscopy follows a structured sequence of steps to ensure safe access, adequate visualization, proper tissue handling, and secure closure. The mnemonic I-VITROS describes the standard workflow of laparoscopic surgery.

I-VITROS =

  • I – Insufflate: create pneumoperitoneum (usually CO₂) to form working space
  • V – Visualise: introduce telescope and confirm safe intraperitoneal access
  • I – Identify: identify anatomy, pathology, and key landmarks
  • T – Triangulate: correct port placement for ergonomic instrument alignment and precision
  • R – Retract: expose operative field safely without tissue trauma
  • O – Operate: perform the intended surgical steps (dissection, clipping, cutting, suturing)
  • S – Seal: ensure hemostasis/secure closure (energy sealing, clips, sutures) and final check

Thus, I-VITROS in MIS refers to “Insufflate, Visualise, Identify, Triangulate, Retract, Operate, Seal” (Option D).

questions.raw_text:
A 62 year old man with moderate COPD and hypertension is undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. After creation of pneumoperitoneum with CO2 at an intra-abdominal pressure of 15 mmHg, the following findings are noted:
-	Sudden rise in EtCO2 from 34 to 54mmHg
-	Increase in peak airway pressure 
-	HR- 50 bpm
Which of the following scenarios can explain these findings?

options.text: CO2 embolism leading to ac​ute right heart obstructi‌on.
Vagal mediated JT reflex d​ue to peritoneal stretch.‌
Absorption of CO2 from per​itoneum causing hypercarb‌ia and respiratory acidos‍is.
Decreased venous return du​e to high IAP causing obs‌tructive shock.

questions.correct_answer: C. Absorption of CO2 from peritoneum causing hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Absorption of CO2 from peritoneum causing hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis.

Creation of CO₂ pneumoperitoneum during laparoscopy increases intra-abdominal pressure and exposes the peritoneum to a highly diffusible gas. CO₂ is rapidly absorbed into the bloodstream, especially at higher pressures (e.g., IAP 15 mmHg), leading to hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis unless ventilation is increased. The most characteristic physiologic response to increased CO₂ absorption is:

  • Rise in EtCO₂ (as seen from 34 → 54 mmHg)
  • Increased airway pressures due to diaphragmatic splinting and reduced lung compliance from pneumoperitoneum

The accompanying bradycardia can occur with acute hypercarbia/acidosis or may coexist with peritoneal stretch reflexes, but the key unifying finding here is the marked rise in EtCO₂, which is best explained by CO₂ absorption from the peritoneum.

This differs from:

  • CO₂ embolism → typically causes a sudden fall in EtCO₂ (due to increased dead space) with cardiovascular collapse.
  • Vagal stretch reflex → causes bradycardia but does not explain a significant EtCO₂ rise.
  • Reduced venous return from high IAP → hypotension/tachycardia; not primarily a large EtCO₂ rise.

  • No pus
  • No spreading erythema

  • Grade I: normal healing (may have mild bruising/erythema only)
  • Grade II: erythema/inflammation only (no discharge)
  • Grade III: discharge present

    • IIIb: seropurulent discharge
  • Grade IV/V: deep or severe infection (abscess/dehiscence/systemic sepsis)

questions.text: A patient with acute pancr​eatitis has BP 84/50, HR ‌140, cold extremities. • ‍PCWP: normal • SVR: high ​• CVP: low • CO: low What‍ is the type of shock?
questions.raw_text:
A patient with acute pancreatitis has BP 84/50, HR 140, cold extremities.
•	PCWP: normal
•	SVR: high
•	CVP: low
•	CO: low
What is the type of shock?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypovolemic

Shock is classified based on hemodynamic parameters such as cardiac output (CO), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), and filling pressures (CVP and PCWP). In acute pancreatitis, massive third spacing of fluid into the retroperitoneum and peritoneal cavity can cause significant intravascular volume depletion, leading to hypovolemic shock.

Hypovolemic shock is characterized by:

  • Low preload → low CVP
  • Low left-sided filling pressure → normal/low PCWP
  • Low CO due to reduced venous return
  • High SVR as a compensatory vasoconstrictive response
  • Clinical findings of cold extremities and poor perfusion

This differs from:

  • Cardiogenic shock: high PCWP, high CVP, low CO, high SVR
  • Distributive shock (sepsis/anaphylaxis): low SVR with warm extremities early
  • Obstructive shock (PE/tamponade): high CVP with low CO

Thus, the given hemodynamic profile (↓ CVP, normal PCWP, ↓ CO, ↑ SVR with cold extremities) confirms hypovolemic shock.

options.text: Continue insufflation as t​he needle is likely intra‌peritoneal

Correct Veress needle placement in the peritoneal cavity is suggested by two distinct “clicks” (fascia then peritoneum), low initial insufflation pressure (<10 mmHg) with free flow of gas, good abdominal distension, and a positive saline drop test (free fall without bubbling).

Therefore, the safest and most appropriate next step is to abort the Veress attempt and switch to an open (Hasson) technique to obtain direct visual entry and reduce the risk of further injury. Continuing insufflation or advancing the needle risks worsening extraperitoneal insufflation or penetrating bowel/major vessels and attempting umbilical entry is unsafe due to likely adhesions from prior surgeries.

• Outer zone
• Increased perfusion and inflammation
• Usually recovers completely

• Maintain perfusion (adequate fluids)
• Prevent infection
• Avoid pressure or hypoxia

  • TBI 0.4–0.7: PAD

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystic artery

In laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the “critical view of safety” (CVS) described by Strasberg requires full clearance of the hepatocystic (Calot’s) triangle, which is bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct, and the inferior surface of the liver. Within this cleared triangle, only two structures leading into the gallbladder should be visible, which are then identified as the cystic duct and cystic artery. The cystic artery itself is not a boundary of the triangle. It lies inside the triangle after dissection.

Learning Points:

  • Hepatocystic triangle – Bounded by cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver, and is the key area dissected for CVS.
  • Original Calot’s triangle – Calot’s original description used the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and cystic artery, but in modern hepatobiliary surgery the superior boundary is taken as the liver edge, not the artery.
  • Critical view of safety – Requires that the hepatocystic triangle is cleared of fat and fibrous tissue and only two structures entering the gallbladder are seen, minimizing risk of bile duct injury.
  • Cystic artery location – The cystic artery typically runs within the triangle and is one of the two structures to be clipped and divided, but it is not a boundary in the modern definition used for CVS.
  • Bile duct injury prevention – Proper identification of the cystic duct versus common hepatic duct within the hepatocystic triangle is essential to avoid catastrophic common bile duct injury.

Other Options:
A. Cystic duct – Correct boundary. Forms the inferior edge of the hepatocystic triangle.
B. Inferior surface of the liver – Correct boundary. The superior border of the hepatocystic triangle in modern usage.
D. Common hepatic duct – Correct boundary. Forms the medial edge of the hepatocystic triangle.
C. Cystic artery – Not a boundary in the modern hepatocystic triangle used for critical view of safety, so this is the correct answer.

Trick points / Common confusions:

  • Exam questions often mix original Calot’s triangle and modern hepatocystic triangle. For a critical view of safety, think cystic duct, common hepatic duct, liver edge, not the artery.
  • A useful memory aid is that the two structures you finally clip (cystic duct and artery) are inside the triangle, whereas the triangle boundaries include only one duct twice and the liver edge.

Neurogenic shock occurs after acute cervical or high thoracic spinal cord injury due to loss of sympathetic outflow, resulting in massive vasodilation and bradycardia.

  • Hypotension is therefore due to vasodilation, not volume loss.

Pathophysiology :-

• Spinal cord injury → interruption of sympathetic pathways (T1–L2)
• Unopposed parasympathetic (vagal) tone → bradycardia
• Loss of peripheral vascular tone → systemic vasodilation
• Leads to hypotension with warm, flushed skin

Key clinical features
• Hypotension despite adequate fluid resuscitation
• Bradycardia (unlike hypovolemic shock → tachycardia)
• Warm extremities
• Normal CVP and negative FAST (no bleeding)

Differentiation from other shocks :-

• Hypovolemic shock: tachycardia, cold clammy skin, low CVP
• Cardiogenic shock: high CVP, pulmonary edema
• Obstructive shock: tamponade, PE, tension pneumothorax signs

  • High SVR as a compensatory vasoconstrictive response
  • Clinical findings of cold extremities and poor perfusion

  • Cardiogenic shock: high PCWP, high CVP, low CO, high SVR
  • Distributive shock (sepsis/anaphylaxis): low SVR with warm extremities early
  • Obstructive shock (PE/tamponade): high CVP with low CO

Thus, the given hemodynamic profile (↓ CVP, normal PCWP, ↓ CO, ↑ SVR with cold extremities) confirms hypovolemic shock.

questions.explanation:

1) Acute Appendicitis
Typical progression:
Visceral pain phase

  • Pain begins around the umbilicus
  • Because visceral afferents from the appendix enter T10 spinal segment

Parietal peritoneal irritation

  • Inflammation reaches parietal peritoneum
  • Pain localizes to right lower quadrant

This is where McBurney’s point tenderness appears.

  • Junction of lateral 1/3 and medial 2/3 of the line between: Umbilicus-Right anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)

2) Ultrasound is preferred in pregnant women and children ✔️

  • Ultrasound has no radiation
  • Safe for pregnancy and pediatrics

It can detect:

  • Inflamed appendix
  • Appendix diameter > 6 mm
  • Peri-appendiceal fluid

3) Ochsner-Sherren regimen is preferred for appendicular mass ✔️
An appendicular mass forms when the body tries to contain infection by surrounding the inflamed appendix with: Omentum and Bowel loops
Instead of immediate surgery, conservative treatment is given.
This is called Ochsner–Sherren regimen, which includes:

  • Nil by mouth
  • IV fluids
  • Antibiotics
  • Observation

Surgery is avoided initially because operating on a mass can injure surrounding bowel.

4) Interval appendectomy is mandatory-This is false.
Earlier practice:

  • After conservative treatment, surgery was done 6–8 weeks later (interval appendectomy).

Current practice:

  • Not mandatory anymore
  • Done only if symptoms recur.

Many patients remain completely asymptomatic.

  • The transversalis fascia/posterior wall is cleared to prepare for mesh placement.

  • A polypropylene mesh is placed over the posterior wall.
  • Fixed to:

    • Conjoint tendon (superiorly)
  • A slit is made in the mesh to accommodate the spermatic cord.

Wound closure
Layers closed sequentially:

  • External oblique aponeurosis
  • Subcutaneous tissue
  • Skin

questions.raw_text: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon carefully dissects to obtain the “critical view of safety”. Which of the following is not a boundary of this triangle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystic artery

In laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the “critical view of safety” (CVS) described by Strasberg requires full clearance of the hepatocystic (Calot’s) triangle, which is bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct, and the inferior surface of the liver. Within this cleared triangle, only two structures leading into the gallbladder should be visible, which are then identified as the cystic duct and cystic artery. The cystic artery itself is not a boundary of the triangle. It lies inside the triangle after dissection.

Learning Points:

  • Hepatocystic triangle – Bounded by cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver, and is the key area dissected for CVS.
  • Original Calot’s triangle – Calot’s original description used the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and cystic artery, but in modern hepatobiliary surgery the superior boundary is taken as the liver edge, not the artery.
  • Critical view of safety – Requires that the hepatocystic triangle is cleared of fat and fibrous tissue and only two structures entering the gallbladder are seen, minimizing risk of bile duct injury.
  • Cystic artery location – The cystic artery typically runs within the triangle and is one of the two structures to be clipped and divided, but it is not a boundary in the modern definition used for CVS.
  • Bile duct injury prevention – Proper identification of the cystic duct versus common hepatic duct within the hepatocystic triangle is essential to avoid catastrophic common bile duct injury.

Other Options:
A. Cystic duct – Correct boundary. Forms the inferior edge of the hepatocystic triangle.
B. Inferior surface of the liver – Correct boundary. The superior border of the hepatocystic triangle in modern usage.
D. Common hepatic duct – Correct boundary. Forms the medial edge of the hepatocystic triangle.
C. Cystic artery – Not a boundary in the modern hepatocystic triangle used for critical view of safety, so this is the correct answer.

Trick points / Common confusions:

  • Exam questions often mix original Calot’s triangle and modern hepatocystic triangle. For a critical view of safety, think cystic duct, common hepatic duct, liver edge, not the artery.
  • A useful memory aid is that the two structures you finally clip (cystic duct and artery) are inside the triangle, whereas the triangle boundaries include only one duct twice and the liver edge.

Inguinal hernias in children are congenital and occur due to failure of obliteration of the processus vaginalis. Volume=Weight (kg)×TBSA burned (%)÷2

  • Blood loses protein → oncotic pressure of blood ↓

  • Creates a pulling force that draws fluid from interstitium → back into vessels

Correct answer: C. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid

  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid, which originate from the neural crest and secrete calcitonin.
  • The pathognomonic histological feature is amyloid deposition in the stroma, which is derived from altered calcitonin molecules produced by the tumor cells.

Key contraindications to BCT

Absolute

  • Prior chest RT
  • Pregnancy (when RT required)
  • Multicentric disease
  • Persistent positive margins
  • Collagen vascular diseases

Relative

  • Large tumour relative to breast size
  • Locally advanced breast cancer (LABC)

The patient has acute limb ischemia (ALI) with a Rutherford Grade IIa (marginally threatened limb).

  • Sudden onset severe limb pain
  • Cold, pale limb
  • Absent distal pulses
  • Sensory loss limited to the toes
  • No significant motor deficit (power 4/5)
  • No fixed mottling or muscle rigidity

A viable but threatened limb requires urgent revascularization to salvage the extremity.

The patient has a salvageable limb with mild sensory loss and minimal motor weakness. The recommended management is:

  • Immediate IV unfractionated heparin
  • Urgent revascularization (catheter-directed thrombolysis, surgical embolectomy, or bypass depending on the cause and anatomy)

Rutherford classification of acute limb ischemia

| Grade | Limb Status | Clinical Features | Management |
| ----- | ----------- | ----------------- | ---------- |
| I | Viable | No sensory or motor deficit | Anticoagulation ± imaging |
| IIa | Marginally threatened | Toe sensory loss, minimal/no motor deficit | Urgent revascularization |
| IIb | Immediately threatened | Sensory loss beyond toes, significant motor weakness | Immediate revascularization |
| III | Irreversible | Profound anesthesia, paralysis, fixed mottling | Amputation |

Why not the other options?

  • A. Intravenous anticoagulation and observation: Anticoagulation is started immediately but observation alone is inappropriate because the limb is threatened.
  • B. Catheter-directed thrombolysis: May be used as a revascularization technique in selected Rutherford I and IIa patients, but the broader and most appropriate answer is urgent revascularization.
  • D. Amputation: Reserved for irreversible ischemia (Rutherford Grade III) with profound anesthesia, paralysis, fixed mottling, and muscle rigidity.

1.	Incision of the skin
2.	Identify the hernia sac and reduce the contents

4.	Mesh placement and fixation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 2 4 3

Standard steps of inguinal hernioplasty (Lichtenstein repair)
Skin incision

  • Oblique inguinal incision parallel to the inguinal ligament.
  • Opens the layers to reach the inguinal canal.

Open external oblique aponeurosis

  • The external oblique aponeurosis is split along its fibers.
  • This exposes the inguinal canal and spermatic cord.

Mobilize the spermatic cord

  • The spermatic cord is isolated and lifted with a sling.
  • This allows clear visualization of the hernia sac

Identify and manage the hernia sac

  • Indirect hernia: sac separated from cord → ligated and excised.
  • Direct hernia: sac reduced back into abdomen.

Prepare posterior wall

  • The transversalis fascia/posterior wall is cleared to prepare for mesh placement.

Mesh placement (tension-free repair)

  • A polypropylene mesh is placed over the posterior wall.
  • Fixed to:
    • Inguinal ligament (inferiorly)
    • Conjoint tendon (superiorly)
  • A slit is made in the mesh to accommodate the spermatic cord.

Wound closure
Layers closed sequentially:

  • External oblique aponeurosis
  • Subcutaneous tissue
  • Skin

While dissecting Calot's triangle, a lateral injury to the common bile duct occurred, leading to significant bile leakage into the operative field. The surgeon has limited experience in laparoscopy. What is the most appropriate intraoperative management step at this stage?

options.text: Continuing laparoscopic re‌pair of the common bile d‌uct
Placing a drainage tube in‌ subhepatic space
Closing the abdomen and ta‌king the patient for ERCP‌ and biliary stenting

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Converting the laparoscopic surgery to open surgery and placing a T-tube through the injured common bile duct

Bile duct injury is one of the most serious complications of laparoscopic cholecystectomy, most commonly occurring during dissection of Calot’s triangle due to misidentification of biliary anatomy. In this case:

  • Lateral injury to the common bile duct (CBD)
  • Significant bile leak
  • Surgeon has limited laparoscopic experience

The safest management is to convert to open surgery and repair the injury over a T-tube, which decompresses the biliary tree and allows postoperative cholangiography.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Continue laparoscopic repair of common bile duct: Not advisable in an inexperienced surgeon; increases the risk of further injury and stricture.
  • B. Place only a drainage tube in subhepatic space: Inadequate for a recognized CBD injury.
  • C. Close abdomen and perform ERCP and biliary stenting later: ERCP is useful for postoperative leaks but recognized major intraoperative bile duct injuries should be addressed immediately.

Correct answer: D. Abdominal discomfort and ascites are the main presenting features.

Budd–Chiari syndrome (BCS) is caused by obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, anywhere from the small hepatic veins to the junction of the inferior vena cava (IVC) with the right atrium. The obstruction leads to hepatic congestion, portal hypertension, and impaired liver function.

The classic clinical triad consists of:

  • Abdominal pain/discomfort
  • Ascites
  • Hepatomegaly

Why not the other options?

  • A. It principally affects young males: BCS is more common in young to middle-aged adults, with a female predominance in many populations due to associations with pregnancy, oral contraceptive use, and myeloproliferative disorders.
  • B. Venous drainage of the liver is occluded by IVC thrombus: The obstruction most commonly involves the hepatic veins. IVC obstruction can occur but is not the defining or usual mechanism.
  • C. Quadrate lobe (Segment 4 and 5) undergoes hypertrophy: The caudate lobe (Segment I) undergoes hypertrophy because it has independent venous drainage directly into the IVC, allowing it to remain relatively spared.

The gallbladder is a storage and concentrating organ for bile. It does not produce bile; bile is synthesized by hepatocytes in the liver. The gallbladder modifies bile by absorbing water and electrolytes and secreting mucus, which protects the mucosa and facilitates bile flow.

The normal functions of the gallbladder include:

  • I. Reservoir for bile: Stores approximately 30–60 mL of bile between meals.
  • III. Secretion of mucus: Mucus protects the gallbladder mucosa and lubricates bile flow.
  • IV. Concentration of bile: The gallbladder absorbs water, sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate, concentrating bile 5–10 times.

Why is II incorrect?

  • II. Production of bile: Bile is produced by hepatocytes in the liver, not by the gallbladder.

The gallbladder may have several congenital anomalies involving its shape, position, number, and development. Most are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally during imaging or surgery, but some predispose to torsion, gallstone formation, or surgical complications.

The following are recognized congenital anomalies of the gallbladder:

  • I. Phrygian cap: The most common congenital anomaly of the gallbladder. It is a folding of the fundus over the body, resembling the cap worn by ancient Phrygians. It is usually clinically insignificant.
  • II. Floating gall bladder: The gallbladder is suspended by a long mesentery, making it unusually mobile and predisposing it to gallbladder volvulus (torsion).

  • Sonographic Murphy’s sign

| Type | Definition |
| ---- | ---------- |
| Primary | Formed de novo within the bile duct itself |
| Secondary | Migrated from the gallbladder into the CBD |
| Retained | Missed at the time of cholecystectomy (found within 2 years of surgery) |
| Recurrent | Found after 2 years of a previous stone-clear CBD |

Why "Primary" is Correct Here

The key detail is the 4-year gap after cholecystectomy:

  • The gallbladder has been removed → stone cannot have migrated from GB → rules out Secondary
  • Discovered 4 years post-op → beyond the 2-year window → rules out Retained
  • Stone formed de novo in the CBD after cholecystectomy = Primary stone

Characteristics of Primary CBD Stones

  • Typically brown pigment stones (vs. cholesterol in secondary)
  • Associated with bile stasis, infection (E. coli, biliary stricture)
  • Often soft, earthy, and friable
  • Seen with biliary stricture, periampullary diverticulum, or biliary dyskinesia
  • E. coli produces β-glucuronidase → deconjugates bilirubin → pigment stone formation

  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid, which originate from the neural crest and secrete calcitonin.
  • The pathognomonic histological feature is amyloid deposition in the stroma, which is derived from altered calcitonin molecules produced by the tumor cells.

  • C. Radioactive iodine ablation: Used after confirmation of differentiated thyroid carcinoma, not before diagnosis.
  • D. Repeat FNAC after 6 months: Repeating FNAC is unlikely to resolve the diagnosis because cytology cannot assess capsular or vascular invasion.

  • Baseline risk halves as you go:
    • Isolated → Dominant → Generalized
  • Within each:
    • Solid = double cystic
    • Male = double female

    o   dissection here risks RLN trauma

  • Done at superior pole, mainly risks EBSLN
  • Does not typically injure RLN, hence does not lead to hoarseness in the classical sense

The diagram illustrates the Monro–Kellie doctrine, which states that the adult skull is a rigid, fixed-volume compartment containing three major components:

When the volume of one component increases, the others must decrease to maintain a constant intracranial volume. Initially, CSF displacement and increased venous outflow compensate for an expanding mass. Once compensatory mechanisms are exhausted, intracranial pressure (ICP) rises rapidly.

In trauma, a patient with transient response to fluid resuscitation (initial BP improvement followed by deterioration) should be assumed to have ongoing hemorrhage until proven otherwise.

  • Occult hemorrhagic shock is characterized by:
    • Transient responder pattern to fluids
    • Low central venous pressure (CVP) → suggests hypovolemia
    • Elevated serum lactate → ongoing tissue hypoperfusion
    • No obvious external or intraperitoneal bleeding → think hidden sources (retroperitoneum, pelvis, long bones, thorax)
  • FAST negative ≠ no bleeding

  • Key differentiation from other shocks:
    • Cardiogenic → high CVP
    • Obstructive → high CVP (e.g., tension pneumothorax, tamponade)
    • Neurogenic → hypotension with bradycardia, not high lactate initially

The Formula:
The total required fluid for a given time period is calculated as:
Volume=Weight (kg)×TBSA burned (%)÷2
The calculated volume is delivered as one "ration." This ration is administered across 6 periods totaling 36 hours, distributed as follows:

  • First 12 hours: 1 ration every 4 hours (3 infusions)
  • Second 12 hours: 1 ration every 6 hours (2 infusions)
  • Third 12 hours: 1 full ration administered over the 12 hours (1 infusion)
Pathophysiology in burns:
  • Capillaries become leaky→ Fluid + proteins leak into tissues → interstitial fluid ↑ →  Fluid stays in tissues as edema
  • Blood loses protein → oncotic pressure of blood ↓

Albumin is the main protein responsible for plasma oncotic pressure

  • It increases oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure in blood
  • Creates a pulling force that draws fluid from interstitium → back into vessels
  • ↓ Interstitial fluid → less edema. ↑ Intravascular volume → better perfusion.

Zone of stasis (Correct answer)
• Surrounds central zone of coagulation
• Characterized by reduced perfusion, vasoconstriction, and microvascular thrombosis

Zone of coagulation:
• Central area of burn
• Irreversible tissue necrosis
• Protein denaturation and cell death

Zone of hyperemia:
• Outer zone
• Increased perfusion and inflammation
• Usually recovers completely

Proper burn management aims to:
• Maintain perfusion (adequate fluids)
• Prevent infection
• Avoid pressure or hypoxia
→ to salvage the zone of stasis

Neurological examination reveals loss of vibration sense and sensory ataxia, suggestive of tabes dorsalis. Urodynamic evaluation demonstrates the following. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atonic bladder

The patient has tabes dorsalis, a manifestation of neurosyphilis involving degeneration of the posterior columns and dorsal roots of the spinal cord. Damage to the afferent sensory fibers from the bladder abolishes the normal micturition reflex.

This results in an atonic (flaccid) neurogenic bladder, characterized by:

  • Large-capacity bladder
  • Poor or absent detrusor contractions
  • Chronic urinary retention
  • Overflow incontinence
  • Increased post-void residual urine

Urodynamic studies (cystometrogram) typically show a large-capacity bladder with markedly reduced detrusor activity, exactly as described.

Why not the other options?

  • A. Automatic bladder: Occurs with spinal cord lesions above the sacral micturition center after the spinal shock phase. Reflex voiding returns, but bladder emptying is involuntary.
  • C. Spastic bladder: Seen in suprasacral spinal cord lesions. The bladder has increased detrusor tone, small capacity, urgency, frequency, and reflex voiding—not a large flaccid bladder.
  • D. Neurogenic uninhibited bladder: Results from frontal lobe or cerebral lesions, causing urgency, frequency, and urge incontinence with preserved detrusor contractions.

High-yield pearl

| Type of neurogenic bladder | Site of lesion | Bladder characteristics |
| -------------------------- | -------------- | ----------------------- |
| Atonic (flaccid) bladder | Sacral cord, pelvic nerves, dorsal roots (e.g., tabes dorsalis, diabetic neuropathy) | Large-capacity bladder, urinary retention, overflow incontinence, ↓ detrusor contraction |
| Automatic bladder | Spinal cord lesion above S2–S4 | Reflex emptying after spinal shock |
| Spastic bladder | Suprasacral spinal cord lesion | Small-capacity, hyperreflexic bladder, urgency |
| Neurogenic uninhibited bladder | Frontal cortex lesion | Urgency and urge incontinence |

An obstructed infected urinary system (obstructive pyelonephritis/pyonephrosis) is a urological emergency. Obstruction prevents drainage of infected urine, predisposing the patient to urosepsis and septic shock.

  • Start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics

  • B. Percutaneous nephrectomy: Nephrectomy is not the initial treatment unless the kidney is non-functioning and infection persists despite appropriate management.
  • D. Elective nephrectomy after the infection subsides: Not indicated as first-line management in an acute obstructed infected kidney.

  • "Obstruction + Fever = Drain first, stone later."
  • Never perform definitive stone removal before decompressing an infected obstructed collecting system.

  • Sudden onset severe limb pain
  • Cold, pale limb
  • Absent distal pulses
  • Sensory loss limited to the toes
  • No significant motor deficit (power 4/5)
  • No fixed mottling or muscle rigidity

Rutherford classification of acute limb ischemia

| Grade | Limb Status | Clinical Features | Management |
| ----- | ----------- | ----------------- | ---------- |
| I | Viable | No sensory or motor deficit | Anticoagulation ± imaging |
| IIa | Marginally threatened | Toe sensory loss, minimal/no motor deficit | Urgent revascularization |
| IIb | Immediately threatened | Sensory loss beyond toes, significant motor weakness | Immediate revascularization |
| III | Irreversible | Profound anesthesia, paralysis, fixed mottling | Amputation |

  • B. Catheter-directed thrombolysis: May be used as a revascularization technique in selected Rutherford I and IIa patients, but the broader and most appropriate answer is urgent revascularization.

  • Type IV = recurrent hernia

• Hypovolemic shock: tachycardia, cold clammy skin, low CVP
• Cardiogenic shock: high CVP, pulmonary edema
• Obstructive shock: tamponade, PE, tension pneumothorax signs

Minimally invasive surgery (MIS)/laparoscopy follows a structured sequence of steps to ensure safe access, adequate visualization, proper tissue handling, and secure closure. The mnemonic I-VITROS describes the standard workflow of laparoscopic surgery.

I-VITROS =

  • I – Insufflate: create pneumoperitoneum (usually CO₂) to form working space
  • V – Visualise: introduce telescope and confirm safe intraperitoneal access
  • I – Identify: identify anatomy, pathology, and key landmarks
  • T – Triangulate: correct port placement for ergonomic instrument alignment and precision
  • R – Retract: expose operative field safely without tissue trauma
  • O – Operate: perform the intended surgical steps (dissection, clipping, cutting, suturing)
  • S – Seal: ensure hemostasis/secure closure (energy sealing, clips, sutures) and final check

Thus, I-VITROS in MIS refers to “Insufflate, Visualise, Identify, Triangulate, Retract, Operate, Seal” (Option D).

A 62 year old man with moderate COPD and hypertension is undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. After creation of pneumoperitoneum with CO2 at an intra-abdominal pressure of 15 mmHg, the following findings are noted:
-	Sudden rise in EtCO2 from 34 to 54mmHg
-	Increase in peak airway pressure 
-	HR- 50 bpm
Which of the following scenarios can explain these findings?

options.text: CO2 embolism leading to ac​ute right heart obstructi​on.
Vagal mediated JT reflex d​ue to peritoneal stretch.​
Absorption of CO2 from per​itoneum causing hypercarb​ia and respiratory acidos​is.
Decreased venous return du​e to high IAP causing obs​tructive shock.

questions.correct_answer: C. Absorption of CO2 from peritoneum causing hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Absorption of CO2 from peritoneum causing hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis.

Creation of CO₂ pneumoperitoneum during laparoscopy increases intra-abdominal pressure and exposes the peritoneum to a highly diffusible gas. CO₂ is rapidly absorbed into the bloodstream, especially at higher pressures (e.g., IAP 15 mmHg), leading to hypercarbia and respiratory acidosis unless ventilation is increased. The most characteristic physiologic response to increased CO₂ absorption is:

  • Rise in EtCO₂ (as seen from 34 → 54 mmHg)
  • Increased airway pressures due to diaphragmatic splinting and reduced lung compliance from pneumoperitoneum

The accompanying bradycardia can occur with acute hypercarbia/acidosis or may coexist with peritoneal stretch reflexes, but the key unifying finding here is the marked rise in EtCO₂, which is best explained by CO₂ absorption from the peritoneum.

This differs from:

  • CO₂ embolism → typically causes a sudden fall in EtCO₂ (due to increased dead space) with cardiovascular collapse.
  • Vagal stretch reflex → causes bradycardia but does not explain a significant EtCO₂ rise.
  • Reduced venous return from high IAP → hypotension/tachycardia; not primarily a large EtCO₂ rise.

The surgeon decides to insert the Veress needle at Palmer’s point. During insertion, the surgeon feels only one click, and on connecting the insufflator, the pressure initially rises to 17 mmHg, then slowly falls to 12 mmHg but does not drop further. There is minimal abdominal expansion, and the saline drop test shows intermittent bubbling, not free fall. A small amount of bloody fluid is aspirated from the needle. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue insufflation as t​he needle is likely intra​peritoneal
Advance the Veress needle ​further until pressure dr​ops
Stop the attempt and switc​h to open (Hasson) techni​que
Withdraw the needle and at​tempt insertion at the um​bilicus

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stop the attempt and switch to open (Hasson) technique

Safe creation of pneumoperitoneum is the critical first step in laparoscopy. Correct Veress needle placement in the peritoneal cavity is suggested by two distinct “clicks” (fascia then peritoneum), low initial insufflation pressure (<10 mmHg) with free flow of gas, good abdominal distension, and a positive saline drop test (free fall without bubbling).

In this obese patient with multiple previous midline laparotomies, the risk of intra-abdominal adhesions and visceral/vascular injury is high, even when using an alternative entry site like Palmer’s point. In this case, multiple findings indicate incorrect/unsafe placement and possible injury: only one click, high opening pressure (17 mmHg) that fails to fall below 12, minimal abdominal expansion, intermittent bubbling on saline drop test, and bloody aspirate (suggesting preperitoneal placement or vascular/visceral trauma).

Therefore, the safest and most appropriate next step is to abort the Veress attempt and switch to an open (Hasson) technique to obtain direct visual entry and reduce the risk of further injury. Continuing insufflation or advancing the needle risks worsening extraperitoneal insufflation or penetrating bowel/major vessels and attempting umbilical entry is unsafe due to likely adhesions from prior surgeries.

questions.raw_text: The principle of adaptation shown in the following diagram is explained by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Monro-Kellie doctrine

The diagram illustrates the Monro–Kellie doctrine, which states that the adult skull is a rigid, fixed-volume compartment containing three major components:

  • Brain tissue
  • Arterial and venous blood
  • Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)

When the volume of one component increases, the others must decrease to maintain a constant intracranial volume. Initially, CSF displacement and increased venous outflow compensate for an expanding mass. Once compensatory mechanisms are exhausted, intracranial pressure (ICP) rises rapidly.

Why not the other options?

  • (a) Moynihan’s aphorism: Relates to surgical principles, not intracranial pressure.
  • (b) Monro–Kellie doctrine — Correct: Explains the relationship between intracranial contents and ICP.
  • (c) Cushing’s law: Describes the physiological response to raised ICP, particularly hypertension with bradycardia and respiratory changes.

Retroperitoneal hematomas are classified by anatomical zone, and management depends on both the zone and the mechanism of injury (blunt vs. penetrating):

| Zone | Location | Blunt trauma | Penetrating trauma |
| ---- | -------- | ------------ | ------------------ |
| Zone 1 (Central/medial) | Aorta, IVC, pancreas, duodenum | Always explore | Always explore |
| Zone 2 (Lateral/perinephric) | Kidney, ascending/descending (retroperitoneal) colon | Explore only if expanding, pulsatile, or ruptured | Explore |
| Zone 3 (Pelvic) | Pelvic vessels | Explore only if expanding or uncontrolled (often better managed by angioembolization) | Explore |

  • The retroperitoneal colon (ascending and descending colon) lies in Zone 2. In blunt trauma, a non-expanding, non-pulsatile Zone 2 hematoma is generally left undisturbed — the retroperitoneum itself provides tamponade, and opening an intact hematoma risks converting a self-limited injury into uncontrolled hemorrhage or missing the chance for the body's own tamponade to work.
  • Since the hematoma is not explored, the underlying retroperitoneal colon is also not visualized or manipulated — so no resection or repair is performed unless there's clear evidence of colonic perforation (free air, succus entericus, fecal contamination, or an expanding/pulsatile hematoma), in which case exploration becomes mandatory regardless of zone.

• Prevent infection

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Connective tissue weakness

The key mechanism is: Weakness of connective tissue in the aortic media. This leads to cystic medial degeneration.
Features include:

  • Fragmentation of elastic fibers
  • Loss of smooth muscle cells
  • Accumulation of mucoid material

The presentation of tearing chest pain radiating to the back with negative cardiac biomarkers is classic for aortic dissection.
Aortic dissection results from medial degeneration with connective tissue weakness, leading to an intimal tear. This allows blood to track between layers of the aortic wall.

| Risk factor | Mechanism |
| ----------- | --------- |
| Hypertension | Most common cause |
| Marfan syndrome | Connective tissue defect |
| Ehlers–Danlos syndrome | Collagen defect |
| Bicuspid aortic valve | Aortic wall weakness |

Fibrinoid necrosis and immune complex vasculitis are seen in vasculitides, not dissection.
A) Fibrinoid necrosis
Seen in malignant hypertension or vasculitis, not typical for dissection.

B) Subintimal lipid infiltration
Mechanism of atherosclerosis, not aortic dissection.

C) Immune complex vasculitis
Occurs in diseases like polyarteritis nodosa, not dissection.

Doppler shows absent dorsalis pedis flow but audible posterior tibial artery flow. Sensation is reduced over the toes, motor sensation is intact. Capillary refill is sluggish. Using Rutherford classification, the limb is what category?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Marginally threatened (category 2a)

Acute limb ischemia (ALI) is a vascular emergency defined by a sudden reduction in limb perfusion (typically <14 days) producing the classic 6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia. Management urgency is guided by the Rutherford classification, which predicts limb viability based on sensory loss, motor deficit, and Doppler signals.

These findings correspond to Rutherford Category IIa (Marginally threatened):

  • No motor deficit
  • Minimal sensory loss (toes only)
  • Arterial Doppler often inaudible at distal vessel, but venous Doppler remains audible (some flow preserved)

This category indicates the limb is salvageable with prompt intervention, but not immediately threatened like IIb.

Key distinctions:

  • Category I (Viable): no sensory/motor deficit; both arterial and venous Doppler audible
  • Category IIa (Marginally threatened): minimal sensory deficit (toes), no motor deficit
  • Category IIb (Immediately threatened): more than toe sensory loss + motor weakness → needs urgent revascularization
  • Category III (Irreversible): profound anesthesia + paralysis; limb non-salvageable

Therefore, this limb is Marginally threatened — Rutherford IIa (Option B).

questions.raw_text: A 62-year-old diabetic patient has an ABI of 1.4. Which of the following is the best next investigation to assess peripheral arterial disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Toe-brachial index (TBI)

ABI is calculated as: ABI = Ankle systolic pressure / Brachial systolic pressure

Normally:

  • 0.9–1.3 = normal
  • <0.9 = PAD
  • >1.3 = non-compressible artery

In diabetes (and elderly/CKD), arteries of the leg often become stiff and calcified, so when the cuff inflates it cannot compress the artery properly. This causes:

  • Falsely high ankle systolic pressure
  • Falsely high ABI (e.g., 1.4)

So the ABI becomes invalid for assessing PAD severity.

Best next investigation: Toe-brachial index (TBI) because:

  • Toe arteries are smaller and are much less affected by medial calcification
  • Hence, toe pressure measurements remain compressible and reliable
  • Therefore, TBI is the preferred test when ABI is >1.3

Interpretation (useful exam values):

  • TBI > 0.7: normal
  • TBI 0.4–0.7: PAD
  • TBI < 0.4: severe ischemia

Consider the following:

II. Hypertension
III. Renal failure
IV. Jaundice

Which of the above are the risk factors for post-operative wound dehiscence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Wound dehiscence (burst abdomen) is the partial or complete separation of a postoperative wound due to failure of fascial healing. It usually occurs between the 5th and 8th postoperative day, when wound tensile strength is at its lowest.

Several systemic factors impair collagen synthesis, wound healing, and immune function, thereby increasing the risk of wound dehiscence. The following are important risk factors:

  • I. Diabetes: Causes impaired leukocyte function, poor collagen synthesis, microvascular disease, and delayed wound healing.
  • III. Renal failure: Uremia, anemia, malnutrition, and impaired immune function delay wound healing and increase wound complications.
  • IV. Jaundice: Associated with impaired collagen formation, malnutrition, immune dysfunction, and increased susceptibility to infection, all of which predispose to wound dehiscence.

Why is II incorrect?

  • II. Hypertension: Hypertension alone is not considered a major independent risk factor for wound dehiscence, although it may contribute indirectly in some patients.

Pilonidal sinus is a chronic inflammatory condition of the natal cleft, usually caused by hair penetration into the skin, leading to chronic sinus formation. The goal of surgery is complete excision of the sinus with off-midline closure, as midline wounds have higher rates of infection, delayed healing, and recurrence.

The following techniques are commonly used to achieve off-midline closure after excision of a pilonidal sinus:

  • I. Limberg procedure: A rhomboid transposition flap that flattens the natal cleft and shifts the suture line away from the midline. It has low recurrence rates.
  • III. Z-plasty: A local flap technique that changes the direction of the scar and moves the wound away from the midline while reducing tension.
  • IV. Karydakis procedure: An asymmetric advancement flap that lateralizes the incision and flattens the natal cleft. It is associated with excellent healing and low recurrence.

  • II. Y-V plasty: Although Y-V advancement flaps are useful in reconstructive surgery, they are not commonly used as standard procedures for pilonidal sinus closure.

Premalignant Conditions of the Stomach:

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Small bowel stricture

Wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) is a noninvasive technique used to visualize the small intestine, particularly areas that are difficult to assess with conventional upper GI endoscopy or colonoscopy. The patient swallows a small camera-containing capsule that transmits images as it passes through the gastrointestinal tract.

The major contraindication to capsule endoscopy is a known or suspected small bowel stricture, obstruction, or fistula, because the capsule may become impacted, leading to capsule retention and possible intestinal obstruction.

Common Indications for Capsule Endoscopy

  • Obscure gastrointestinal bleeding after negative upper and lower endoscopy
  • Iron deficiency anemia of unknown source
  • Suspected or known small bowel Crohn disease
  • Small bowel tumors
  • Celiac disease (selected cases with suspected complications or refractory disease)
  • Positive fecal occult blood test with negative conventional evaluation

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

  • A. Coeliac disease
    • An indication in selected patients, especially when complications are suspected.
  • C. Obscure gastrointestinal bleeding
    • One of the most common and important indications for capsule endoscopy.
  • D. FOBT positive but CT negative
    • Capsule endoscopy may be useful to evaluate an occult small bowel source of bleeding.

questions.text: LIFT procedure in fistula ​surgery stands for:
questions.raw_text: LIFT procedure in fistula surgery stands for:
questions.correct_answer: C. Ligation of intersphincteric fistula tract
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ligation of intersphincteric fistula tract

LIFT (Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract) is a sphincter-preserving procedure used for the treatment of fistula-in-ano.

Principle

  • The fistulous tract is identified in the intersphincteric plane.
  • The tract is ligated close to the internal opening.
  • The tract is divided, thereby disconnecting the internal opening from the external tract.
  • This eradicates the fistula while preserving the anal sphincters.

Advantages

  • Preserves continence (minimal risk of fecal incontinence).
  • Suitable for complex transsphincteric fistulas.
  • Less sphincter damage compared with fistulotomy.
  • Good healing rates with low morbidity.

High-Yield MCQ Points

  • LIFT = Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract.
  • Indicated mainly for transsphincteric fistula-in-ano.
  • A sphincter-saving procedure.
  • Preferred when preservation of continence is important.

questions.raw_text:
A patient diagnosed with acute appendicitis was brought to the hospital within 24 hours of symptom onset. Which of the following statements is/are true regarding this condition?

1.	McBurney's point tenderness is a reliable clinical sign
2.	Ultrasound (USG) is the preferred investigation in pregnant women and children
3.	Ochsner-Sherren regimen is preferred for appendicular mass
4.	Interval appendectomy is mandatory after conservative management
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

1) Acute Appendicitis
Typical progression:
Visceral pain phase

  • Pain begins around the umbilicus
  • Because visceral afferents from the appendix enter T10 spinal segment

Parietal peritoneal irritation

  • Inflammation reaches parietal peritoneum
  • Pain localizes to right lower quadrant

This is where McBurney’s point tenderness appears.

  • Junction of lateral 1/3 and medial 2/3 of the line between: Umbilicus-Right anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)

2) Ultrasound is preferred in pregnant women and children ✔️

  • Ultrasound has no radiation
  • Safe for pregnancy and pediatrics

It can detect:

  • Inflamed appendix
  • Appendix diameter > 6 mm
  • Peri-appendiceal fluid

3) Ochsner-Sherren regimen is preferred for appendicular mass ✔️
An appendicular mass forms when the body tries to contain infection by surrounding the inflamed appendix with: Omentum and Bowel loops
Instead of immediate surgery, conservative treatment is given.
This is called Ochsner–Sherren regimen, which includes:

  • Nil by mouth
  • IV fluids
  • Antibiotics
  • Observation

Surgery is avoided initially because operating on a mass can injure surrounding bowel.

4) Interval appendectomy is mandatory-This is false.
Earlier practice:

  • After conservative treatment, surgery was done 6–8 weeks later (interval appendectomy).

Current practice:

  • Not mandatory anymore
  • Done only if symptoms recur.

Many patients remain completely asymptomatic.

• risk of bowel leak
• bleeding
• postoperative adhesions/obstruction

• narrow neck (higher obstruction/diverticulitis risk)
• induration/thickening or palpable ectopic tissue
• fibrous bands
• inflammation/ulceration
• bleeding or symptoms

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T3 N1c M0

In colon cancer staging, two findings are crucial: depth of invasion (T stage) and presence of nodal disease or tumor deposits (N stage).
• A tumor that invades through muscularis propria into subserosa/pericolic tissue is staged as T3 (it has not penetrated the serosal surface, which would make it T4a).
• Tumor deposits are discrete cancer nodules in the mesocolic/mesenteric fat that lack identifiable lymph node tissue. Importantly, when tumor deposits are present but no regional lymph nodes are involved, the nodal stage is classified as N1c (even if all lymph nodes are negative).
• Absence of distant spread corresponds to M0.
Therefore, adenocarcinoma invading subserosa with mesenteric tumor deposits, no lymph node involvement, and no metastasis = T3 N1c M0.

However, his bowel movements abruptly stopped yesterday, and the diffuse abdominal discomfort and distension worsened. The abdomen is distended, tympanic, and mildly tender to palpation with no guarding or rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds are decreased. Abdominal CT scan shows diffuse colonic dilation with nondilated small bowels. Which of the following most likely contributed to this patient's current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Electrolyte abnormality

This patient’s presentation is classic for acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome), characterized by massive colonic dilation without a mechanical obstruction.

Ogilvie syndrome occurs due to autonomic dysfunction of colonic motility (↓ parasympathetic / ↑ sympathetic tone), leading to impaired colonic peristalsis and progressive dilation.

A major precipitating factor is electrolyte abnormalities, especially after diarrheal illness:

  • Hypokalemia
  • Hypomagnesemia
  • Hypocalcemia

These electrolytes are essential for normal smooth muscle contraction and intestinal motility, so their depletion can trigger colonic pseudo-obstruction.

Why other options are incorrect
A. Adhesions → usually cause small bowel obstruction, not isolated colon dilation.
B. Colonic hypoperfusion → causes ischemic colitis (bloody diarrhea, pain).
C. Colonic mass → causes true mechanical large bowel obstruction with a transition point, not diffuse dilation without small bowel dilation.

The choice of surgery for rectal adenocarcinoma depends primarily on the distance from the anal verge and whether the anal sphincter complex can be preserved while achieving an adequate distal margin and oncologic clearance.

A tumor located very low in the rectum (2 cm from the anal verge) and extending to involve the anal sphincters is not amenable to sphincter-sparing surgery. In such cases, the appropriate curative operation is Abdominoperineal resection (APR)

This involves en bloc removal of: rectum, anal canal, sphincter complex followed by a permanent end colostomy.

Why other options are not appropriate:

A. Total mesorectal excision (TME) is a technique (part of oncologic rectal surgery) but does not specify the required operation when sphincters are involved; APR includes TME.
B. Low anterior resection (LAR) is used for upper/mid rectal tumors where sphincters can be preserved.
D. Hartmann’s procedure is typically for obstructed/perforated cases or high-risk patients; it is not the standard definitive surgery for a very low sphincter-involving tumor.

Correct answer: B. CT angiography of abdominal vessels

Progressive post-prandial abdominal pain (intestinal angina) beginning 20–30 minutes after meals, lasting 1–2 hours, associated with food fear and significant weight loss in an older patient with major atherosclerotic risk factors (smoking, diabetes, hypertension) is classic for chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) due to atherosclerotic stenosis/occlusion of mesenteric arteries (most commonly SMA ± celiac). A faint epigastric bruit further supports vascular disease. Because endoscopy and routine labs are often normal in CMI, diagnosis requires vascular imaging.

The most appropriate confirmatory investigation is CT angiography (CTA) of abdominal vessels, as it provides rapid, high-resolution visualization of the celiac, SMA, and IMA, identifies the site and severity of stenosis, evaluates collateral flow, and simultaneously aids planning for revascularization (endovascular stenting or bypass). Duplex mesenteric Doppler can be used as a screening test but is operator dependent and limited in obese/bowel gas; CTA is the preferred confirmatory test in most patients.

Biopsy reveals intestinal-type epithelium with goblet cells. Which of the following classification is used to know the extent of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prague criteria

Barrett esophagus is a complication of chronic GERD in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia). Endoscopically it appears as salmon-colored mucosa extending proximally above the gastroesophageal junction. To describe the extent of Barrett’s esophagus, the standard system used is the Prague C & M classification, which reports:

  • C (Circumferential extent): length of continuous circumferential Barrett mucosa
  • M (Maximal extent): maximum length of Barrett mucosa including tongues

This classification provides a reproducible way to document disease length, guide surveillance, and assess risk of progression to dysplasia and esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Other Options:

A. Milan criteria:

  • Used in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
  • Determines eligibility for liver transplantation (single tumor ≤5 cm or ≤3 tumors each ≤3 cm).
  • Not related to esophageal disease.

B. Tokyo criteria:

  • Used in acute cholangitis and cholecystitis.
  • Helps in diagnosis and severity grading (Tokyo Guidelines).
  • No role in Barrett esophagus or dysphagia evaluation.

C. Chicago criteria:

  • Used in esophageal motility disorders based on high-resolution manometry.
  • Classifies disorders like achalasia, distal esophageal spasm, EGJ outflow obstruction.
  • Applies to motility disorders, not mucosal metaplasia like Barrett.

The gallbladder may have several congenital anomalies involving its shape, position, number, and development. Most are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally during imaging or surgery, but some predispose to torsion, gallstone formation, or surgical complications.

The following are recognized congenital anomalies of the gallbladder:

  • I. Phrygian cap: The most common congenital anomaly of the gallbladder. It is a folding of the fundus over the body, resembling the cap worn by ancient Phrygians. It is usually clinically insignificant.

| ---- | ---------- |
| Primary | Formed de novo within the bile duct itself |
| Secondary | Migrated from the gallbladder into the CBD |
| Retained | Missed at the time of cholecystectomy (found within 2 years of surgery) |
| Recurrent | Found after 2 years of a previous stone-clear CBD |

The key detail is the 4-year gap after cholecystectomy:

  • The gallbladder has been removed → stone cannot have migrated from GB → rules out Secondary
  • Discovered 4 years post-op → beyond the 2-year window → rules out Retained
  • Stone formed de novo in the CBD after cholecystectomy = Primary stone

Characteristics of Primary CBD Stones

  • Typically brown pigment stones (vs. cholesterol in secondary)
  • Associated with bile stasis, infection (E. coli, biliary stricture)
  • Often soft, earthy, and friable
  • Seen with biliary stricture, periampullary diverticulum, or biliary dyskinesia
  • E. coli produces β-glucuronidase → deconjugates bilirubin → pigment stone formation

• Treatment: Endoscopic sphincterotomy or medical therapy (e.g., nitrates, CCBs).

options.text: Milan criteria is applicab​le for single tumor up to​ 5 cm or three tumors eac​h less than 3 cm

questions.correct_answer: B. A FLR (future liver remnant) of at least 40% normal liver is a pre-requisite for resection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A FLR (future liver remnant) of at least 40% normal liver is a pre-requisite for resection

Management of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC/hepatoma) depends on tumor burden, liver function, and the feasibility of curative therapy (resection, transplantation, ablation). Key concepts:

  • Milan criteria define eligibility for liver transplantation in HCC: single tumor ≤5 cm OR up to 3 tumors each ≤3 cm, with no vascular invasion or metastasis.
  • Percutaneous ablation (RFA/MWA) is a curative option for small HCC (typically ≤3 cm, selected up to 5 cm).
  • Liver metastasis from colorectal cancer is often resectable, and metastasectomy can be curative in selected patients.

Future Liver Remnant (FLR) requirement

The amount of liver that must remain after resection depends on baseline liver quality:

  • Normal liver: FLR ≥ 20–25%
  • Steatosis/chemotherapy-injured liver: FLR ≥ 30%
  • Cirrhotic liver: FLR ≥ 40%

Thus, saying FLR must be at least 40% in normal liver is incorrect (40% is required for cirrhosis, not normal liver).

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Portal vein occlusion

TIPS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt) is an interventional radiology procedure that creates a low-resistance channel between the portal vein and a hepatic vein, thereby reducing portal hypertension. It is used in patients with portal hypertensive complications such as:

  • Refractory variceal bleeding not controlled with endoscopic + medical therapy
  • Refractory/intractable ascites (important indication)

For TIPS to be performed, there must be patent portal venous inflow so that blood can be shunted into systemic circulation. Therefore, Portal vein occlusion is a major contraindication (often absolute/technical), because the shunt cannot function if the portal vein cannot be accessed or has no flow.

questions.text: A 58-year-old female has B​ismuth Type IIIa Klatskin​ tumor. What is the prefe​rred surgical procedure?
questions.raw_text: A 58-year-old female has Bismuth Type IIIa Klatskin tumor. What is the preferred surgical procedure?
questions.correct_answer: B. Right hepatectomy + caudate lobe resection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right hepatectomy + caudate lobe resection

Klatskin tumor refers to perihilar cholangiocarcinoma arising at the hepatic duct confluence. Surgical planning is guided by the Bismuth–Corlette classification, which describes the longitudinal extent of biliary duct involvement and determines which hepatic resection is needed for an R0 (margin-negative) resection.

In Bismuth Type IIIa, the tumor involves:

  • the common hepatic duct and confluence, and
  • extends into the right hepatic duct (right secondary biliary radicals), while the left duct is relatively spared.

Therefore, the preferred curative operation is Right hepatectomy + caudate lobe resection with en bloc bile duct excision and biliary reconstruction.

The caudate lobe (segment I) drains directly into the hilar bile ducts and is frequently involved early in perihilar cholangiocarcinoma; removing it improves chances of complete clearance.

Other options are incorrect because:

  • Left hepatectomy is preferred for Type IIIb (left duct involvement).
  • Whipple’s procedure is for distal bile duct/pancreatic head tumors, not perihilar tumors.
  • Simple bile duct excision has high positive-margin rates and is inadequate for Type III lesions.

Thus, Type IIIa Klatskin tumor → Right hepatectomy + caudate lobe resection (Option B).

questions.text: During surgery for a hydat​id cyst of the liver, the​ surgeon removes the endo​cyst and drains the cyst ​cavity. To prevent residu‍al cavity complications, ‍he performs spiral suturi‌ng of the hydatid cavity ‍walls. This surgical step​ is known as:
questions.raw_text: During surgery for a hydatid cyst of the liver, the surgeon removes the endocyst and drains the cyst cavity. To prevent residual cavity complications, he performs spiral suturing of the hydatid cavity walls. This surgical step is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Capitonnage

In hepatic hydatid disease (Echinococcus granulosus), after endocystectomy (removal of the germinal membrane/endocyst) and evacuation of cyst contents, a large residual pericyst cavity may remain. This cavity can lead to postoperative complications such as infection, bile leakage, prolonged drainage, hemorrhage, and residual cavity abscess. To prevent these residual cavity problems, surgeons may obliterate the cavity by in-folding and suturing the cavity walls in a spiral/continuous manner, thereby collapsing the space and eliminating dead space. This technique is called capitonnage.

Key differentiations:

  • Marsupialization: exteriorization of cyst cavity by suturing it to the skin/open wound for continuous drainage.
  • PAIR: percutaneous aspiration–injection–reaspiration (image-guided minimally invasive technique).
  • Cystojejunostomy: internal drainage procedure connecting cavity to jejunum (rarely used; for selected complicated cysts).

Thus, spiral suturing of the hydatid cavity walls to obliterate the residual cavity = Capitonnage.
